en: Preface to the Profound Meaning of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra:

Now, the core meaning of the sūtras is not easily pointed out. Only the Great Master Zhizhe, having awakened to the *āvartanī-dhāraṇī* and begun by following the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, fully expounded the ten profundities (*daśa-miāo*).
Consequently, every aspect of the net of the teachings was made brilliantly clear and detailed; thus it is called "profound" (*xuan*).

The Commentary states: "Nevertheless, the entire body of the *Mohe zhiguan* (Great Calming and Contemplation) embodies the ten subtleties (*shimiao*) of the *Lotus Sūtra*. Thus we know that although the teachings and contemplations are distinct volumes, their underlying principle follows but a single track.

Indeed, the World-Honored One, the Great Awakened One, further revealed the *dhāraṇī* at the summit of the Buddha’s head; the objective realm and contemplation therein are in profound accord. However—"

This scripture was later introduced to China, yet it had not yet been formally categorized or explained. At that time, as its flavors were both partial and perfect, people did not know which way to turn.
My late teacher, Master Baishong, once composed the "Hundred Questions" (*Baimen*) to initiate the gradual approach to the profound mystery;

he ultimately lamented that those who could listen to the celestial music of Mount Dongting were but few. My elder brother, Master Deng, disregarding worldly opposition, composed the *Lengyan jing xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra) in four fascicles.

Does this scroll perhaps assist the intent of those who, through the *dhāraṇī*, vow to behold [the Buddha] day and night? Or does it ultimately fulfill the intent of our late master to exhaustively investigate and resolve deep-seated doubts?
Together with my brother Dēng and I, the Unwise One, we practiced the *samādhi* repentance method; by means of this scroll, we attained entry into the stage of the stream (*srotāpanna*).

Therefore, regarding the three contemplations, the ten stages of the vehicle, and the principles of teaching, practice, and realization within the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning), there is nothing that has not been thoroughly investigated and clearly elucidated herein.
Thereupon, Lingshan and Dasu nodded their heads in mutual agreement. My own humble words at the beginning of this composition are perhaps like the saying:

"Even a thatched cottage is not excluded from the school of learning. Yet, at that time, those of the same class as the many-heard (bahuśruta) were already ignorant of the One Truth and had cast aside the myriad practices;

they dismissed the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) as mere worldly wisdom and took the encounter with Dhanagarga as a realm of pleasure. Thus, whenever they encountered the teachings or contemplation, they harbored much doubt.
Frowning with distress, the Tathāgata called them those who are to be pitied. Thus, though one cannot help but repeatedly hearken to the sacred teachings of the Sage, what can I alone do?
Written by the śramaṇa Chuánrú in the spring of the Dīngyǒu year of the Wànlì era, at Jiūsā Chànshì in Xīxī.
The Profound Meaning of the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Śūraṅgama Sūtra, Volume One, with Preface.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Chuandeng of Youxi on Mount Tiantai.
As for the Dharma of the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Śūraṅgama: coming and going are one; arising and ceasing are eternally as they are. Its nature...

The seven elements are vast and mutually pervasive; the three categories are subtle and equally entered. Regarding true emptiness and true form, the four views of "conditioned" and "natural" are perfectly transcended.
As for the nature of form and the nature of emptiness, the two extremes of conventional existence and ultimate non-existence are utterly severed.
Like a precious mirror, like a mani jewel, the multitude of images of the Three Truths return to it, and the profusion of treasures of the ten realms rains down upon it. It serves as...
It is the numinous treasury of all wonders and the profound foundation of myriad virtues. Vast and expansive, it cannot be named, yet is forcibly called the *tathāgatagarbha*;
rare and serene, it cannot be designated, yet is metaphorically termed the "ever-abiding mind. Alas, the nature of sentient beings is inverted;
they are obscured from this single principle of interpenetration, becoming confined by their own divergent cognitions and views. Some paint over the void...
There are divisions and confusions regarding the gateway of cultivation; some disparage the extremes while esteeming the middle, or they become entangled in the kalpas of the *Saṃghāṭa*.
Among ordinary beings, they calculate the internal and the external; among non-Buddhists, they cling to annihilationism or eternalism.

In all such cases, they mistake true knowledge for false knowledge—like one who is lost and pursues the reflection of their own head—and mistake false views for true views, as if discarding [the real].
To mistake a bubble for the ocean—the Tathāgata calls such a person pitiable. This is precisely what is taught in this *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra* of the Great Buddha-Crown.
This scripture proclaims only the ultimate truth and is intended solely for those of perfect capacity;

it discerns the eternal mind amidst birth and death, points to the rushing current as still water, and realizes the nature of the storehouse within form and emptiness—like applying ointment to a sore on the forehead.
It serves as the crest-jewel. It recompenses the Bodhi of all Buddhas and realizes that the aggregates, sense bases, and elements are fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha;

its essence is the Divine. It interrogates the Sahā world’s fundamental root of perfect penetration—the dharmas of arising and ceasing within the faculties, objects, consciousness, and wisdom—and causes them to vanish, so that all are stilled in quiescence.
To state the essentials: hearing, contemplation, and cultivation are all wondrous; precept, concentration, and wisdom are all perfected. Right...

Accompanied by its auxiliaries, it gallops forward; manifest and hidden, it moves in tandem. Traversing the stages from cause through fruit, from beginning to end, the gentle breeze propels the boat upon the rushing river.
It crushes the Māra of birth-and-death, views, and craving; its fierce flames melt the snow upon the atoms of space.
Truly, this is what is called the authentic exposition of the *vaipulya* and the true nature (*dharmatā*), the precursor to the Great Matter (*mahākārya*). Sound...
I have heard that in the past the teaching was spread until the present; in the final five hundred years, it will be as one under the single sun of the Buddha.
At that time, just as there was Ānanda of wondrous realization at the Jetavana Monastery, how could this land of Mahācīna lack men of superior roots and capacity?

It is only because the phrasing of the scriptures is fluid and the intent of the Buddha’s meaning is profound that those who understand merely weave a net while keeping the main cord secret; thus, students...

This is like casting away the main net and throwing oneself into a fine-meshed snare. Thus, there are those who spend their entire lives studying the garden of teachings (*śikṣā-vana*), investigating the subtle nuances (*ji*), yet fail to achieve integration.
How much less could one who spends a lifetime searching for hidden mysteries at the gate of meditation (*dhyāna*) attain liberation?

(Lamp) Having had the honor of beholding the secret edicts and having studied them for many years, it was as if entering the ocean to count its sands—merely becoming dazed and exhausting oneself in vain. Thereupon, he closed [the volume].
Set aside contemplation of meaning and set down the analytical study of the sutras; only by concurrently reading the Tiantai school will there be further ground for understanding.

Not only does this lead to the realization that the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* constitutes the essential framework of the *Lotus Sūtra*, but it also reveals how Zhizhe’s insights accord with the original intent of the Tathāgata.

When discussing the *tathāgatagarbha*, his words perfectly coincide with the doctrine of the inherent nature (*xingju*). When expounding on *śamatha-vipaśyanā*, they implicitly harmonize with the principles of the Great Samādhi. This extends even to... [suspended]
He adjudicated the stages of realization and warded off the demons of the dark realm; there was no name or expression that he did not fully penetrate and accord with. Alas!

Although the compassionate rain from Yuquan Temple poured forth tens of millions of words, no one could verify them. That the Buddha remained at Longxi for over a dozen years was surely for this very reason.
Now, I have taken up this ocean of meaning to reverently comment upon this king of sutras. To seal the Buddha-mind with the Buddha-mind—is this not like adding oil to nourish the light?

Thus, explaining the *Śūraṅgama* by means of the *Śūraṅgama*, who could say that this is like diluting milk with water? I have briefly drafted these discursive remarks to examine the text and establish its principles.
My learning is ashamed of its rusticity and my phrasing is apologetic for its lack of elegance; my words may be loose and fragmented, yet I hope the meaning may occasionally hit the mark.

I have compiled this into four fascicles and submitted it for the consideration of my fellow students. It is not intended to seek a shortcut through the Dragon Gate; rather, I merely wish to attach my humble dust to the hooves of the noble steed.

Regarding the exegesis of this sutra, there are five profound themes: first, the explanation of the title; second, the discernment of its essence; third, the clarification of its core principle; fourth, the discussion of its function.
The fifth section concerns the characteristics of the five teachings. This chapter is divided into two major parts: first, a general explanation; second, a detailed explanation.
The general explanation further consists of two sub-sections: first, the sequential arising; second, the differentiation. Regarding the sequential arising, the *Guangming xuanyi* states:

"In this Sahā world-realm, the Buddha’s work is carried out through sound. One may hear the names [of the teachings] from a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), or one may hear them from within the scriptures."
It is called "name. Therefore, name is placed first. Because one hears the name, one next cognizes the essence of the dharma. Once the essence is revealed, there follows practice;
practice is precisely the thesis (*siddhānta*). When the thesis is established, it possesses power; power is precisely function (*prayojana*). Function is able to benefit sentient beings.

Because it benefits sentient beings, one teaches others. Hearing the name is the beginning of self-cultivation; bestowing the teaching is the end of transforming others. Only those who have both a beginning and an end [are truly complete].
O Sage! The sequence of the arising of these five chapters is as follows. Next, regarding the differentiation: "differentiation" (jian) means to examine and analyze.
Question: If abbreviated, there is only one; if expanded, they are immeasurable. Now, these five chapters are neither expansive nor abbreviated.
For what reason are there five? Answer: They are neither abbreviated nor expansive. Because they are not abbreviated, they are not one; because they are not expansive, they are not... [immeasurable].
If too extensive, it causes the intellect to retreat; if too concise, the meaning is not comprehensive. I shall now speak with moderation, so that the meaning may be easily understood.

Within the five chapters, the meaning is thus: the first chapter takes the three dharmas collectively as its title; the next three chapters divide the three dharmas into their particulars; and the final chapter clarifies both the collective and the particular. "Distinct" (*bie*) means differentiation.

The preceding chapter provides a general designation for the three dharmas together; the subsequent three chapters branch out the three dharmas to establish distinctions; and the last chapter elucidates them by combining both the general and the particular.

This is the classification of the teachings (*śāsanavyavasthāna*). Furthermore, the first chapter, "Revealing the Essence," clarifies principle (*li*), while the remaining four chapters clarify phenomena (*shi*).

Moreover, the first three chapters constitute the cause (*hetu*), and the latter two chapters constitute the fruit (*phala*). Additionally, the first four chapters constitute practice (*pratipatti*), and the final chapter constitutes the teaching (*deśanā*).

Furthermore, the first four chapters constitute practice for one's own benefit (*svārthacaryā*), and the final chapter constitutes practice for the benefit of others (*parārthacaryā*). Finally, the first four chapters represent the "sage’s silence" (*āryatūṣṇīmbhāva*).

The final chapter is the Holy One’s exposition of the Dharma. Such various distinctions and analyses (and so forth). Second, regarding the separate explanation, this refers to the separate explanation of the five chapters.
First, the explanation of the chapter on the title is divided into two parts: first, a detailed determination of the scripture’s title;
second, the explanation of the scripture’s title. Regarding the first, the detailed determination: according to the scripture, it is as the Tathāgata answers Mañjuśrī’s question concerning its name.
There are five titles: first, "The Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa-Sitātapatra Unsurpassed Jewel Seal, the Pure Ocean-Eye of the Tathāgatas of the Ten Directions";

second, "The Savior and Protector of Kinsmen, Delivering Ānanda and the Bhikṣuṇī of this Assembly by Nature, Causing Them to Attain the Bodhicitta and Enter the Ocean of Universal Knowledge"; third, "The Secret Cause of the Tathāgata’s Cultivation and Realization."
The definitive meaning [of this scripture] is as follows: first, it is called the *Mahāvaipulya-saddharmapuṇḍarīka-rāja-daśadig-buddha-mātṛkā-dhāraṇī-mantra*;
second, it is called the *Abhiṣeka-pada-sarvabodhisattva-sahasracaryā-śūraṅgama*. In the present translation, the translator has retained three titles while concealing two;
this is what is meant by "the concise encompassing the extensive. Indeed, the Tathāgata’s intention in establishing these names must necessarily correspond to the specific context.
It is explained and established as follows: the essential purport of this scripture does not exceed its essence, doctrine, power, and function. Now, among these five names, the first states:
"The Great Buddha-Crown *Siddhārthabhadra* Unsurpassed Jewel Seal, the Pure Ocean-Eye of the Tathāgatas of the Ten Directions."
These two [titles] are established based on the essence, the virtues, and the function [of the teaching]. It is also named "Saving and Protecting the Kinsmen and Causes;
Delivering Ānanda and the Bhikṣuṇī of this Assembly so that She Attains Bodhicitta and Enters the Ocean of Universal Knowledge.

This is established based solely on its merit. It is also named "The Definitive Meaning of the Secret Cause and Cultivation-Realization of the Tathāgata. This is established based solely on its central doctrine.

These names are established based on the essential qualities of its substance and its fundamental doctrine. It is also called the *Mahāvaipulya-saddharma-puṇḍarīka-rāja-daśadig-buddha-mātṛkā-dhāraṇī-mantra*;
these two titles are established based on both its substantial qualities and its fundamental doctrine.
It is also called the *Abhiṣeka-pada-sarva-bodhisattva-sarva-caryā-śūraṅgama*; this title is established solely based on its fundamental doctrine. Now, as for that "fundamental doctrine":
The Sūtra is the sovereign; the essential nature and virtues are that to which the core tenets converge;

and merit is that which arises from the convergence of the core tenets upon that essential nature. Since merit arises spontaneously, even if it proceeds slowly and is not actively promoted, it does not constitute a fault.

One must realize that the essence and the virtues are fundamental pillars that cannot be neglected in isolation. Therefore, I have now extracted the essentials of these virtues and designated them as "The Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa" (Dàfódǐng).
Although it consists of only three characters, it is already capable of encompassing all virtues. Why is this?

For "The Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa" is an alternative designation for the secret treasury of the Three Virtues (*triguṇa*). Thus, "Great" (*mahā*) is named according to the very nature of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
The Buddha takes the universal protection of *prajñā* as his essential meaning; the "Crown" (*uṣṇīṣa*) is designated by virtue of liberation and freedom from defilement.
This is the Great White Parasol of *Sītātapatrā*. This Great Buddha-Crown definitively establishes all phenomena and is free from all demonic activities;
it is the supreme jewel-seal of the single true reality (*ekalakṣaṇa*). This Great Buddha-Crown is vast, expansive, and perfectly complete. Its ritual procedure...
It upholds all dharmas; dwelling amidst defilement without being stained, it is sovereign and honored as the Great Vaipulya Wondrous Lotus King.
This Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa obstructs all evils and sustains all virtues, giving birth to the Buddhas of the ten directions;
it is the Dhāraṇī that is the Mother of the Buddhas of the ten directions. As for the consecration verses (*abhiṣeka-pada*), they originate from the source where this sūtra flows forth.
Even when speaking according to the esoteric terminology, it does not go beyond the two characters "miji" (esoteric cause).

This is because "mi" (esoteric) encompasses both the sense of being subtle and profound (*sūkṣma-guhya*) and the sense of being secret (*rahasya*). This is likely due to the skillful mastery of the translators and their methodical approach to condensation.

Within these mere nineteen characters, they have briefly set forth the essential qualities of its substance while fully capturing the core tenets; thus, they have mastered the designations of five names to invoke this single sūtra.

This is the ultimate purport [of this scripture]. Therefore, it is titled *The Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa, the Tathāgata’s Secret Cause for Cultivation and Realization, the Definitive Meaning of the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas, the Śūraṅgama*.

Second, the explanation of the title of the scripture is divided into two parts: first, a combined explanation of the general and specific titles; second, separate explanations of the general and specific titles.
Regarding the first point, the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning) of the *Fahua Wenju* states: "Now, teachings have both general and specific aspects. Based on the teachings, one clarifies practice."

Practice has both general and specific aspects; through practice, one manifests the principle. The principle also has both general and specific aspects. For now, setting aside practice and the principle, let us clarify the general and specific aspects of the teaching alone.
Now, the principle is devoid of names and words, yet names and words manifest the principle. It is like empty space, which has no measurements, yet measurements are applied to empty space.
As the *Tianwang Prajñā* states: "Dhāraṇī is without letters, yet letters manifest dhāraṇī. If we follow this capacity...
The term "text" (*vyañjana*) refers to that which manifests [meaning] and is thus general; however, when considered from the perspective of what it manifests, this term becomes specific.
What is meant by "general"? As the Noble One has taught: a single sūtra, a single time, a single location, a single section, a single verse, a single line, or a single word—all these are "texts.
From these texts, they are generally designated as "sūtras. What is meant by "specific"? Specifically, there are...

Fourth: First, it prevents the confusion of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and brings joy that delights the ear. Second, it accords with what is appropriate for conversion, intermittently awakening latent roots of goodness (*kuśala-mūla*).

Third, it confronts karmic obstructions so that evil is extinguished and transgressions are removed. Fourth, it points out the underlying principles so that one attains sudden and wondrous realization.
Because the reasons for these joys, accommodations, confrontations, and awakenings differ respectively, they are termed "distinct. This is like the blending of salt and plum.
Various flavors are synthesized; patterns are woven crosswise and lengthwise to form diverse embroideries.

Because they arise from distinct causes, there are nineteen characters—such as "Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa"—which mark how this teaching differs from all other teachings. This is according to the common terminology.

Therefore, the single character "jing" (sūtra) serves as the general designation for all scriptures. In this case, the general and specific titles are presented together; thus it says, "The Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa... (and so forth).
Next, the general and specific titles are explained separately in two parts: first, the explanation of the specific title; second, the explanation of the general title.

The explanation of the specific title is further divided into two: first, determining the name; second, providing the interpretation. Regarding the determination of the name, our school’s method of explaining the specific names and characteristics of various sūtras is most [thorough].
In general, when establishing titles based on essential points, they do not exceed three types: namely, those based on persons (*pudgala*), dharmas, or similes.
Within these three, there are further seven distinct categories consisting of three single [types], three compound [types], and one complete [type].

Now, among these seven titles, this sutra is determined to be titled according to the "person-dharma" category within the compound types. Within the person-dharma category, each has its own cause and effect. The Great Buddha...

The *uṣṇīṣa* is the dharma of the fruit; the Tathāgata is the person of the fruit. The secret cause is the causal dharma of the myriad practices; the various bodhisattvas are the persons of the cause.
When one cultivates and realizes the definitive meaning of the *Śūraṅgama*, it encompasses both cause and fruit. This sutra combines the cause, the fruit, the person, and the dharma in its title;
therefore, it is called the *Mahābuddhoṣṇīṣa* (and so forth). Next, the explanation is divided into two parts. First, the explanation of "the Great Buddha-uṣṇīṣa" and so forth.
Sixteen characters. Next, the explanation of *Śūraṅgama*. First, regarding "The Secret Cause of the Tathāgata’s Cultivation and Realization of the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa":
Now, "secret" (*mi*) possesses both the sense of "subtle secret" (*weimi*) and "hidden secret" (*mibimi*). This present "secret cause" encompasses both meanings.
The first refers to the wondrous *śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna* requested by the interlocutor; to mention one is to include all three, and to speak of the three is likewise so.
First, it is called "wondrous" (miao). "Wondrous" is synonymous with "esoteric" (mi). Because this serves as the cause, it is termed the "esoteric cause" (miyin).

This one [practice] is a divine mantra proclaimed by the Tathāgata, a secret word of all Buddhas that no human can fathom; therefore, it is called "esoteric. It causes practitioners to uphold this and ascend to the fruit of sainthood;
therefore, it is called the "esoteric cause. Although the practices of the Exoteric and Esoteric differ, that upon which they rely...

This principle is identical to the *tathāgatagarbha*. Furthermore, it is only through the simultaneous cultivation of both the Exoteric and Esoteric teachings that one can realize the stage of fruition;
thus, a single name is used to designate two practices. Regarding what is called the "Secret Cause of the Tathāgata":
from the perspective of the Exoteric, this refers to the so-called *śamatha* and other methods by which the Tathāgatas of the ten directions attain *bodhi*. From the perspective of the Esoteric...
That which is called this *Śītātapatrā* is that by which the Tathāgatas of the ten directions have attained perfect enlightenment through its upholding.
That which is called the "Great Buddha-Crown Tathāgata" refers to the transformation Buddha who proclaimed this divine mantra.
He is a manifestation produced from the hundred-jeweled, fearless radiance emitted from the World-Honored One’s crown; therefore, he is called the "Great Buddha."
Regarding the Tathāgata "Maha" (Great): the Buddha refers to him as "Mahā," which in the language of India is *mahā*.

Ancient scholars have sometimes said it cannot be translated, because it contains the three meanings of great (*mahat*), much (*bahu*), and superior (*viśiṣṭa*). Therefore, the *Śāstra* states: "In the language of India, *mahā* means great, much, and superior."

Because the meaning of the word "da" (大) in this region does not encompass the full range of meanings [of the original term], it cannot be translated [in its entirety]. For now, in the title, we have translated it simply as "Da" (Great).
This is because the character "Da" in this region, though its literal form does not contain all the meanings, is in fact vast and comprehensive.

As Laozi said: "Within the realm there are four greatnesses, and the King occupies one of them. These are what are called the Greatness of the Dao, the Greatness of Heaven, the Greatness of Earth, and the Greatness of the King. However, the King...
This is merely a person. Yet the reason he is greater than Heaven and Earth is truly because he attains *zhonghe* (harmony and centrality) through the Way, thereby securing his preeminent position;
thus, Heaven and Earth find their proper stations and the myriad things are nourished. That he secures the station of Heaven and Earth by attaining *zhonghe* means he is as great as Heaven and Earth.
That the myriad things are equally nourished means he is great by virtue of his abundance. Furthermore, that he secures his preeminent position—this...
"Great" (mahat) signifies "superior. Furthermore, as worldly people refer to parents and elders as "great persons" (mahājana), this also takes superiority as the meaning of "great.
When śramaṇas refer to a large number [of people] as a "great assembly" (mahāsaṃgha), this takes plurality as the meaning of "great. Thus, the meaning of the word "great" in this region is manifold.
Although translating it with a single term does not lose its essential principle, we shall now first explain it according to the Sanskrit sound.

The term "Great Buddha" (*Mahābuddha*) is explained through both a combined and inclusive interpretation, followed by an interpretation based on the literal meaning of its constituent parts. First, regarding the combined and inclusive explanation:
the *Śāstra* states that *mahā* signifies great, much, and superior. "Great" refers to encompassing vastness; "much" refers to inclusion and subsumption;
and "superior" refers to excellence and eminence. Zhanran (Zhang’an) says: "The Dharma-body and the Dharma-realm pervading all places constitute the meaning of 'vastness. The Reward-body..."
The sense of "containing" (*saṃgraha*) is that the correspondence between the realm of wisdom and its manifestation is inexhaustible.

The sense of "surpassing" (*abhibhava*) is that the mastery of the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body) cannot be obstructed or cut off. Thus, the Dharma-body, the Reward-body, and the Response-body are all equally termed "Great Buddha.

Now, if one were to explain this "Great Buddha" of the *Saṃdhinirmocana* and the *Āgamas* solely by way of the excellence of the response-body, or solely by way of the multiplicity of the reward-body—
This explains the Great Buddha of the Separate Teaching (Bie-jiao). It is solely by way of the greatness of the Dharma-body that this Great Buddha of the Perfect Teaching (Yuan-jiao) is explained.
Since this sūtra being expounded is a perfect sūtra, the Teacher who expounds it must accordingly be a perfect Buddha.
Although he is a perfect Buddha, when observed according to his manifested traces, he belongs to the Response-body (Nirmāṇakāya). However, this Response-body has its origin; its...

What is the "fundamental" (hon)? It refers to the Dharma-body and the Reward-body (hō-hon). The response-body (ō-shin) manifested from this entirety of the Dharma and Reward bodies is such that the response-body itself is precisely the Dharma and Reward bodies.
Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "The pure and wondrous Dharma-body is serene, responding to all things. Tiantai says:
Mercury and pure gold can be used to paint various images; likewise, the merit and the Dharma-body manifest and appear everywhere.

Thus we know that there has never been a time when the Dharma-body and Reward-body did not manifest as response-bodies, nor has there ever been a response-body that was not identical to the Dharma-body and Reward-body.

It is only according to the capacities of sentient beings that their perceptions differ, resulting in variations of superior or inferior. Now, this sutra is suited to the specific needs of those present.
Thus, it is perceived through the consciousness of karma (*karmavijñāna*). Consequently, the Buddha manifests in accordance with the Middle Principle (*madhyama-naya*) by relying upon that Middle.

Is this not precisely the identity of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) and the Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*)? Therefore, a verse of praise in the Sūtra states: "Wondrously profound, all-holding, the Honored One of Immovability.

"Wondrously profound" praises the Absolute Truth (*paramārtha-satya*), which is the Reward-body. "All-holding" praises the Conventional Truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), which is the Response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*). "Immovable" praises the Middle.
The Way is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). This is because, through wondrous awakening according to the capacity of the occasion, one penetrates and perceives the source of the Dharma;

thus, it is expressed in words as praise that accords with the nature of reality. Here, the title serves as the general [heading], for how could the general not permeate the particular? Therefore, this "Great Buddha" must be explained by means of three meanings:

namely, the greatness of the Dharma (*dharmamahattva*), the greatness of the recompense (*vipākamahattva*), and the excellence of the response (*nirmāṇamahattva*). Regarding the greatness of the Dharma:
This refers to what is called "great grasping" (*mahā-upādāna*), which is vast and expansive. The meaning of "vastness" is that the *dharmakāya* and the *dharmadhātu* pervade all places.
The *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-sūtra* states: "Vairocana pervades all places. This sutra also says: "Emptiness arises within the Great Awakening, like a single bubble emerging from the ocean.
This is precisely the meaning of the vastness of the *dharmakāya*. Regarding "many rewards" (*vipāka-bahutva*), this refers to what is called "much grasping," which contains...

It is "comprehensive" (*saṃgraha*). The illumination and manifestation of the wisdom-realm of the *saṃbhogakāya* are correspondingly inexhaustible; this is the meaning of inclusion. As the Sūtra says:

thus, it is established as "contemplative penetration" (*guāndá*). When contrasted with "non-contemplative contemplation" (*bùguān guān*), although the terminology applies generally to both, their meanings are fundamentally distinct.

Regarding the former two types of contemplation, they are discussed in terms of penetrating through the dense obscurity of birth and death; regarding "contemplative penetration," it is discussed in terms of piercing through delusion and blindness.

This has been explained generally by clarifying contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) through the mutual dependence of wisdom (*jñāna*) and abandonment (*prahāṇa*). Now, it is explained specifically according to the principle of the Truths (*satya*):

ignorance (*avidyā*) is itself the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), and the dharma-nature is itself ignorance. Ignorance is neither contemplation nor non-contemplation, yet ignorance is called "non-contemplation.
The dharma-nature is likewise neither contemplation nor non-contemplation, yet the dharma-nature is called "contemplation. As the Sūtra says: "The dharma-nature is neither illumination..."

To call the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), which is dark, "light," and to call the ultimate emptiness (paramārtha-śūnyatā), which is neither wisdom nor folly, "wisdom"—this constitutes the clarification of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) through contrast with non-contemplation (*avipaśyanā*). Therefore, *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* each derive their names from three meanings.

(There is further text regarding the absolute transcendence, the convergence of differences, and the universal penetration of the three virtues; it is not cited here in full. Next, the explanation of the essence (*svabhāva*) of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* is divided into three parts. First, the sequential [explanation].

Cessation (*śamatha*). Second, the sequential cultivation of both cessation and contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). Third, the three types of cessation and contemplation within a single mind. Regarding the sequential three cessations:

first, cessation that accords with reality (*tattva-śamatha*), which brings rest to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*); second, cessation that follows conditions through skillful means (*upāya-anu-pratyaya-śamatha*), which brings rest to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*);

third, cessation that quiets the discrimination of the two extremes (*anta-dvaya-vikalpa-śamatha*), which brings rest to the Middle Way, the primary ultimate truth (*madhyamā pratipad paramārtha-satya*). As for cessation that accords with reality: all phenomena arise from conditions.
Because causes and conditions are empty and without a master, and because the mind has ceased and reached the source, one is called a *śramaṇa*.

Knowing that causes and conditions are a provisional confluence and that their illusory nature is void, this is termed "substance" (*tǐ*). When攀緣 (*pānyuán*) and deluded thoughts attain emptiness, they immediately cease;

since emptiness is itself the truth, it is called "stopping in the truth of substance" (*tǐzhēnzhǐ*). Regarding "stopping by following conditions through skillful means" (*fāngbiàn suíyuán zhǐ*): if the two vehicles likewise employ the path of ineffable speech...

By severing afflictions (*kleśa*), one enters the Truth (*tattva*); once in the Truth, there is no difference. It is only said that there is exhaustion or non-exhaustion regarding the afflictions and their residual habits (*vāsanā*).

If the followers of the Two Vehicles realize the Truth and require no further expedient means (*upāya*), the Bodhisattvas enter into the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) and ought to practice its application. Because they know that emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is not [inherently] empty, it is called "expedient means.

Because they distinguish between medicines and diseases, it is called "following conditions" (*pratyaya*). Because the mind rests in the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), it is termed "calming" (*śamatha*).
The Sūtra says: "Whether moving or resting, the mind is always one. This also serves to verify this meaning. Regarding the cessation of dualistic discrimination:

the flux of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) and the fixed security of nirvāṇa are both one-sided practices that do not accord with the Middle Way. Now, knowing that the conventional is not conventional, one rests in the quiescence of the conventional extreme;
yet, one does not attain the quiescence of the empty extreme of non-conventionality. This is called the cessation of the two extremes. These three—[the movement, the rest, and the cessation]—are...

Although the specific names for the three types of cessation (*śamatha*) have not been seen in the sūtras or śāstras, they are established according to their meaning by analogy with the three contemplations (*vipaśyanā*). The *Śāstra* states:
"When a bodhisattva relies on the scriptural teachings to assign names [to phenomena], this is called the gift of Dharma (*dharma-dāna*); there is no fault in establishing such names.

If one can seek out the names within the sūtras, it will immediately correspond to this intent. (The *Yunjian Lengyan Buyi* states: "Since Gushan used the Master’s three cessations to explain the text of the present sūtra, we know that Tiantai [established] the three cessations...")

There is indeed a profound correspondence. Thus, the *Zhiguan* (Stopping and Contemplation) states: "Although these three names for 'stopping' (*śamatha*) are not explicitly found in the sūtras or śāstras, they are established according to their meaning in relation to the three types of 'contemplation' (*vipaśyanā*), and so forth.

Now, we have indeed found them in the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra*. I maintain that the three names in the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* (*Ratnabhijñā-sūtra*) clearly designate this as meditative concentration (*samādhi*); it is also a sūtra translated during the Tang dynasty, and thus it is the most closely related [to the *Zhiguan*]. Therefore, one knows that the three types of stopping correspond precisely to the two sūtras. Furthermore, according to the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*: "Good son, one cultivates *śamatha* for three reasons.

What are the three? First, to prevent negligence; second, to adorn great wisdom; third, to attain mastery. Furthermore, one cultivates *vipaśyanā* for three reasons. What are the three? First, to contemplate the evil retributions of birth and death..."

Second, for the sake of increasing all roots of goodness; third, for the sake of destroying all afflictions (*kleśa*). According to this scriptural passage, *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight) each open up three meanings; this is the explicit textual evidence for the "three *śamathas* and three *vipaśyanās*. The sequential correspondence of these meanings is exact in the text. Thus, the *Guxiang Chao* states:

"The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says that one cultivates *śamatha* for three reasons. This is clear proof that the three are contained within *śamatha*. Moreover, it accords perfectly, like a tally, with the three [reasons] requested by Ānanda.

Yet, although the Great Master personally saw the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, he did not point to it—was this not because he wished for students to realize it for themselves? Examining these three types of *śamatha* in detail, they are similar in name to the previous explanation of their titles.

Their names are the same, but their characteristics differ. "Cessation" (zhi) that accords with reality is like the realization of the true essence (*tattva*). "Cessation" that accords with skillful means is like following conditions (*pratyaya*).
"Non-cessation" that accords with cessation is like quelling the two extremes. Their characteristics are distinct; these are what are called the characteristics of the three truths (*trīṇi satyāni*).

The first three establish the subsequent three, and the final one encompasses all three. Why is this? It is because when one abides in the cessation that accords with reality, one penetrates dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

The provisional name "emptiness" refers to the cessation of the flow of the primary essence; this is the meaning of "stopping. To settle the mind within principle is precisely to penetrate dependent origination;
this is the meaning of "abiding. This principle is itself reality; reality is itself the source.

The source is neither subject to stopping nor non-stopping; this is the meaning of "non-stopping as stopping. These three meanings together constitute the essence of True Stopping (*tathatā-viśrāma*). If, by means of skillful means...
When one abides, there is mastery in illuminating the conventional; when distraction and ignorance cease, this is the meaning of "cessation" (*śamatha*).

Stilling the mind within the conventional principle—just as Vimalakīrti entered samādhi to observe the faculties and natures of the bhikṣus and distinguish between the medicine and the illness—is the meaning of "stopping.

The immovability within the conventional principle is the meaning of "non-stopping" within stopping. These three meanings together constitute the characteristics of the skillful means of "stopping according with conditions."
When the conceptualizations of the two extremes are stilled, the two characteristics of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are both stilled; this is the meaning of "stopping" (śamatha).

The *prajñā* that enters into principle is called the Middle Way within the mind that takes conditions as its object; this is the meaning of "abiding. This reality of the true mark (*dharmatā*) is neither stopping nor non-stopping;
this is the meaning of "non-stopping-stopping. These three meanings together constitute the characteristic of stopping the two extremes. Therefore, it is [identical] with the former...
These are fundamentally different and are not what is employed in the present [teaching]. Regarding the three successive contemplations:

first, the contemplation of entering emptiness from the conventional, also called the contemplation of the two truths; second, the contemplation of entering the conventional from emptiness, also called the contemplation of equality;
third, taking the contemplation of the two emptinesses as a skillful means to enter the contemplation of the Middle Way, the primary truth, wherein every thought is quiescent and naturally flows.

One enters the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge). This is called the *Sutra on the Emergence from the Garland*. I shall now explain its meaning. "The provisional" (*jia*) refers to the false conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

"Emptiness" (*kong*) refers to the verified ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Since one now wishes to leave the conventional and return to the ultimate, it is said that one "enters the contemplation of emptiness from the provisional.
The provisional is the means for entering emptiness; first, one must contemplate the provisional, realize that the provisional is false and illusory, and thereby attain union with the ultimate.

Therefore, it is called the contemplation of the two truths (*satyadvaya*). If this contemplation is perfected, one realizes all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*). Regarding the contemplation that enters the provisional from emptiness (*śūnyatā*):
if one dwells in emptiness, how would this differ from the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*)? One would not accomplish the Buddha-dharma, nor benefit sentient beings.

For this reason, one contemplates emptiness without dwelling in emptiness, but enters the provisional to know the illness, recognize the medicine, and administer the medicine according to the illness, so that [sentient beings] may attain [liberation].

Because one practices by conforming to this, it is called the "contemplation of entering the provisional from emptiness. As for the term "equality," it is called equality in relation to what preceded it.

Previously, one used emptiness to destroy the provisional; now, one uses the provisional to destroy emptiness. Since the application of destruction is balanced, it is called the "contemplation of equality.

When this contemplation is perfected, one realizes the knowledge of the paths and their varieties (*mārgajñatā*). Regarding "the two emptinesses as the means": first, one contemplates the emptiness of saṃsāra; next, one contemplates [the emptiness of]...

Nirvāṇa. These two types of emptiness serve as the skillful means for simultaneous negation (*dvaya-pratiṣedha*). First, one contemplates the emptiness of function; next, one perceives the conventionality of function.

These two functions serve as the skillful means for simultaneous illumination (*dvaya-avabhāsa*). With every thought-moment returning to and entering the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge), one simultaneously illuminates the two truths.
When this contemplation is perfected, one realizes the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*). This is the third contemplation in the sequence.
These three contemplations share names that appear similar at first glance to the previous three contemplations, yet their meanings and characteristics differ.

The previous "contemplation of penetration" involves contemplating all things as illusory, appearing to be an entry from the conventional into emptiness; the "contemplation of thorough understanding" involves thoroughly understanding principles so that principles are harmonized, and thoroughly understanding phenomena so that phenomena are harmonized.
It is as if entering the conventional from the empty; it is a non-contemplative contemplation that resembles the contemplation of the Middle Way. As for their differences in characteristics:

the former is the characteristic of one truth, while the latter is the characteristic of the three truths. Furthermore, the first three can collectively establish the latter three, and the latter three fully possess the first three. Why is this so?
For example, when entering the empty from the conventional to shatter the solid rock of the four abidings, this is the "puncturing contemplation" (piercing through). As for that which is entered...
The emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*) is precisely the wisdom of principle (*li-jñāna*), which is capable of manifesting that principle;

this is the contemplation of penetration (*guan-da-guan*). This principle of emptiness is the meaning of "contemplation through non-contemplation. These three meanings together constitute the characteristics of entering the contemplation of emptiness. Entering the conventional from emptiness likewise possesses these three meanings:

as one recognizes conventionally designated phenomena (*prajñapti-dharma*), one destroys the obstacle of ignorance; this is the meaning of "pervasion" (*guan-chuan*). It illuminates the principle of conventional designations and distinguishes... [the text continues].
There is no error in this; it is precisely the meaning of "penetrating through observation. The provisional principle is always thus; this is precisely the meaning of "observation without observing.

These three meanings together constitute the characteristics of provisional observation (*prajñapti-vipaśyanā*). The observation of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*) likewise possesses these three meanings:

being empty of the two extremes is the meaning of "pervasive penetration"; correctly entering the Middle Way is the meaning of "penetrating through observation"; and the dharma-nature of the Middle Way is the meaning of "observation without observing."

In this way, these three meanings together constitute the characteristics of the Middle Way contemplation (*madhyamā-pratipad*). Regarding the three types of cessation-and-contemplation within a single mind:

according to the aforementioned Mahāyāna teachings on the characteristics of the three cessations and three contemplations, their meanings follow their respective characteristics and are distinct from one another.

If one discusses the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*), there are distinctions of provisional and real, as well as shallow and deep. If one discusses the three knowledges (*trividya*), there are distinctions of superior and inferior, as well as prior and posterior.
If one discusses the three types of persons, there are distinctions of various stages, great and small. These represent sequential classifications and are not what is employed here.
As for the characteristics of the Perfect and Sudden *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*: when *śamatha* takes the truths (*satya*) as its object, then one truth is the three truths; by means of the truths...
When bound to cessation (*śamatha*), there is one cessation and yet three cessations. It is like the three characteristics existing within a single moment of mind;

although it is a single moment of mind, it possesses the three characteristics. The same applies to cessation and truth: the phenomena that are ceased are one yet three, and the mind that effects the cessation is three yet one.
When observing through insight (*vipaśyanā*) with respect to objects, there is one object and yet three objects. By means of the object...
When arising from contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), one contemplation is three contemplations, like the three eyes on the face of Maheśvara;
though they are three eyes, they reside upon a single face. Contemplation and object are likewise: contemplating the three is the one, and giving rise to the one is the three.
This is inconceivable. It is neither provisional nor real, neither superior nor inferior, neither before nor after, neither simultaneous nor distinct. It is not...
This is not insignificant. Therefore, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "Phenomena born of causes and conditions are themselves emptiness, themselves the provisional, and themselves the Middle.
The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "It is as if a person with eyes sees various forms when the sun shines; if the eye alone could see, it would not require the sun.
If there were no forms, even with the sun and the eye, nothing would be seen. Thus, these three factors are not distinct.
At that time, they are inseparable. The eye is like *śamatha* (calm abiding); the sun is like *vipaśyanā* (insight); and form is like the object.
These three factors do not precede or follow one another; they are discussed as a triad simultaneously. It is likewise when discussing one within the triad. If one perceives this meaning:

This is precisely the characteristic of the perfect and sudden *śamatha-vipaśyanā*. Why stop at "three-in-one" or "one-in-three"? All the preceding meanings are, in their entirety, contained within a single mind.
What are its characteristics? To realize that the essence of ignorance and delusion is itself the reality of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is called "True Cessation of Essence.
When this true mark pervades all places, remaining unmoved as it settles the mind while following conditions and passing through objects, it is called "Cessation Following Conditions."
The provisional cessation [of conceptual proliferation] is called the "cessation that stills the two extremes," as it brings rest to the quiescence of *nirvāṇa* and the dispersion of *saṃsāra*.

To realize that all conventional designations are entirely empty, and that this emptiness is itself the true nature (*dharmatā*), is called "entering the contemplation of emptiness. When one penetrates this emptiness, one contemplates the profound Middle Way;
being able to know the characteristics of the arising and ceasing of worldly phenomena as they truly are, this is called "entering the contemplation of the provisional. Such emptiness...

Wisdom (*prajñā*) is itself the Middle Way, non-dual and undifferentiated; it is called the contemplation of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratyavekṣā*). At the moment of realizing its true essence, the massive boulders and gravel of the five abodes (*pañca-vāsabhūmi*) all come to rest;
this is the meaning of "cessation" (*śamatha*). When the mind takes the Middle Way as its object and enters the wisdom of the true reality (*dharmatā*), this is the meaning of "stopping.
The nature of true reality is neither stopping nor not stopping. Furthermore, this single thought-moment is able to pierce through...
The fifth dwelling reaches the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). This true mark is neither contemplation nor non-contemplation.
Such meanings as these exist solely within a single thought-moment; without moving from the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), there are various distinctions. As the Sūtra says:
"One is well able to discern the characteristics of all phenomena, yet remains unmoved in the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Although there are many names, they are all merely one dharma of Prajñā.

The Buddha taught various names, all of which are perfect; their meanings are likewise perfect. Whether in terms of mutual dependence or absolute transcendence, they are inconceivable in their very essence.
Because they are inconceivable, there is no obstruction; because there is no obstruction, they are fully complete without deficiency.
This is the essence of the Perfect Sudden (yuanton) manifestation of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. Mount Gu said: "Ānanda first made his request based on these three dharmas."

Having received this instruction, upon reaching full understanding, he again praised the Buddha by means of three dharmas. Thus the Sūtra says: "The Wondrously Profound, the Universal Retainer, the Unmoving Honored One.

"Wondrously Profound" refers to the wisdom of emptiness (*śūnyatā-jñāna*). "Universal Retainer" refers to the wisdom of the provisional (*prajñapti-jñāna*). "Unmoving" refers to the wisdom of the Middle (*madhyama-jñāna*).
Furthermore, when the Buddha spoke for Pūrṇa of the Tathāgata-garbha as the fundamentally wondrous, perfect, and circular mind that is not a mind.

"Non-empty is precisely mind, and mind is precisely empty; transcending both, one transcends non-transcendence. The three truths are as vividly clear as pointing at something in the palm of one's hand.

Furthermore, when explaining to Ānanda that "the six dissolve and the one perishes," he concludes with a praise, saying: "This is called the Wondrous Lotus, the Adamantine King, the Jewel-Awakening, and the Illusion-like Samādhi.
The metaphor of "the flower opening and the flower appearing" illustrates "precisely the Middle Way. The metaphor of the "adamantine" illustrates "precisely [the nature of] firmness and sharpness."

It is emptiness. That it possesses a metaphorical form like an illusion is precisely its provisional nature. Even when Mañjuśrī selected the perfect organ of realization (*avavāda*), he praised it using this very same principle.
Thus it is said: "Ānanda, listen attentively; empowered by the Buddha’s majestic authority, I shall proclaim the Vajra-King, the Illusion-like, Inconceivable Mother of Buddhas, the True Samādhi.
It differs from other metaphors for the Middle Way only in that it employs the "Mother of Buddhas" as its analogy. Regarding this...

Throughout these various texts, the teachings are expounded in successive layers, each section refuting delusion. Sometimes they employ the perspective of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), sometimes they discuss the provisional (*prajñapti*), and sometimes they reveal the Middle Way (*madhyamā*).
Though the expressions may seem partial, their intent is perfect, as they all fully embody the three dharmas. This was intended to respond to Ānanda’s request for the three types of cessation.

Now, it may be said that the three dharmas—wondrous stillness, total retention, and wondrous observation—may also be interpreted as the three distinct names for cessation, contemplation, and meditation respectively. For example, "wondrous... [and so forth].
"Profound stillness" (*zhan*) and "Vajra King," etc., refer to the cessation of penetration. "Dhāraṇī" and "like an illusion," etc., refer to the suspension of contemplative penetration.
"Immovable" and "Wondrous Lotus," etc., refer to neither ceasing nor stopping, and neither contemplating nor observing.
Thus, among the three—śamatha and so forth—whichever one is mentioned possesses the three meanings of wondrous stillness and the rest. As the Sūtra says: "This..."
This is what is meant by the statement in the Abhidharma that one "transcends the stage of no-more-learning in the snap of a finger.

It is precisely because of this perfect integration (*yuanrong*) that it is called "wondrous" (*miao*). "Wondrous" is synonymous with "esoteric" (*mi*). Regarding the phrase "cultivating and realizing the esoteric cause," the Sūtra states:
"All these various stages are gradually entered through the cultivation and realization of the various Tathāgatas' *vipaśyanā* within *śamatha*. Therefore...
The explanation of the "Secret Cause for Cultivation and Realization" is complete. Next, regarding the "Secret": this refers to entering the *maṇḍala* and reciting and upholding the divine mantra.
After the Sūtra has clarified the four kinds of discipline (*vinaya*), it says:

"If there are those with past habitual tendencies who cannot eliminate them, you should instruct such a person to single-mindedly recite my supreme divine mantra, the *Buddhoṣṇīṣa-vijaya-mahā-sitātapatra*."

It even provides instructions for the method of establishing the ritual altar (*maṇḍala*) and fixes the period for attaining realization. This is the most detailed account regarding the cultivation and progress of practitioners.
However, establishing an altar strictly according to the scriptures requires great wealth; those with meager conditions in this degenerate age are rarely able to provide for it.
Within this practice, the established periods consist of four stages totaling one hundred and twenty-one days, followed by seated meditation (*dhyāna*).

One hundred days. Since it is stated that one should sit upright in *samādhi* and dwell in peace, the method for entering the Way—relying on *śamatha* to cultivate the Great Samādhi—is known without waiting for further instruction.
As previously mentioned in the "First Seven Days," one should with utmost sincerity prostrate to the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, the great Bodhisattvas, and the Arhats;
constantly reciting mantras at the six periods of the day and night while circumambulating the altar with a sincere heart.
When practicing the path, one should constantly recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times at each session.
During the second week, one should single-mindedly and exclusively resolve upon the bodhisattva vow without interruption; in our Vinaya, there is already a teaching regarding such vows.

During the third week, throughout the twelve periods of the day and night, one should single-mindedly maintain the Buddha’s *bentuo* (pañcara) dhāraṇī (and so forth). In the past, Master Yue of Wuxing once examined this according to these principles.

The *Shuchouxengyi* (A Manual for Cultivating and Realizing [the Path]) in one fascicle is now rarely heard of; however, by following the general procedures of the various repentance rituals of Tiantai, it may be roughly understood.

Since the period of practicing the path and reciting mantras involves many causes of distraction and movement, if one does not guide these ritual actions with contemplation of principle (*li*), it may be difficult to extinguish transgressions.
This is all the more true regarding the rules for establishing the altar and the various symbolic representations described therein.
It is not a vain bestowal; thus, masters such as those of Wēnlíng have all drawn upon its underlying meaning to elucidate the manifestation of the Dharma.
What is called the "Dharma-king’s Dharma-speech" is precisely the identity of phenomenon and principle. Furthermore, the secret power of this divine mantra is realized only by the Buddha;
it is a cryptic exposition of the realm of the Three Truths, and for this reason, it is titled the *Mahā-sitātapatra-hṛdaya-mantra*. There is indeed a profound basis for this.
Therefore, when a practitioner ascends the altar, they must ensure that both principle and practice are carried out together, and the manifest and the secret are integrated.
As the Master of Siming stated regarding the three types of repentance: "Although there are three methods, the practice occurs at one time.

It is better to omit the preceding ones than to fail in the succeeding ones. The method of non-arising is most essential, while the method of taking signs is more flexible. This is because it is subtle.
Contemplating this principle is the core of the Mahāyāna. The destruction of hindrances is like overturning the great earth, where grasses and trees all wither;

the manifestation of virtues is like illuminating a clear river, where the myriad phenomena appear in their entirety. If one guides ritual practice with this contemplation of the principle, then a single prostration or a single circumambulation will extinguish the sins of kalpas as numerous as motes of dust;
a single lamp or a single offering of water will bring merit equal to empty space. This is precisely the essence of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*.

This refers to meritorious achievement. Since that is so, this should likewise be understood as such. It is because the mantra is expounded through the union of single-minded concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).

First, the forty-four minds are clarified herein; subsequently, one must maintain the divine mantra by upholding both concentration and wisdom, relying upon both the Exoteric and Esoteric teachings to traverse the stages of the sages.
Furthermore, regarding "definitive meaning" (*nītārtha*): it praises the fact that the meanings taught in this sutra are entirely without anything that is not fully realized.
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*, the *Ratnakūṭa*, and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa* sūtras all state: "Rely on the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), not on the non-definitive meaning (*neyārtha*).
In the *Ratnakūṭa*, Śāriputra asks: "In which sūtras is the definitive meaning spoken of? In which sūtras is the non-definitive meaning spoken of? The Buddha tells Śāriputra:
"If, within various sūtras, there is the proclamation of conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*), it is called non-definitive."
Teaching the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is called definitive (*nītārtha*). Teaching karma and afflictions (*kleśa*) is called non-definitive (*neyārtha*).
Teaching the exhaustion of afflictions and karma is called definitive. Teaching weariness with saṃsāra and the pursuit of nirvāṇa is called non-definitive.
Teaching that saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are non-dual and without distinction is called definitive. Teaching various...

The differentiation of literal phrases is called "provisional meaning" (neyārtha). That which proclaims the profound, which is difficult to see and difficult to realize, is called "definitive meaning" (nītārtha).
Now, this sutra states: "Today, the Tathāgata universally proclaims for this assembly the true nature of the ultimate within the ultimate.
This refers to the *Ratnakūṭa* proclaiming the ultimate as definitive meaning. The sutra says: "Entering the ocean of wondrous adornment, it is perfected."
Enlightenment returns to non-attainment; thus, it is proclaimed that the exhaustion of afflictions and karma is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). A sutra says:

"The aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha"; thus, it is proclaimed that birth-and-death and nirvāṇa are neither two nor distinct, which is the definitive meaning.
A sutra says: "I unite non-arising and non-ceasing with the Tathāgatagarbha" (and so forth); this proclaims the profound.
That which is difficult to see, difficult to understand, and difficult to awaken to is called the *nītārtha* (definitive meaning). Next, regarding "the myriad practices of all bodhisattvas":
