From the *Xinbian jian* (Discernment of the Mind) up to the fourth fascicle, the exposition of the perfect principle (*yuanli*) is nothing other than the meaning of the "principle-as-such" (*lijì*) Tathāgatagarbha.

If one follows the textual sequence and takes the passage concerning the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) as being inherently the Tathāgatagarbha, and judges this to be the "principle-as-such," its meaning becomes even more manifest.

Although the aggregates, bases, and elements are textually restricted to the six classes of ordinary beings within the context of the Three Truths, their meaning actually extends throughout the ten realms.

Regarding the *dhātu* (element/realm): because there exist the five aggregates (*skandha*) of the *dharmatā* outside the realm, the *tathāgatagarbha* has three aspects according to the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra*:
first, the empty *tathāgatagarbha*, which is separated from and not liberated from all afflictions (*kleśa*);

second, the non-empty *tathāgatagarbha*, which possesses inconceivable qualities as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; and third, the empty-and-non-empty *tathāgatagarbha*, which manifests in accordance with form.
Emptiness universally responds to all things. Although this sutra speaks only of the *tathāgatagarbha* (Buddha-nature) in its singular form, the fourth fascicle fully sets forth three meanings.
As it says: "The *tathāgatagarbha* is fundamentally the wondrous primordial mind; it is neither mind nor emptiness," etc.—this refers to the empty *tathāgatagarbha*.
Furthermore: "The *tathāgatagarbha* is originally luminous and the mind is wondrous; it is both mind and emptiness," etc.—this refers to the non-empty [tathāgatagarbha].
It is the *tathāgatagarbha*. That is to say, the wondrously luminous fundamental mind of the *tathāgatagarbha* is detached from both "is" and "is not," being neither identical nor non-identical.

This is the empty-yet-not-empty *tathāgatagarbha*. As for the term "original *tathāgatagarbha*," it means that the form and mind of both the sage and the ordinary person are fundamentally perfect and pure, equal to the *tathāgatagarbha* without any difference. This is what the Great Master [Zhiyi] meant by "this is the perfect wisdom, the perfect..."
One awakens to all dharmas as pervading all places, such that there is nothing not clearly understood. Although the five *ānantarya* [sins] exist, they are all characterized by liberation.
Although one may be obscured, blind, inverted, or deluded, this principle remains. This principle is manifest and eternally abiding in the world;

it cannot be diminished by the absence of a Buddha, nor can it be increased by the presence of a Buddha. To attain it does not constitute loftiness; to lose it does not constitute lowness. Therefore, it is called the *skandhas* and *āyatanas*.

The aggregates, sense bases, and elements (*skandha-āyatana-dhātu*) are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha. Now, I shall further explain their meaning. The Sūtra says: "The nature of form is true emptiness.

This means that these aggregates, sense bases, and elements are fundamentally the empty Tathāgatagarbha. "The nature of emptiness is true form. This means that these aggregates, sense bases, and elements are fundamentally the non-empty Tathāgatagarbha.
"Pure and originally so, pervading the Dharma-realm. This means that these aggregates, sense bases, and elements are fundamentally both empty and...
It is the empty *tathāgatagarbha*. Through the "original name" (*benming*), its meaning becomes even more manifest. Second, regarding the "name-as-identical-to-the-*tathāgatagarbha*":
at the beginning of cultivating merit, one hears the names that can express the aforementioned principle and nature. However, there is both inclusion and exclusion.

In terms of inclusion, those whose ears pass over the sounds of the Dharma—regardless of whether they are clear or obscure—are included in this stage, provided they differ from those who do not hear at all. In terms of exclusion, those who have not yet attained perfection are excluded.

I have heard that the "Distinct" and "Shared" stages within the stage of Ordinary Beings still belong to the level of Principle-Identity (*li-ji*), because those at the seven stages of expedient means have not yet understood the ultimate name of the *Śūraṅgama* Samādhi and do not know the principle of the eternally abiding *tathāgatagarbha*. As the Sūtra says:

"The continuous succession of birth and death for all sentient beings is entirely due to their failure to know the eternally abiding true mind. This is what is meant. The three contemplations constitute the stage of Practice-Identity (*xing-ji*) of the Tathāgata.

Regarding "the treasury," the Sūtra says: "If you now cultivate and realize the Buddha’s samādhi, you must first establish three gradual stages to eliminate the fundamental causes of your original deluded thoughts" (and so forth). These three gradual stages are:
first, cultivation to eliminate auxiliary causes; second, true cultivation to excise the primary nature; and third, further advancement to counteract manifest karma. This is...

This refers to the stages of advancement through names. One is not only able to understand the names but can also practice contemplation (*vipaśyanā*); however, as long as one has not yet entered the formal stages (*bhūmi*), it is not yet the stage of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-caryā*).
If these three types [of cultivation] are practiced without ceasing, in the near term they can subdue the five abodes (*pañca-vāsana*) and enter the stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-jñāna*);

in the distant term, they can shatter the three delusions and ascend to the True and the Counterfeit [Stages]. Thus the Sutra says: "Because the mind does not flow outwardly, it returns to the source itself; the dust..."

"Since they no longer take the sense organs as objects, there is nothing with which they may be coupled; the flow returns to its entirety as one, and the six functions cease to operate (and so forth). ...

Eventually, this person attains the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Now, among the three gradual stages, it is clearly stated in the Sūtra that one must 'eliminate auxiliary causes and hollow out the primary nature.
Furthermore, regarding the third stage, which opposes their manifest karma—by what dharma is this opposition achieved? One must know..."

The methods for avoiding these transgressions are scattered throughout various sutras; however, to synthesize and put them into practice, they reside precisely here. Now, that which is expounded by a single sutra consists of understanding (*parijñā*), practice (*pratipatti*), and realization (*sākṣātkriyā*).
Understanding is likened to the eyes, and practice is likened to the feet; because the eyes and feet rely upon one another, one can reach the Lake of Coolness (*śītavana*).

Thus, when the Great Master Tiantai commented on the *Lotus Sutra*, he first elaborated the Ten Profound Subtleties (*daśa-prakarṣa*) as the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning) to reveal the Perfect [Teaching].
[The author] explains: Next, he establishes the ten vehicles as the foundation for calming and contemplation (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*) to clarify the practice of the Perfect [Teaching].
It can be said that these two approaches fully provide both the eyes and the feet. Now, following that intent, I shall take the eight dharmas expounded in a single sutra to explain *Śūraṅgama*.

Although it is said that both practice and realization are contained therein, the methods for cultivating and constructing the gates of practice are not yet fully complete; therefore, one must further...
Based on the principles of what is to be expounded (*vācya*), ten vehicles (*daśayāna*) are established as the foundation for counteracting present karma and entering the stages (*bhūmi*).
Among these, the names and meanings bear much resemblance to those of the Eightfold Dharma; however, while that [system] is detailed, this is concise, and the intent is not in vain.
As for the ten vehicles: first, contemplating the inconceivable realm (*acintyaviṣaya*); second, truly and correctly generating the bodhicitta; third, skillful...
1. Skillfully settling the mind in *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*; 2. Thoroughly destroying all phenomena; 3. Recognizing what is permeable and what is obstructed;
4. Harmonizing the factors of the path (*mārga-aṅga*); 5. Applying remedies to assist in opening the way; 6. Knowing the successive stages; 7. Being able to practice patient endurance; 8.

Detaching from attachment to the dharmas that accord with the Path. These ten dharma-methods are fully present in both the words and meaning of this present sutra. If one contemplates the empty mind...

These do not transcend matter and mind; matter is produced from the mind, and its entire substance is mind. Therefore, a sutra says: "In the three realms there are no separate dharmas;

(Text) This sutra clarifies that within the *tathāgatagarbha*, the ten realms are both "neither" and "both," and through these simultaneous negations and affirmations, [all dualistic extremes] are sublated. All...

This is the meaning. Furthermore, it is said: "The principle is fully possessed by all sentient beings, and has been perfected by all Buddhas. Between this perfection and this possession, there is no difference in their equality.

The same applies to the sensory objects (*viṣaya*). This sutra states: "In the Tathāgatagarbha, essential form is true emptiness, and essential emptiness is true form;

Being without nature, they originally transform according to things; therefore, while they interpenetrate one another, their phenomenal activities remain eternally distinct. Hence, I...
The body and mind pervade all lands and atoms; so too do all Buddhas and sentient beings. (Text) This sutra says:
"You join the mind of birth and extinction with the Tathāgatagarbha, and thus the Tathāgatagarbha accordingly becomes form and emptiness, pervading the Dharma-realm.
I join the non-extinguishing and non-arising [mind] with the Tathāgatagarbha, and thus the Tathāgatagarbha is solely wondrous, enlightened clarity, perfectly illuminating the Dharma-realm."

The meaning can be understood by examining the text. Furthermore, it says: "Each and every body and land are eternally identical in essence; how could this hinder the distinction between mind, Buddha, and sentient beings?

Because they are distinct, there is the differentiation of ultimate defilement and purity as conditions. Yet the essence of these conditions is fundamentally empty; emptiness is not non-empty. (Text) This sutra clarifies that within the Three Truths:
because of their difference, the ten realms are all identical; because of their sameness, the ten realms are all non-existent; and because they are empty...

It is said that the nature of clouds is true emptiness; because it is not empty, the nature of clouds is true form within emptiness. It is further said: "The three truths and the three contemplations are neither three nor one;
three, one, and one have no place of reliance. Although the names 'truth' and 'contemplation' differ, their essence is the same. Therefore, the duality of subject and object is non-dual.
(Text) Because these three truths in this sutra are identical to the Tathāgatagarbha, the three truths are neither three nor [not-three]. This is the wondrous *śūnyatā*.
Because of *mātr̥-samādhi* (contemplation through cessation), one contemplates that the three are not three. The entire Tathāgatagarbha gives rise to the three forms of cessation (*śamatha*).
The entirety of these three cessations resides within the Three Truths. That is to say: "Only the wondrous, awakened clarity completely illumines the Dharma-realm.

Therefore, their essence is identical and not two. Furthermore, it says: "One who contemplates in this manner is said to contemplate that birth-and-death is itself nirvāṇa, and that afflictions are themselves bodhi."
(Text) The aggregates, bases, sense-fields, and elements of this sutra are themselves birth-and-death and afflictions;
because they are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha, they are themselves nirvāṇa and bodhi. I unite my wondrous clarity—neither extinguished nor arising—with the Tathāgatagarbha;
thus, I contemplate that birth-and-death is itself nirvāṇa, and afflictions are themselves bodhi. All nine vehicles that follow below shall take this phrase as their governing framework.
Second, regarding the genuine arousal of the bodhicitta: one gives rise to objectless compassion and formulates the Four Great Vows.
Knowing that nirvāṇa is identical to saṃsāra, and that this suffering can be transcended, one thinks: "For those who have not yet crossed over suffering, I shall cause them to cross.

Therefore, the vow is made: "Sentient beings are boundless; I vow to deliver them all. This is formulated based on the objective realm of the Truth of Suffering. Furthermore, knowing that bodhi is identical to afflictions (kleśa)...

This [truth of] origination can be understood. For those who have not yet understood origination, I shall cause them to understand it; therefore, the vow states: "I vow to sever the innumerable afflictions.
This arises based on the objective realm of the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*). Knowing that afflictions are themselves bodhi, this path is easily settled.

For those who have not yet settled in the path, I shall cause them to settle in it; therefore, the vow states: "I vow to study the immeasurable dharma-gates. This arises based on the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*).

It arises from the objective realm (*viṣaya*). One knows that birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) is itself nirvāṇa; this cessation is easy to attain. For those who have not yet attained cessation, I shall cause them to attain it;
therefore, the vow is made: "The unsurpassed path of the Buddha, may I vow to accomplish it. This arises from the objective realm of the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*).
Thus, compassion is without conditions and without conceptualization, universally covering all beings like a great cloud; it requires no effort, just as a magnet attracts iron.

[The Master] said: "This is called truly and authentically giving rise to the bodhicitta. (Text) Having realized the inconceivable realm of the Tathāgatagarbha according to his capacity through this sutra, he then spoke verses in praise of the Buddha and made a vow, saying:
"May I now attain the fruit and become a Treasure King, returning to save as many beings as there are grains of sand in the Ganges.
He further said: "I vow to enter first into the evil world of the five turbidities; until even a single sentient being has [attained liberation]..."
Having attained Buddhahood, one shall ultimately not enter *nirvāṇa* here. To become a Treasure King is the vow to accomplish the Buddha-way;

to "gather" the Dharma-gates is the vow to study them, for one must study the Dharma-gates before attaining the fruit. To "return" to deliver the multitude of beings is the vow to deliver sentient beings;
to "gather" the afflictions is the vow to sever them, for only by severing the afflictions can one deliver beings.

Once the practitioner has realized that the aggregates (*skandha*), sense bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) are fundamentally the *tathāgatagarbha*, they give rise to this vow; this is precisely the true arousal of the *bodhicitta*.

However, while the vow itself is thus formulated, there are varying depths in its stages. As the *Zhaolun* states: "One arouses the *saṃnāha* (armor) at the initial mind and brings forth great compassion when responding to hardships.
This refers to the arousal of the mind at the stage of the nominal designation (*nāmadheya*). The *Renwang jing* speaks of ten [stages]...

The "Good Bodhisattva" who has resolved upon the Great Mind (mahācitta) is forever parted from the ocean of suffering in the three realms; this is the resolve of the stage of semblance (*sādṛśya-bhūmi*).
The *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra says, "At the very moment of first resolving the mind, one attains perfect enlightenment"; this is the resolve of the stage of partial realization (*pradeśa-prativedha-bhūmi*).

What is now being addressed to the capacity of the audience is a stage situated within partial truth (*bhūtārtha-pradeśa*); even if it is not yet the stage of partial truth, one has nonetheless ascended to the stage of semblance. Third, the Good [Bodhisattva].

Regarding those who skillfully settle the mind in *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*: the initial vehicle is called "seeking the supreme," and the subsequent vehicle is called "transforming through downward guidance. By means of what dharma does one ascend and descend?

It is by means of skillfully cultivating *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. Through *vipaśyanā*, one realizes that birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) is itself nirvāṇa, and the mind of birth-and-death comes to rest.
This very nature of mind is called the Great Nirvana, the profound cave of dhyāna; this is the skillful cultivation of śamatha (calm abiding).

To contemplate that afflictions are themselves bodhi and thus shatter the afflictive mind—this very nature of mind is called the wisdom of the true mark (dharmatā); this is the skillful cultivation of vipaśyanā (insight).
Just as when yin and yang are harmonized, all things flourish and mature, so too, if one skillfully cultivates śamatha and vipaśyanā, one can possess them both within a single mind.
It completes the ten thousand practices. The *Lotus Sūtra* says: "Adorned by the power of concentration and wisdom, one delivers sentient beings by means of this.

Is this not ascending upon *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* to seek the Way above and transform others below? Therefore, it is called the "skillful method for settling the mind through *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*" (text).

This marks the beginning of the main body (*abhidharma*) of this sūtra. With earnest and respectful entreaty, he requests the single-minded *śamatha-vipaśyanā*, the Great *Śūraṅgama* Samādhi. Tianru says: "Although [the Buddha] uses the Great..."
This is certainly a request for instruction. However, as shown in the subsequent passages of the Tathāgata’s teaching, there is no other method presented;

from the initial discernment of the true and the false, through the subsequent harmonization of the true and the false, up until the fourth fascicle, it is entirely a matter of elucidating the perfect principle (yuanli).

Indeed, this perfect principle is the foundation of the Great Samādhi. This perfect principle is precisely the Tathāgatagarbha, which is fundamentally identical to the aggregates, sense bases, and elements.
One cultivates the Great Samādhi by relying upon this perfect principle; this is equivalent in meaning to the teaching that observing birth and death is itself nirvāṇa.
It is further stated that by skillfully practicing śamatha and vipaśyanā, one can single-mindedly fulfill the myriad practices. Moreover, this is consistent with the samādhis described in this sūtra.

The perfection of the ten thousand practices is like the matching of a tally and its seal. Fourth, regarding the "Pervasive Destruction of Dharmas": previously, one proceeded upward through *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.

If proceeding upward, one should have attained the fruit; if proceeding downward, one should have attained deliverance (*tāraṇa*). Now, neither fruit nor deliverance is attained—what obstacle is there?
It is simply that the destruction of dharmas was not pervasive. Furthermore, one must investigate that birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) is itself nirvāṇa.

Horizontally breaking through the obstructions of the ten dharma realms: afflictions are investigated and found to be none other than bodhi. Vertically breaking through the obstructions of the ten dharma realms:

fundamentally they are not identical to the ten dharmas; how then could they suddenly be identical to the ten dharmas? For this reason, they must be broken through. Fundamentally they are not separate from the ten dharmas;

how then could they suddenly be separate from the ten dharmas? For this reason, they must be broken through. When neither identical nor separate, the path of bodhi is accomplished. It is like a turning wheel.
The Sage-King is able to shatter all powerful enemies, yet there is nothing that is actually shattered. The Prajñāpāramitā is also like this:
it can shatter all things, yet there is nothing that is actually shattered. This sutra says: "I unite the non-extinguished and non-arising with the Tathāgatagarbha;
yet the Tathāgatagarbha is neither mind nor emptiness," and so forth. How could the ten realms not be [of this nature]?
If the ten dharmas are themselves the *tathāgatagarbha*, why must they be destroyed? Furthermore, it is said that the *tathāgatagarbha* is itself mind and itself emptiness;
since the ten realms are not separate from the ten dharmas, why must they be destroyed because they are separated from them?
Moreover, it is said that the *tathāgatagarbha* is "separated from identity and separated from non-identity," being neither identical nor non-identical; is this not itself non-identity?
Is it not the case that one does not depart from the path of Bodhi to achieve [enlightenment]?

If you say that this refers to the state of the Tathāgata’s fruition and has no bearing on the universal penetration of dharmas through the causal mind, how can this be reconciled with the following passage:

"If, at the stage of the causal ground, one takes a mind of arising and ceasing as the fundamental practice for cultivation and seeks the fruit of the Buddha-vehicle—which is neither arising nor ceasing—there is no such possibility"? Please [explain].
It is appropriate to seek through principle and not be obstructed by emotion. Fifth, regarding the penetration or obstruction of consciousness:
once the three contemplations have thoroughly destroyed all phenomena, this mind should accord with the principle; why then does it still fail to penetrate? One must examine more minutely:
within all phenomena there is the nature of peace and bliss, so why are they suddenly all destroyed together? Within all phenomena there are the nets of Māra.

If you suddenly wish to grasp it all at once, you must clearly discern what is open and what is obstructed. If you mistake birth-and-death for non-nirvana and mistake afflictions for non-enlightenment, then all ten realms will be obstructed.
If you realize that birth-and-death is itself nirvana and realize that afflictions are themselves enlightenment, then they are all open.
Thus, all ten realms are mutually pervasive; hence it is called "the consciousness penetrating the obstructed and the unobstructed. (Text) This sutra states:

"You cause the characteristics of form and emptiness to tilt against and usurp one another within the Tathāgatagarbha, yet the Tathāgatagarbha accordingly manifests as form and emptiness, pervading the entire Dharma-realm.

This is because delusion regarding birth-and-death and afflictions is itself nirvāṇa and bodhi; for by means of afflictions and birth-and-death, the characteristics of form and emptiness tilt against one another.

They compete for possession, resulting in the ten realms all becoming obstructed. This is also the fault of not understanding that within all dharmas there are entirely the nets of Māra, yet grasping at them all together.
Furthermore, it says: "I unite non-extinction and non-arising with the Tathāgatagarbha;
and the Tathāgatagarbha is solely wondrous, enlightened clarity, perfectly illuminating the Dharma-realm. This is precisely realizing that birth-and-death and afflictions are [the Tathāgatagarbha].

Because *nirvāṇa* and *bodhi* are present, all ten realms are universally permeated. This is also the function of awakening to the fact that within all phenomena there exists the nature of peace and bliss, rather than simultaneously negating them.

Furthermore, regarding the three truths (*triratna*) across the ten realms—whether they are neither identical nor different, and so forth—all share the meaning of neither being collectively grasped nor collectively negated.
Moreover, "to establish knowing upon knowing" is the very root of ignorance; it is to be open yet obstructed.

Furthermore, when one knows that seeing is non-seeing, this is itself nirvana; it is to be obstructed and yet be unobstructed. Because one is turned by external things, within this state one perceives the great as small;
this is to be unobstructed and yet be obstructed. If one can turn things over, one is identical to the Tathāgata; this is to be obstructed and yet be unobstructed.
Sixth, regarding the skillful cultivation of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*): once the practitioner has recognized obstruction and unobstruction, how [should they proceed]?
While practicing the factors of enlightenment on level ground, one should contemplate the impurity of the body;
thus, through impurity, one cultivates purity, neither purity nor impurity. This extends even to cultivating permanence through impermanence, neither permanence nor impermanence.
This is neither flourishing nor withering; within this interval, one enters nirvana. Even so it is for all the various factors of enlightenment.
This is so. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "From the first generation of the mind, one constantly contemplates nirvāṇa.
Practicing the path and possessing the hundred phrases of liberation is called the 'hundred-pound-gold' afflictions being identical to bodhi; this is named the Śūraṅgama Samādhi.
Cultivating and purifying the mind so that it is like empty space is also named the King of the Twenty-five Existences Samādhi. This is called skillfully cultivating the factors of the path. (Text)
This sutra states: "There is a samādhi called the Great Buddha-Crown Śūraṅgama King, which is fully endowed with the myriad practices.

This is precisely the meaning of the statement that contemplating afflictions as being identical to bodhi is named the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, through which one cultivates and rectifies the mind, and so forth.

Seventh, regarding the "Aids to Opening through Antidotes": once one has skillfully cultivated the factors of the path (mārga-aṅga), one will necessarily be able to flow into [the ultimate realization].
Regarding the three gates of liberation: if difficulties arise before one has entered them, or if difficulties arise while one is in the midst of saving others, how should one apply the antidotes?

If the difficulty of stinginess arises, one should contemplate that stinginess itself is bodhi. Whether one accepts or does not accept, whether one both accepts and does not accept, or even up to the fivefold non-acceptance—this non-acceptance is *dāna* (generosity).
*Dāna* is the *dharmadhātu*. The meaning of *dāna* encompasses the six [perfections]; it provides the necessities of life... [text ends].

"Fearing the Dharma. Herein, one, two, or three [categories] apply; the remaining deficiencies are likewise so. Furthermore, there are the counteractive measures (*pratipakṣa*), the transformative counteractives, and those that do not transform, and so forth.
This is called "the aids to the opening of the counteractives" (text). This sutra first speaks of the single mind, clarifying the four kinds of restraint within concentration and wisdom.
Once the three trainings are complete, the remaining perfections (*pāramitā*) are contained therein; it even says they are fully endowed with the myriad practices.

How much more so, then, for the six perfections? Furthermore, if sexual depravity is difficult to guard against due to long-standing habitual tendencies, the Buddha commanded the exclusive recitation of divine mantras;

this is yet another supreme method of remedial treatment. Since sexual depravity is difficult to guard against, if its recitation can eliminate it, then other forms of depravity are merely slight and trivial.

To employ spiritual power (*ṛddhi*) for the purpose of melting it away is the most easy method. Therefore, when weariness or difficulty arises, the practitioner should skillfully grasp the essential meaning and apply it as an antidote.

If one clings to the literal text and remains bound by fixed notions, failing to recognize the necessity of adaptability, one will remain satiated with [the mere taste of] the nectar while suffering injury;
this is what is meant by "seeking long life while being lost in youth. How can one not be cautious? (Section Eight)

Regarding "skillfully knowing the stages and positions": if a practitioner does not recognize these stages and positions, they will fall into the error of overweening pride (*adhimāna*), claiming to have attained what they have not attained and claiming to have realized what they have not realized.
One should know that birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) is itself *nirvāṇa*; this is the identity of principle (*li*). To be able to understand in this way is to accord with the *Sūtras*;
this is the *nirvāṇa* of words and letters. When that which is contemplated accords with the text and the text accords with contemplation, this is contemplation.
It is the practice of Nirvana. When the delusions of views and thoughts are first shattered and the six sense organs become pure, it is the semblance Nirvana.

When ignorance is partially shattered and the Buddha-nature is partially revealed, it is the partial true Nirvana. When wisdom is equal to that of all Buddhas and severance is identical to the Great Enlightenment, it is the ultimate Nirvana.
You should personally observe and deliberate: among these six stages of "being thus," to which position does what you have now attained belong?
Next, be careful not to beat your breast and argue about the mind, thereby deceiving yourself and others. This is called "skillfully knowing the stages and positions" (the text).
The stages and positions clarified in this present sutra are precisely what is meant by this. Ninth, the accomplishment of patience (*kṣānti*): when the practitioner practices the Way...
At that time, there will be many obstacles and difficulties arising from what is mature and what is not yet mature; one must always practice patient endurance (*kṣānti*).

If one knows that birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) is itself nirvāṇa, then one will not provide an opportunity for the aggregates (*skandha*), sense-bases (*āyatana*), elements (*dhātu*), the objects of the senses, the objects of illness, the objects of karmic signs, the objects of demonic activities (*māra-karman*), the objects of meditative states (*dhyāna-citta*), the objects of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), or the objects of the bodhisattva stages to gain access.
If one knows that afflictions (*kleśa*) are themselves awakening (*bodhi*), then one will not provide an opportunity for the objects of affliction.

When one gains mastery over the objects of all views and the objects of overweening pride, and is able to endure this suffering and its accumulation which are without action (*anabhisaṃskāra*), then birth and death cannot ensnare them, and afflictions cannot defile them.
The views and attachments of the ten dharma-realms all become their attendants, and the *pariccheda* (segmented) and *pariṇāma* (transformative) deaths become their servants;
this is called the accomplishment of patience (*kṣānti*). This sutra clarifies that the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) are fundamentally suchness (*tathatā*).

The *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness) is the realm of the aggregates (*skandha*), sense bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*). The ten causes of habitual action (*daśa-vyasanahetu*) and the sixfold mutual retribution (*ṣaḍ-vyavahāra-vipāka*), along with the various heavens and so forth, are the realms of the marks of karma (*karma-lakṣaṇa*).
The devas of the form and formless realms (*rūpa-ārūpya-dhātu*) are the realms of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). The realms of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*) are also included therein.

Furthermore, the latter two types within the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) are likewise the realms of the two vehicles. Moreover, they encompass the realms of the bodhisattvas. These fifty kinds of demonic obstacles of the aggregates (*pañcāśad-skandha-māra*) are all [included].

The sphere of demonic activities (*mārakarman*) includes the increase of afflictions (*kleśa*), various views (*dṛṣṭi*), and overweening pride (*abhimāna*). Only the single sphere of illness does not fall outside the great refuge.

Although the various spheres elucidated in the sūtras and śāstras differ in their extent—some being more detailed and others more concise—in sum, they all do not transcend the afflictions of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
For instance, the various views, afflictions, and overweening pride belong to the category of affliction (*kleśa*), while the remainder all belong to birth and death.

Therefore, the Dharma of patience according to Tiantai merely states that when one realizes that birth-and-death and afflictions are themselves nirvana and bodhi, one will not be defiled by the nets of various sensory objects.
This sutra, however, says: "The accomplishment of disruption arises from the master of the five aggregates within your own mind.
If the master is deluded, the guests will gain the advantage; if you awaken to dhyāna right where you are, there will be no fault. Thus...
Those demonic activities can do nothing to you; while remaining in *dhyāna*, one immediately contemplates the mountain terrace—that birth-and-death is itself *nirvāṇa*.
As the *Śūraṅgama Samādhi Sūtra* says: "To know that the realm of Māra is like the realm of the Buddha, that they are one suchness and not two suchnesses"—this is what is meant.
Tenth, regarding being free from attachment to dharmas (*dharmatṛṣṇā*): being able to practice the various vehicles mentioned above, and furthermore being able to abide in...

Whether forceful or gentle, one must necessarily accord with the *dharmatā*. If, regarding this, one gives rise to attachment and remains stationary without moving forward, it is as if one were to collapse just as one is about to ascend, or fall just as one is about to pass through. Is this not a great loss? Therefore, it is said:
"Nirvāṇa is precisely saṃsāra," because of the craving for nirvāṇa; and "saṃsāra is precisely nirvāṇa," because one advances without retreating. For this reason, one should contemplate thus.
Birth-and-death is itself nirvana; it gives rise to all meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), samādhis, and various merits.

Viewing afflictions as themselves bodhi, it gives rise to all dhāraṇīs, the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), and other such Buddha-dharmas.
If one can act in this way, it is called "following craving so that it does not arise, yet giving rise to prajñā."
Therefore, it is said: "one is free from attachment to dharmas" (text). This sutra says: "Sentient beings are crazed and deluded, lacking self-reflection.
Encountering this [state] appearing before them, each rests according to their own cherished habitual delusions, taking it to be the ultimate ground of refuge and peace.
They claim for themselves that they have attained the fulfillment of unsurpassed bodhi; thus, Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas fail to progress further. You all must maintain..."

With hearts upholding the Way of the Tathāgata, you shall transmit this Dharma-gate after my parinirvāṇa to the final age, causing all sentient beings everywhere to awaken to and understand its meaning.

You shall cause their bodies and minds to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, so that from beginning to end they do not encounter false paths, and ultimately enter the ocean of wondrous adornment to perfect Bodhi and return to the state of non-attainment. This is called "Leaving Accordance."
The Way’s Dharma is one of loving-kindness. The Great Master said: "These ten grave precepts encompass both the horizontal and vertical dimensions with subtle refinement and exquisite skill.

At the beginning, they distinguish between the authenticity and falsehood of objects; in the middle, the primary and auxiliary practices complement one another; and at the end, there is patient endurance and non-attachment.

Their intent is perfect and their method is ingenious; they are all-inclusive and exhaustive. As a standard for beginners, they escort the practitioner to that state of *sārvajña* (omniscience); this is not a matter of obscure realization."
The Chan Master is what a scholar-monk can understand. It is like Viśvakarman constructing the Hall of Victory:

neither too sparse nor too dense, with gaps narrow enough to admit a thread; towering and majestic, it stands loftily in the heavens, beyond the ability of a clumsy craftsman to measure its proportions.
Or again, it is like a skilled painter who delineates the outlines and renders the likeness with such fidelity that the skeletal structure is exquisite and lifelike.

The vital energy (qi) soars and moves; how could it be something for a mere colorist to embellish? (And so forth. If you wish to understand this thoroughly, you should consult the *Mahā-śamatha-vipaśyanā*.
To know that is to know this; once you know this sutra, you will then come to know the Tathāgata and the Wise One (Zhìzhě).

This Dharma begins with the stage of names (*nāmamātra*) when first practiced, and reaches the stage of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-caryā*) upon its completion. Contemplative practice consists of the five ranks (*pañca-varga*).
Furthermore, this sutra is titled "The Stage of Dry Wisdom" (*śuṣka-prajñā-bhūmi*). The sutra says: "The grasping mind is empty and luminous, consisting purely of wisdom.
The nature of wisdom is bright and perfect, illuminating the ten directions. Possessing wisdom while being 'dry' [of moisture] is called the Stage of Dry Wisdom.

This is because one uses inconceivable contemplation to observe the inconceivable realm, realizing that the aggregates (*skandha*), sense bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) are fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha; thus, the two attachments to self and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-ubhaya-grāha*) are seen to be utterly devoid of reality.

Because its nature is thus, it is said that the grasping mind is empty and luminous, being purely wisdom; and because the Tathāgata-garbha is solely wondrous, enlightened, and luminous, perfectly illuminating the Dharma-realm, it is said that the nature of wisdom is luminous and perfect, polishing the ten directions.
These are all signs of the initial accomplishment of the Tathāgata-garbha at the stage of contemplative practice (*guanxing*), wherein the five abodes of delusion are completely suppressed.
This is what is called the initial drying up of desire and love, yet not yet having attained the Dharma of the Tathāgata.
"Flowing water" refers to "reception. The third stage, "semblance," corresponds to the *tathāgatagarbha* at the level of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*).

Regarding the term "semblance": by contemplating the empty *tathāgatagarbha*, one attains a semblance of resonance; by contemplating the non-empty *tathāgatagarbha*, one attains a semblance of resonance;
and by contemplating the both-empty-and-non-empty *tathāgatagarbha*, one attains a semblance of resonance. Tiantai says: "Semblance..."
Two things may resemble one another, like brass appearing similar to gold, or a melon compared to a gourd; likewise, fire is first warm, and the waters of the sea are initially level.
One knows the nature of water only when it is cold and drinks it; if one is thirsty, what is the use of listening to talk about digging a well? I have briefly set forth these essentials.

The characteristics of this stage are as described in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* regarding the purification of the six sense faculties. This stage consists of ten levels: first, the mind of faith; second, the mind of mindfulness;

and so on, up to the tenth, the mind of aspiration. Regarding these ten stages of faith within the perfect teaching (*yuanwei*) of the *Lotus Sūtra*, Tiantai correlates them with the ten minds of the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* through the Ten Modes of Practice (*shicheng*).
He states: "By practicing the equality of the Dharma-realm, one enters the mind of faith. Through skillful cultivation...
Compassion immediately enters the mind of mindfulness; continuing thus until the skillful cultivation of non-attachment, one enters the mind of aspiration.

This is explained in terms of vertical correspondence, whereby the One Vehicle is paired with a single stage of faith. If discussed in terms of horizontal correlation, each and every stage of faith contains all ten vehicles.
Therefore, the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* states: "One faith has ten; ten faiths have a hundred. The hundred dharmas are the root of all dharmas."

This is the fundamental principle. Jingxi said: "In each of the ten faiths, the phrase 'skillfully cultivating' refers to practicing the five repentances by taking true reality as the object of focus, exerting oneself with diligent vigor, and thereby attaining entry into the ten faiths upon reaching the fifth stage; this is called 'skillful cultivation.
Because of this skillful cultivation, a semblance understanding arises. Therefore, the ten dharmas, as they function within the stage of semblance, are designated as 'faith,' and so on up to 'vow.'"

When the fuel is exhausted and the fire is extinguished, he enters [this] skillful means.

Pure Nirvāṇa. According to the Separate Teaching (*pratyeka-yāna*), one destroys the twelve grades of ignorance, realizes the *sarvākārajñatā* (all-aspect wisdom), and enters the stage of Sublime Enlightenment (*miao-jue*).

This corresponds to the two practices of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*): sitting beneath the great king of jewel-flowers at the foot of the seven-jeweled Bodhi tree in the Lotus Treasury World (*padmagarbha-lokadhātu*), one achieves the perfect reward-body (*pūrṇa-sambhogakāya*) and dwells in the land of True Reward and Non-obstruction, entering the Perfectly Pure Nirvāṇa. This...
Although the stages of Buddhahood differ among the three teachings, in essence, none have reached ultimate perfection.

Only the Perfect Buddha of the present has exhausted the forty-two grades of ignorance, entered the stage of Subtle Enlightenment (*sūkṣmasaṃbodhi*), and realized that all phenomena do not arise and that *prajñā* does not arise.

This non-arising of non-arising is called Great Nirvāṇa. Taking empty space as his seat, he has perfected the pure *dharmakāya* and dwells in the Light of Constant Quiescence (*nityapraśāntaprakāśa*).
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "In this manner, through successive layers of the twelve [stages], both single and double, one exhausts the wondrous enlightenment and achieves the Unsurpassed Way.
It also says: "Entering the ocean of wondrous adornment, one perfects Bodhi. Third, regarding that which is attained and that which is unattained:

Regarding the first three teachings: because they do not understand that birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and afflictions (*kleśa*) are themselves awakening (*bodhi*) and nirvāṇa, one must eliminate birth-and-death and afflictions in order to realize the new attainment of nirvāṇa and awakening; therefore, upon reaching the stage of fruition, it appears as if there is something to be gained.
Now, for the person of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanren*) in this sutra, since they already know that birth-and-death and afflictions are themselves nirvāṇa and awakening, then birth-and-death—
Because afflictions (*kleśa*) are not "old," they are not old; because Nirvāṇa and Bodhi are "new," they are not new.

Thus, if they are not old, even while remaining within saṃsāra and affliction, what is there to lose? Therefore it is said: "The aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha.
If they are not new, even upon realizing Nirvāṇa and Bodhi, what is there to gain? Therefore it is said: "Perfectly complete."
Enlightenment returns to non-attainment; this is called the ultimate consummation of the fruit (*phala-paryavasāna*).
Regarding the eighth, the ultimate consummation of the teaching (*deśanā-paryavasāna*): the teaching serves as the means of expression (*vyañjaka*).

Since it possesses no separate essence or characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), the seven kinds of ultimate consummations previously analyzed are already included within this ultimate consummation of the teaching. However, although their distinct characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) are manifest, [they are subsumed] under the general...
As these characteristics have not yet been fully understood, three further points are established to clarify them: first, whether the seven factors are complete or incomplete;
second, whether the seven factors are all perfected or not all perfected; third, whether the path of teaching is dispensable or indispensable. Regarding the first point:

these seven meanings are distributed throughout the Tathāgata’s entire career of teaching, across both the Great and Small Vehicles, as well as the partial and perfect teachings. Within the various sutras, they may appear...
There are those that are complete and those that are incomplete. Now, among the seven meanings, those cited above are the most complete.

Next, regarding those that are both perfect and not both perfect: sometimes all seven are perfect, which is the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*); when the seven are partial and small, this is the Prior Teaching (*qianjiao*).

Sometimes the prior is partial and the subsequent is perfect, which is the Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*). Or it may be the Perfect connecting to the Prior, the Distinct, and the Separate; or it may be the prior and the subsequent...
When both [aspects] are complete, they are provisionally designated by one or two partial names; this is the intent behind the Round Teaching’s use of borrowed names.

For instance, within the stages of realizing the first and third fruits as appropriate for the occasion in this sutra, it borrows the name of the "Stage of Dry Wisdom" from the Shared Teaching and the "Four Degrees of Applied Practice" from the Treasury Teaching.
Although these are partial names, their meaning is entirely complete; thus, while the three [partial teachings] may be discarded, they cannot be denied.

Regarding "abandoned": since the seven types of teachings expounded by the three preceding vehicles are not ultimate, they are either abandoned through being rebuked by the Vaipulya (Vaipulya-sūtras) or abandoned through being winnowed out by the Prajñāpāramitā.
If these two [stages] do not abandon them and cause them to turn toward the truth, they must await the opening and revealing of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* before they are abandoned.
If they are not abandoned during the three weeks of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, then they must further be gathered up by the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*.
To pick up and discard [the teaching] is exemplified by the śrāvakas who withdraw from their seats. Furthermore, during the first two periods, one could only discard the person but not the teaching;
even if some discarded it, because their faculties were not yet mature, they soon established it again. It must wait until the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* for its ultimate abandonment.
If this sutra is purely perfect, then within the Vaipulya and Prajñā [periods], it is that which is upheld by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
How much more so, then, could it be sublated? Even the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* itself cannot sublate it. Thus the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* says:

"These people, having heard what I have taught, have entered the Buddha-wisdom," and so forth. Among the four periods [of the Buddha’s teaching], there is nothing that surpasses the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* for providing the complete and perfect integration of the framework of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. This is called the ultimate of the teachings.

The explanation of the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* by way of the sequential arrangement (*pindubhāva*) of the eight dharmas is now complete. Next, the explanation by way of the perfect interpenetration (*yuanrong*) of all characters is as follows:
since the preceding clarification of the eight dharmas has shown them all to be ultimate, the cause transcends the ocean of fruition, and the fruition reaches back to the source of the cause;
thus, wisdom, principle, practice, and stages enter into one another in layers. Therefore, the Dharmakāya, Sambhogakāya, and Nirmāṇakāya Tathāgatas are vast, great, and supreme. This is *śamatha*.

The samādhi-dhyāna is the most supreme among secret causes; entering the ocean of the Tathāgata’s wondrous adornments, one perfects bodhi and returns to non-attainment—this is the most supreme among practices and realizations. With the three types of bodhi, one seeks the Buddha-way above;
with the three types of compassion, one transforms sentient beings below—this is the most supreme among all bodhisattvas. Therein lies samādhi.

It is named the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Śūraṅgama King, which is fully endowed with the myriad practices (*sāhasra-caryā*). These myriad practices are the most vast and supreme. The fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*) is the Dharma-body;
the initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*) constitutes the two virtues (*guṇa*). Since the initial and the fundamental are non-dual, it is the Tathāgata of the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa.

The Middle Way belongs to the nature (*prakṛti*); emptiness and the provisional belong to cultivation (*bhāvanā*). Since cultivation and nature are non-dual, it is the Tathāgata of the Secret Cause. Cultivated evil is...
In its nature, good and evil are non-dual; throughout the six stages of practice, there is nothing that is not immediately the Principle—this is the Tathāgata of cultivation and realization.

The initial aspiration and the ultimate goal are not two distinct things—this is the Tathāgata of all Bodhisattvas. Conditions are themselves the realization of the correct, and the realization of the correct is itself conditions—this is the Tathāgata of the myriad practices.
The secret treasury of the three virtues is like the three eyes of the Lord of Heaven; it is the Great Buddha-Crown.
It is the secret cause (*guhyahetu*). The three—Dharma-body, Reward-body, and Response-body—are like the three dots of the world-character *i*;

this is the secret cause of the Tathāgata. "Afflictions are themselves awakening, and awakening is itself afflictions; the six [sense objects] do not obstruct, and the six [faculties] are not obstructed";

this is the secret cause of cultivation and realization. The Mahāyāna cause is the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) of all phenomena; this is the secret cause of all Bodhisattvas. Therein lies samādhi...

"Attaining" (*ti*) refers to the fulfillment of the ten thousand practices; it is the secret cause of the ten thousand practices. The "True Cause" (*zhengyin*) belongs to the nature (*xing*), while the "Conditioned" (*yuan*) and "Developed" (*liao*) belong to cultivation (*xiu*).
Cultivation arises entirely from nature, and cultivation is entirely contained within nature; this is the cultivation and realization of the Great Buddha-Topknot (*Mahā-uṣṇīṣa*).

"As" (*ru*) is original enlightenment (*benjue*); "come" (*lai*) is initial enlightenment (*shijue*); this is the cultivation and realization of the Tathāgata. The three types of cessation (*zhi*) and the three virtues (*de*) are identical in essence but differ in name. "Cultivation" means cultivating these.

"Realization" refers to realizing this: it is the cultivation and realization of the secret cause. "The nature possesses all dharmas, yet apart from the nature there is no person": this is the cultivation and realization of the Bodhisattvas.

"Original existence" (benyou) is termed "possession" (*ju*); this belongs to the realm of principle (*li*). "Pervasive inclusion" (*gai she*) and "accumulation" (*ji ju*) belong to the realm of phenomena (*shi*).
This is the cultivation and realization of the myriad practices. The subtle and wondrous Three Virtues pervade the ten realms; this is the Bodhi of the Great Buddha-Crown.

The Bodhisattva of the *Sāya* [Samaya] stage is one who fully realizes the fundamental nature of the principle of all beings through the integration of the fruition-ground of all Buddhas; such is the Bodhisattva of the Tathāgata.
The Bodhisattva of the *Miyin* [Secret Cause] stage is one who, through skillful means, accords with conditions and brings cessation to rest within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

The Bodhisattva of the stage of cultivation and realization is one who, neither extinguishing nor arising, merges with the Tathāgatagarbha, wherein the wondrous, sublime awakening shines forth universally to illuminate the entire Dharma-realm. This is the state of that which is originally present.
One who possesses the nature and is endowed with the ten realms is a Bodhisattva of myriad practices. The three kinds of endowment are precisely the three virtues;
these are the myriad practices of the Great Buddha-Crown. Furthermore, there is one practice which is the practice of the Tathāgata;

though it is a single practice, it encompasses five practices—these are the myriad practices of the Tathāgata. There is samādhi that fully embodies the myriad practices; this is the myriad [practices] of the secret cause.

It is practice. Before entering the stages (*bhūmi*), one practices them perfectly; upon entering the stages, one realizes them perfectly. These are the myriad practices of cultivation and realization.
They are the ocean of Samantabhadra’s vows, the adornment of the myriad practices, and the myriad practices of all Bodhisattvas. The subtle and profound purport of the *Śūraṅgama* is such as this;
no teaching of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) surpasses it. Therefore, it is called "The Great Buddha-Crown, the Tathāgata’s Secret Cause, the Definitive Meaning of Cultivation and Realization."
The *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*, the foremost among the myriad practices of all Bodhisattvas—this concludes the explanation of its specific name.

Next, regarding the explanation of its general name: it is the single character "sūtra. In Sanskrit, it is called *sūtra*. Regarding the traditional Chinese translations, there are those that provide a literal rendering and those that do not.

There are five meanings—such as "thread" (*sūtra*) and so forth—and each of these is applied to the categories of teaching, practice, and principle to form fifteen meanings, as detailed in the *Miaoxuan*.
Now, I shall briefly explain this in two parts: first, clarifying the essence of the teaching by means of the general and the specific;
second, instructing on the meaning of the sūtra by means of their mutual substitution. Regarding the first point, the *Shenbao ji* states: "The sūtra is that by which the Sage provides instruction.

Through this instruction, one awakens to the Way; thus, there is both the general and the specific. The general refers to the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, wherein all six sense objects are [the teaching]."
Because it constitutes the substance of the teaching, the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa* states: "To bestow a single meal upon all beings—those who are equal regarding food are also equal regarding the Dharma;
those who are equal regarding the Dharma are also equal regarding food. This, then, takes exclusively that which is encountered by the faculty of the tongue as the sūtra.
In some lands, one may attain the Way simply by the touch of celestial robes upon the body; these take the sense-object of touch as their primary teaching.
Or, one may attain the Way by seeing the Buddha’s radiance; these take the sense-object of form as their primary teaching. Or, one may attain the Way through silent contemplation of the mind;

these take the sense-object of mind as their primary teaching. Just as in the Land of Universal Fragrance, where fragrances perform the work of the Buddha, these take fragrance as their primary teaching.

Fragrance serves as a sūtra. This is because the faculties and consciousnesses of those from other realms are sharp and keen; thus, they are able to take all six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) as sūtras.
Furthermore, if one extends this principle broadly, each and every sense object possesses the six faculties, and each and every faculty possesses the six sense objects.
Throughout the entire *dharmadhātu*, every faculty and every sense object can serve as an entryway into the Way; there is nothing that is not a sūtra. Even if... [the teaching]...

The external separate transmission of the essential mind reaches the point where there is neither speech nor words; yet, that which is a single dharma whether it accords with the mind or does not accord with the mind is itself the body of the teaching.
Where, then, and what dharma constitutes the "separate transmission"? Were it not for a profound insight into this principle, [one could not understand].

It is difficult to express this fully with pen and tongue. Regarding the second distinction: in other lands, the six sense-faculties and consciousnesses are sharp, so all six sense-objects may serve as the Sūtra.

In this land, however, only three faculties and consciousnesses are sharp; thus, only visible forms, sounds, and mental objects (dharmas) serve as the Sūtra. Concerning sound serving as the Sūtra, the *Miaoxuan* states:
"For example, when the Buddha was in the world, he expounded the teachings from his golden mouth; there were only sounds that explained and analyzed for those who listened."
One attains the Way; therefore, sound is taken as the sūtra. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "That which is heard from a spiritual friend.

Using form as the sūtra means that while when the Buddha was in the world sound could serve as the sūtra, now that the Buddha has passed away and the teachings are preserved through paper and ink, one should use form as the sūtra.
As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "That which is heard from within the scriptures. Using the Dharma as the sūtra refers to the internal mind.

Contemplating, the mind merges with the Dharma; it does not depend on the instruction of others, nor does it rely on paper and ink. Rather, when the mind itself attains awakening, the Dharma becomes the Sūtra.
Therefore, it is said: "Those who cultivate my Dharma shall realize it through their own knowledge. These three objects of the senses (dharmas) constitute the Sūtra as bestowed upon this land.
Personally, I maintain that using form as the Sūtra is only possible after the [Buddha’s] parinirvāṇa. If sound were the primary Sūtra, [it would have been so from the beginning].
This is not restricted to the Buddha’s era; even now, there are those who do not know written characters yet attain awakening through sound.

Nevertheless, those who can explain [the Dharma] ultimately derive it from material phenomena—namely, paper and ink. Therefore, the Great Master specifically discussed this in reference to the Buddha’s era.

As for the third method, using the Dharma as the sūtra, this may be discussed both during the Buddha’s lifetime and after his parinirvāṇa. Furthermore, these general and specific [distinctions] are indeed...
This statement is made because the *hetuvidyā* (logic) defines the essence of the teaching (*deśanā*).

If both practice and principle were designated as "sūtra," then in this land, the three—sense faculties, objects, and consciousness—would also universally qualify as sūtras. This is as when the twenty-five sages attained realization through the eighteen elements (*dhātu*);
such is the pervasiveness of the sūtra of practice. The *Samantabhadra-dhyāna-sūtra* states: "Vairocana pervades all places; all dharmas..."
There is nothing that is not the Buddha-dharma. The treasury of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is profound, solid, and remote, such that no one can reach it;

this principle pervades all things. Therefore, we know that if one discusses it in terms of the principle of practice, every sense organ and every sensory object throughout the entire dharma-realm may serve as a sūtra.
Next, regarding the definition of "sūtra" (*jing*) by way of its characteristics: in the past, *sūtra* was translated as "sūtra" (*jing*). [The following] opens [the discussion].

Master Shanyun said: "This is not a direct translation; it is merely using this term to replace that one. In this land, what the sages speak is called a *jing* (sūtra), while what the worthies speak is called a *zi* (treatise) or *shi* (history).

In that land, what the sages call a *jing*, the Bodhisattvas call a *lun* (śāstra). Since it cannot be translated, it is appropriate to use this term to replace that one; therefore, it is called a *jing*.
Since this term replaces that one, and since in this land the meaning of *jing* is defined as 'dharma' and 'constancy,' and *dharma* [endures] for ten thousand generations..."

The rules and regulations are constant; thus, for a hundred generations of kings, they have not been altered. The Buddhist scriptures are likewise: neither celestial Māras nor external paths can obstruct or destroy them—this is the constancy of the teaching (*śāsana*).

Being authentic, unmixed, and unsurpassable—this is the constancy of practice (*pratipatti*). Being profoundly still and immovable, with no possibility of divergent paths—this is the constancy of principle (*tattva*).
"In this place, the essence of the true teaching is pure and resides in sound and hearing. This is called [the constancy of the vehicle].

The "Method of Instruction" refers to the single path to *nirvāṇa* taught by the Bhagavans of the ten directions; this is called the "Method of Practice. The nature of the ocean of awakening is clear and perfect;
this clarity and perfection of the nature of awakening is fundamentally subtle and wondrous; this is called the "Method of Principle. The explanation of the names is concluded.
The second major section, "Discerning the Essence," concerns the essence (*tattva*), which is the primary substance.

While the preceding text explained the twenty-odd characters such as "Great Buddha-Crown" (*mahā-uṣṇīṣa*) as the names that express [the meaning], this section now discerns the essence expressed by those names.

This is intended to enable students to catch the fish by means of the trap and discover the essence through the name. The purpose of seeking the name is to forget the name; by discovering the essence, one realizes there is no separate essence apart from it. This...

This is precisely the subtle meaning of the *Shiming* (Explanation of Terms) regarding the clarification of the essence [of the Dharma] within the household of the Buddha. It is divided into three major sections: first, clarifying the universal essence of all sutras;

second, revealing the specific name of this sutra; and third, uniting the specific with the universal. Regarding the first, the universal essence of all sutras, Master Tiantai cites the *Śāstra* (Treatise), which states:
"Except for the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, everything else is the work of Māra. Mahayana sutras take this true reality as...

The *xiàngyìn* (character-seal) constitutes the primary substance of a sūtra. It is adorned by immeasurable merits, toward which all diverse practices converge, and it is elucidated through discourse and dialogue.
This is like the myriad stars encircling the North Star, or as the ten thousand streams find their source in the Eastern Sea;
therefore, the true mark (*shixiang*) is taken as the substance of the sūtra. Calligraphers and those who explain the rites (*li*) likewise define "substance" (*ti*) in this manner.
In essence, there are distinctions of honor and humility, as well as seniority and juniority. The essence of a sovereign or a father is honorable, while the essence of a minister or a son is humble.
One should know that the explanation of "essence" (*ti*) as "etiquette" (*li*) is a designation for the ultimate pinnacle of nobility. Furthermore, "essence" (*ti*) means "bottom.

To exhaust the source and reach the very bottom, where principles are fully realized within the profound depths, and to thoroughly fathom the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), is what is called the "bottom. The *Śāstra* states: "The great ocean of the *Prajñāpāramitā* is exhausted only by the Buddha."
Therefore, "bottom" (*di*) is used to explain "essence" (*ti*). Furthermore, "essence" has the meaning of "penetration.

When one attains this essence, the mind penetrates without obstruction, just as wind moving through space encounters no impediments whatsoever. All various names and distinct explanations do not contradict the true mark (*dharmatā*).
As the *Śāstra* says: "Prajñā is a single dharma; the Buddha speaks of it by various names. Therefore, [it is so explained].
"Realizing the essence" refers to the essence of the commentary on the sūtra. Next, regarding the specific titles of this sūtra:

although all Mahāyāna sūtras generally take *tathatā* (the true mark) as their primary essence, the essence of *tathatā* is pervasive and universally receives various names. Thus, the *Śāstra* states:
"Prajñā is a single dharma, yet the Buddha speaks of it under various names. If one can establish these various names based upon *tathatā*, then [the name]...
There is nothing that is not perfect; its meaning is entirely real. Therefore, Siming said: "Vairocana pervades all places;

there are no phenomena that are not the Buddha-dharma. Thus, from the two deaths and five abodes of the mundane and supramundane worlds, up to the *vairūḍhaka* hell, crawling insects, flying creatures, and those in the five *ānantarya* hells—whether cause or effect—all are none other than the ultimate, supreme primary truth (*paramārtha*).
Therefore, all these names are real and not false. Even the five abodes and two deaths are merely different names for the true aspect (*dharmatā*);

how much more so, then, could names such as the "limit of reality" (*bhūtakoṭi*) not be the true aspect? Thus, when Tiantai explains the essence of various Mahāyāna sūtras, he sometimes also analyzes them by means of their specific names;
for example, in the *Guanyin xuán*, he defines the essence as the union of numinous wisdom with the Dharma-body. Light...

"Clarifying the Profound takes the dharma-nature as its essence," and so forth. Now, regarding the essence of this present sutra, between these two pillars of the general and the specific, to which must it ultimately belong?
Among those of antiquity who followed the Tiantai teachings in their exegesis of this sutra, there were no fewer than ten or more schools.

Among those who have examined the fivefold profound meaning (*wǔzhòng xuányì*) established [herein], we find only Master Yuán of Gūshān’s *Sūtra Commentary* and Master Yuè of Wǔxīng’s *Explanation of the Title*.
As for Gūshān, he takes the eternally abiding true mind as the essence (*tǐ*); as for Wǔxīng, he takes the empty Tathāgatagarbha as the essence.
Although the Jing and Wei rivers are thus clearly distinguished and the orchids and hawthorns vie in their splendor, regarding that which lies between them...

Whether one adopts the partial or the orthodox interpretation may still be subject to discussion. For instance, Gushan takes the eternally abiding true mind as the essence [of this teaching], asserting that at the very beginning of the main body of this sutra, the Buddha told Ānanda: "You should know that the cycle of birth and death continues for all sentient beings."
All this arises from not knowing the eternally abiding true mind, the essence that is inherently pure and luminous, yet employing various false thoughts.

Because these thoughts are not true, there is cyclic existence. Nevertheless, it is upon this [true mind] that [the teaching] is established; thus, one grasps the correct substance of the sutra. However, one should not say:

"Since the sutra text explicitly states 'eternally abiding true mind, inherently pure and luminous essence,' how could one not take this as the substance? [For the text refers to the essence of the mind, not the substance of the sutra.]

Now I say: if one were to establish something as a "substance" (tǐ) simply because its substance is explicitly mentioned, then there are numerous instances throughout the sutra where "substance" is so stated.

For example, the first fascicle says: "The beginningless bodhi and nirvana have as their fundamental substance primordial purity. The second fascicle says: "It is fundamentally the wondrously pure and luminous substance of bodhi," and further:
"Its nature is truly the wondrously enlightened and luminous substance. All of these are explicit statements from the sutra text.

Regarding its essence: why discard that [the *tathāgatagarbha*] and adopt only this? Wu-xing takes the empty *tathāgatagarbha* as the essence because the *tathāgatagarbha* is the preeminent theme of this sutra.

If one were to establish what is the preeminent theme of a sutra as its essence, then throughout the beginning and end of this single sutra, there is nothing but the expression of the eternal essence and the eternal principle. Thus, it is eternally abiding.
Discussions regarding the true mind are particularly abundant; how could one obscure its meaning by focusing solely on the words?
One must understand that the permanently abiding true mind is precisely the empty *tathāgatagarbha*. As the Sūtra says:

"Although the seven designations, such as the 'empty *tathāgatagarbha*,' differ from one another, their pure and perfect essential nature is firm and solid like a diamond-king, eternally abiding and indestructible. This is it.
It is so. Thus we know that if one takes the permanent mind as the essence (*tattva*), both name and meaning are correct. This permanently abiding essence is pervasive and encompasses all things;

it now simultaneously incorporates the views of both schools, precisely taking the permanently abiding true mind as the essence, while secondarily adopting the textual explanations of the *Tathāgatagarbha* to clarify its meaning.
There are several intentions behind taking the permanently abiding true mind as the essence; the first is that it is at the very beginning of the Sūtra.
First, as stated at the very beginning of the sutra: "Because all sentient beings do not know the eternally abiding true mind, the nature of pure clarity.

Second, this is a prominent theme throughout the sutra; from the examination of the unshakability of vision through the finger-snap and the flying light, to the observation that the vision of the river does not shift with age—even up to the fourth fascicle—it clarifies the eternally abiding true mind. Third, by means of wisdom...
Verification through the Truths (*satya*). This essence is the dharma of the Tathāgata’s wondrous wisdom that exhaustively reaches the ultimate.

Since it is said, "I unite my wondrous clarity—which is neither extinguished nor born—with the Tathāgata-garbha, and am thus able to exhaustively reach the ultimate," and since this is that which is constantly reached to its ultimate limit, how could it not be eternal?
Fourth, verification of the essence by means of the doctrine (*siddhānta*). This essence is that to which the doctrine returns; if the doctrine is eternal, the essence should likewise be so.

Regarding "Permanence" (*nitya*): A sutra states, "If, during the stage of the causal ground, one takes a mind subject to arising and ceasing as the fundamental practice for seeking a fruit that is neither born nor extinguished, such a thing is impossible.
Since the principle of cause and effect must necessarily be eternally abiding, how could the essence to which one returns not be permanent?

Furthermore, the reasons for the practitioner’s arousal of the aspiration and their subsequent practice possess the three meanings of being perfect, pervasive, and constant; thus, permanence is especially required.
It abides with the true mind as its substance. Regarding the explanation of the text of the *Tathāgatagarbha* by taking it in a comprehensive sense:
the eternally abiding true mind is the universal substance of all phenomena (*dharmas*). Apart from this eternal mind, there are no phenomena to be discussed;
likewise, apart from all phenomena, there is no eternal mind to be discussed. Therefore, the Sūtra says: "The Tathāgata constantly teaches that all phenomena are manifested solely by the mind. All...
The world of cause and effect, with its subtle atoms, takes form through the mind. Furthermore, it is said:
"I have always taught that all conditions of form and mind, as well as the mental factors and all objects of perception, are manifested solely by the mind.

Your bodies and your minds are all things manifested within the wondrously bright, true essence of the wondrous mind. Why, then, do you neglect and lose this fundamentally wondrous, perfectly wonderful, and luminous mind?"

The wondrous nature of the jewel-like clarity is to be deluded within awakening. It is further said: "This seeing and its objects are all the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence of bodhi" (and so forth).

This is truly because the true mind of the ultimate reality (*dharmatā*) is fully endowed with all phenomena (*dharma*). Since all phenomena are such by their very nature (*dharmatā*), their nature is fundamentally unarisen.

Therefore, in the *Tathāgatagarbha-sūtra*, the eternally abiding and wondrously luminous nature is extensively elucidated through the analysis of the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*).
The meaning of "immovable and all-pervading" is difficult to comprehend unless one is fully endowed with the realization that the nature of all dharmas is fundamentally non-arising.

Nevertheless, while the texts of the four categories are voluminous, their meaning remains somewhat general and concise; only the text on the seven elements fully elucidates the meaning of the eternally abiding true mind.
This is what is meant by: "the nature of form is true emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is true form; it is pure."
This is precisely what is meant by "naturally pervading the Dharma-realm. To be "constant" means to transcend the three periods of time vertically, being neither born nor extinguished.
To be "abiding" means to span the ten directions of space horizontally, being neither departing nor arriving. To be "true" means that its essential nature is pure and untainted by delusion.
Now, when it is said to be "pure and naturally pervading the Dharma-realm," this purity is itself the purity of the essential nature.
It is not subject to false defilement. Being "primordially thus" means it vertically exhausts the three periods of time; it is neither born nor extinguished.

Being "all-pervasive throughout the dharma-realm" means it horizontally spans the ten voids; it neither goes nor comes. Since this is so for the one great element, the same applies to the other elements.
By using the latter to verify the former, the four categories—namely, the "permanently abiding, wondrously luminous," and so forth—can likewise be understood.

Regarding the text on the seven elements (*mahābhūta*): the first four are distinguished in relation to emptiness, stating, "the nature of form is true emptiness; the nature of emptiness is true form," and so forth.
The fifth, the element of space, is distinguished in relation to awakening, stating, "the nature of awakening is true emptiness; the nature of emptiness is true awakening.

The sixth, the element of seeing, is distinguished in relation to the clarity of awakening, stating, "the nature of seeing is the clarity of awakening; the essence of the clarity of awakening is true seeing."

Furthermore, the great seventh consciousness is distinguished in contrast to the "clear knowing" (ming zhi). It is said: "The nature-consciousness is clear knowing; it is the awakened clarity, the true consciousness.

Why is it that these contrasting distinctions are explained differently? Answer: This arises because sentient beings, from time immemorial, have been deluded regarding true awakening and have taken it to be the root-consciousness.

They confine themselves within the internal body while neglecting external objects; they distinguish between the great and the small by confronting emptiness and form. As the sutra says: [as cited in the *Awakening of Faith*].

What is called "dark obscurity" is emptiness becoming obscured; within this dark obscurity, darkness coalesces to form matter. Matter mixes with deluded thoughts, and these thoughts and their appearances combine to form a body.
Gathering conditions, it stirs inwardly; rushing outward, it scatters wildly. This state of turbid confusion is taken as the nature of the mind.
Once deluded, one takes this as the mind and becomes certain that it resides within the physical body, unaware that it extends beyond the body to the mountains, rivers, and empty space.
The entire great earth is, in truth, a thing within the wondrously luminous true mind.

It would be like casting aside hundreds of thousands of clear, vast oceans and instead recognizing only the substance of a single bubble, taking that to be the entirety of the tide and exhausting the whole expanse of the sea.

Out of compassion for such people, the Tathāgata intends to provide a finger-pointing to dispel their delusion so they may immediately awaken; therefore, he must lead them from the shallow toward the deep, first using the boundless void.
This passage contrasts emptiness with the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) that possess boundaries; thus, it is expressed through a series of dialectical exchanges. It states:

"The nature of form is true emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is true form," continuing up to "the nature of wind is true emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is true wind. The reason for this is as follows:

the form of the earth element possesses a solid substance and occupies a specific location, whereas empty space is pervasive and interfused, and therefore lacks any fixed location. This applies likewise to water and fire.
The wind-element is subject to agitation and thus possesses arising and ceasing. Space is eternally constant and therefore free from agitation.
Wherever there is arising and ceasing, coming and going, there is delusion; because it is devoid of arising and ceasing, coming and going, its nature is truly perfect and harmonious.
Now it is said: "The nature of form is true emptiness; the nature of emptiness is true form. This means that the nature of emptiness is form, and form is also the nature of emptiness;
true form is also truly [empty]. Form and emptiness are fundamentally without distinction. Therefore, within the fifth section on the Great Element of Space, it is harmonized by saying:
"If this empty space is perfect, pervasive, and fundamentally unmoving, you should know that the earth and water presently before you..."
Fire and wind are likewise named among the five great elements; their nature is truly perfect and harmonious. All are the Tathāgatagarbha, fundamentally free from arising and ceasing.
