Ānanda, your mind is deluded and confused, failing to realize that the four great elements are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha. You should contemplate whether space emerges or enters, or whether it neither emerges nor enters.
In this way, the four great elements and space are equally and eternally abiding; though their appearances seem different, their nature is one.
Fundamentally they are one. There is nothing that is not pure by nature and all-pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm; is it not fitting to call this "Great"?
Furthermore, although the permanence and pervasiveness of form and emptiness are fused, the non-differentiation of body and environment has not yet been realized.

Moreover, within the passage on the Great Emptiness, it says: "The nature of true awakening is emptiness; the emptiness of nature is true awakening. As for what is called "awakening," speaking generally...

These refer to the sense organs (*indriya*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*). The reason they are distinguished by contrasting emptiness and awareness is that the organs and consciousness possess awareness, whereas empty space lacks awareness.
While this is the case regarding phenomena (*dharma*), it is not so in terms of ultimate principle (*tattva*). Therefore, I have discussed this back and forth, saying:

"The nature of awareness is true emptiness; the nature of emptiness is true awareness. This is like saying that the nature of awareness is emptiness, and [the nature of] emptiness is also [awareness].
Awakening is also truly empty, for emptiness and awakening are fundamentally no different from one another. In the section on "Seeing the Great," it is harmonized and explained thus:

"If the nature of seeing, hearing, and knowing is perfect, pervasive, and fundamentally unmoving, you should know that boundless empty space, along with its movements, and earth, water, fire, and wind—all are equally called the six great elements whose natures are truly perfect and interfused; they are all the Tathāgata."
In the Treasury [of the Dharma], there is neither arising nor ceasing. This means that the sense organs and consciousnesses are equal to space.

Not only is space not insentient, but earth, water, fire, and wind are likewise not insentient. Since space is equal to the sense organs and consciousnesses, not only is space eternal and pervasive, but the sense organs and consciousnesses are also eternal and pervasive.
Is it not therefore appropriate to call them "Great"? Furthermore, regarding the internal and external...

Since the body and its objects have already been shown to be perfectly interfused, yet emotional attachments to the two paths of truth and falsehood still persist like those between a crown and shoes, [the text] further states within the two major sections on "Vision" (*dṛṣṭi*) and "Cognition" (*vijñāna*):
"The nature-vision is the clarity of awareness; the clarity of awareness is the essence of awareness; the essence of awareness is the clarity of vision.

The nature-cognition is the knowing clarity; the knowing clarity is true cognition. The nature-vision and the clarity-vision are the pure six sense-faculties. The clarity of awareness and the essence of awareness are sentient beings."

The six are the faculties of reception (*vedanendriya*). Nature-consciousness and true-consciousness refer to the eighth and ninth consciousnesses (*vijñāna*). Clear knowledge and awakening-knowledge refer to the sixth and seventh consciousnesses.

All of these are the total substance giving rise to function, and the total function abiding within the substance; therefore, they are discussed through mutual interplay. For this reason, an ancient master said:
"According to the gate of the various consciousnesses, although the one and the many are not fixed, all are the dependent origination of substance and function."
Root and branch mutually encompass one another. From the root toward the branches, it is quiescent yet constantly active; from the branches toward the root, it is active yet constantly quiescent.
Because it is quiescent yet constantly active, it is still without stagnation. Because it is active yet constantly quiescent, it is moving without confusion.
Because it is still without stagnation, suchness is dependent origination. Because it is moving without confusion, dependent origination is suchness. Suchness...
Because this is dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), there is neither nirvāṇa nor saṃsāra; thus, the eighth and ninth [consciousnesses] become the sixth and seventh.
Because dependent origination is suchness (*tathatā*), there is neither saṃsāra nor nirvāṇa; thus, the sixth and seventh [consciousnesses] become the eighth and ninth.
Because there is neither nirvāṇa nor saṃsāra, the entire dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is saṃsāra. Because there is neither saṃsāra nor nirvāṇa, the entire dharma-realm is nirvāṇa (and so forth).

Since consciousness is thus, the sense organs are likewise so. How could it be only the six organs? Indeed, the aforementioned five great elements (pañca-mahābhūta) are such that their essence and function are mutually identical.
This is because the three realms are mind-only and all things are consciousness-only. Therefore, within the section on the element of consciousness, it is harmonized as follows:
"If this conscious mind originally has no source from which it arises, one should know that its discernment of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing is perfect."
The pervasive, profound nature does not arise from external conditions; together with space, earth, water, fire, and wind, these are equally termed the "Seven Great Elements.
Their nature is truly perfect and harmonious; all are the Tathāgatagarbha, fundamentally devoid of arising or ceasing. Indeed, when the true permanence of all dharmas is thus perfectly realized.

Is it not fitting to call this "Great"? Therefore, when the Sage’s words reach this point, the elucidation of principle is exhaustive; the deluded attachments of those present are instantly dissolved.

Thus, the Sūtra records that Ānanda and the great assembly, having received the subtle and wondrous instruction of the Buddha-Tathāgata, found their bodies and minds cleared away, attaining freedom from all obstructions. Each member of the great assembly then came to know their own mind for themselves.
Pervading the ten directions, one sees the emptiness of the ten directions as clearly as observing a leaf held in one’s hand.

All things that exist within all worlds are none other than the wondrously luminous, primordial mind of Bodhi. This essence of mind is all-pervasive and perfect, encompassing and enveloping the ten directions.
When one looks back at this body born of one's parents, it is like a single mote of dust blown into the void of those ten directions—barely existing.
If it were to perish, it would be like a single bubble rising and ceasing upon a vast, still ocean, leaving no trace of its origin or destination.

One clearly knows for oneself that one has attained the fundamental, wondrous mind, which is eternally abiding and indestructible. (Text) Contemplating this wondrous awakening and verifying it against the previously explained perfect teaching, one not only perceives the profound mystery of the interpenetration of the *tathāgatagarbha* nature, but also comes to know the wondrous excellence of the inherent nature of the Sūtra’s essence. This is because all that has been proclaimed thus far clarifies only...
Regarding the nature of the *tathāgatagarbha*, even if one wishes to examine its permanence in detail, it must still be sought through its meaning. Now, in this account of awakening, it is stated:
"All things that exist in the world are themselves the wondrously luminous, primordial mind of bodhi. Furthermore, at the conclusion of the text, it says again:

"One attains the original, wondrous mind, which is eternally abiding and indestructible. Is this not because the true, eternally abiding mind is inherently endowed with all phenomena? It is precisely this.
The nature of all phenomena is fundamentally non-arising; yet it is called the eternally abiding true mind, the essence of pure and luminous nature.

Therefore, the substance of this present sutra is universal and perfect in its meaning. That which was previously described as "dualistically encompassing the meanings of both schools" is also seen here.
Question: While it is indeed so that the principle of the eternally abiding True Mind is thus, can this be demonstrated by examining actual phenomena? Answer:
Although the three—sense organs, sense objects, and consciousness—are in principle eternally abiding, it is difficult to point them out definitively when examining actual phenomena.

This is truly because sentient beings have followed their karma for so long that the distinction between the subjective mind and the objective world has become firmly established; even the various organs such as the nose and tongue do not compare to those of oxen or horses, let alone the six sense objects.
Now, if we select from among those currently available for discourse that which is most easily accessible according to the Dharma, it is simply the faculty of hearing and the faculty of sight.

These may perhaps serve as a semblance [of the teaching]. Although it is said that the visual faculty illuminates what is before it but not what is behind, and lacks half of the four directions, when one contemplates the nature of seeing (*darśana-svabhāva*), it is profoundly clear;
yet even regarding the principle of non-extinction and non-arising, it still does not require [external mediation].
In leisurely seclusion, he discerned that this [faculty] seems to surpass even the faculty of hearing. Now, I shall extract its essential points and explain them.

As the Sūtra states: after first using the metaphor of a blind man staring into darkness to show that seeing is not the eye, the Tathāgata, intending to reveal to Ānanda this ground of non-arising and non-ceasing, first inquired regarding the meaning of adventitious defilements (*āgantuka-kleśa*), saying: "When I first attained the Way..."

"In the Deer Park, for the sake of Ājñāta-kauṇḍinya, the five bhikṣus, and you fourfold assembly, I declared that all sentient beings fail to achieve the state of Bodhi and Arhat solely because they are deluded by adventitious afflictions (*āgantuka-kleśa*).
By what means did you then attain awakening and now achieve this holy fruit? At that time, Kauṇḍinya rose and addressed the Buddha: "I have now [attained] long..."
Among the great assembly, you alone have attained the name of "Understanding. Because of your realization of the two characters "guest" (*āgantuka*) and "dust" (*rajas*), you have achieved fruition.

World-Honored One, it is like a traveler who stays at an inn, either to sleep or to eat. Once the tasks of sleeping and eating are finished, he packs his bags for the road ahead and no longer dwells there.
If one is the actual host, they have no need to go anywhere. Reflecting in this way, that which does not abide is called a "guest" (*āgantuka*). It abides [only] temporarily.
It is called the "host. That which does not abide is defined by the meaning of being a "guest. Furthermore, it is like when the clear sun rises after a fresh clearing of the weather;
its light enters through a crack in a wall, illuminating the various forms of dust within the void. The substance of the dust wavers and moves, yet empty space remains tranquil.

Reflecting upon this, that which is limpid and still is called "space," while that which wavers and moves is called "dust. Thus, that which wavers and moves is defined by the meaning of being "dust. The Buddha...
"So be it" (evam). (Text) What Kauṇḍinya said refers to the adventitious dust (*āgantuka-rajas*), which is a metaphor for the dharmas of afflictions that arise and perish.
The host and the space are metaphors for the unarisen, undying, eternally abiding true mind (*akṣara-tathatā-citta*).
Since Kauṇḍinya’s answer was already perfectly clear, this could directly illustrate the meaning of the adventitious dust and the host-space to Ānanda. Therefore, the Sūtra says:
At that moment, the Tathāgata, amidst the great assembly, bent his five fingers, having bent them he opened them, and having opened them he bent them again, saying to Ānanda:
"What do you see now? Ānanda replied: "I see the Tathāgata’s palms, adorned with the hundred jewels, opening and closing amidst the assembly.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "What you see as my hands opening and closing amidst the assembly—is it that my hands possess [this power]?"

[The Buddha asked: "There is opening and closing. Is it your seeing that has opening and closing? Ānanda replied, "World-Honored One, the precious hands [of the Buddha] open and close within this assembly.
I see the Tathāgata’s own hands opening and closing; it is not my faculty of seeing that has opening and closing. The Buddha said, "What moves and what is still?
Ānanda replied, "The Buddha’s hands do not remain still, but as for my faculty of seeing, it does not even possess stillness—how much less could it move?"
"It is for the sake of non-abiding. The Buddha said, "It is so. Thereupon, the Tathāgata emitted a single jewel-light from the palm of his wheel-marked hand, which hovered to Ānanda’s right;
immediately, Ānanda turned his head to look to the right. He then emitted another light to Ānanda’s left, and Ānanda again turned his head to look to the left.
The Buddha asked Ānanda, "For what reason is your head shaking today? Ānanda replied:
"It is difficult to say. I saw the Tathāgata emit wondrous jewel-light coming from my left and right; because of this, I looked left and right and my head moved of its own accord.
Ānanda, when you gaze at the Buddha’s light and your head moves left and right, is it your head that moves, or is it what you see that moves?"
“World-Honored One, my head moves of its own accord, yet my nature of seeing has no cessation; what, then, could cause it to shake? The Buddha said, “It is so.
(Text) Ānanda’s answer, “I see the Tathāgata’s hand opening and closing,” refers to the meaning of the adventitious.

His statement, “It is not that my nature of seeing opens and closes,” refers to the meaning of the permanent. His statement, “My head moves of its own accord,” refers to the meaning of the defilement. Yet his...
Since the nature of seeing itself has no stillness, what could cause it to shake? This is the meaning of emptiness.
Having thus attained an intimate and direct realization, the Tathāgata then addressed the great assembly, saying:
"If sentient beings were to call that which shakes 'dust' and that which does not abide 'a guest,' then you should observe that while Ānanda’s head moves, his seeing does not."
Furthermore, observe my hand as it opens and closes; you see no expansion or contraction there. Why, then, do you now take motion to be the body and motion to be the object?
From beginning to end, moment by moment, you arise and perish, losing the true nature and acting in delusion. Consider this:
when you observe Ānanda’s head moving of its own accord, is that not an external object (*dharma*)? Your vision itself remains unmoving.
Is it not empty? When the Tathāgata’s hand opens and closes of its own accord, is it not a guest? That Ānanda sees neither expansion nor contraction—is this not the host?
Thus, the meaning of the host and emptiness being without birth or extinction applies to Ānanda; since it is so for him, it is surely inherent in all people.
One should truly realize the true permanence through this very state of non-movement. Why, then, do you now take movement to be [the self]?
The body takes movement as its object; from beginning to end, it arises and perishes moment by moment.
Thus one loses the true nature and acts in delusion. Furthermore, a body that moves is not the true body, and an environment that moves is not the true environment.
Yet people today take this as their body and take this as their environment; this is what is called losing the true nature of the mind and mistaking external objects for the self.

Within this cycle of saṃsāra, one takes up the flow for oneself. In this passage and those that follow, King Aṅga’s vision of the river—his reaching down to grasp it without fail—is entirely a clear manifestation of the meaning that the nature of seeing is neither born nor extinguished.

However, although the subsequent text uses the king’s vision of the river over sixty years to verify its non-transmigration, it still seems somewhat [incomplete] regarding the direct pointing to the meaning of the nature of seeing.
This is too lax. It is better to test for immovability here by counting one’s fingers and observing the flight of light;

this is a matter directly manifest before one’s eyes, and the profound meaning of the eternal abiding is easily grasped. Students should carefully examine this for themselves, rather than imitating the poor who count the wealth of others.
An ancient master said: "This uses coarse appearances as a subtle discourse on true seeing, revealing it through discrimination."
The full details are provided in the subsequent text. These words seem too easy; let the wise examine them.

The sutra continues from here by distinguishing the eight returns, selecting among various objects, and seeing through the ten directions without expansion or contraction, thereby clarifying that the nature of vision is all-pervasive.
The Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī and the great assembly: "The Tathāgatas and great Bodhisattvas of the ten directions..."
While abiding in his own samādhi, he saw that the seer, the objects of seeing, and the characteristics of what is conceived are like flowers in the sky—fundamentally non-existent.
This seeing and its objects are originally the pure, wondrous, and luminous essence of bodhi. How could there be such things as "is" or "is not" within them?
This is the true purity of the nature of seeing. However, the wondrous constancy of the nature of seeing must necessarily...
It is universally and necessarily pure; however, it is not manifested all at once. Therefore, there is this sequential great return.

From the first fascicle, beginning with "The blind man gazes into darkness," through the second fascicle, which distinguishes that the nature of seeing is neither conjoined nor disjoined—all of these clarify the meaning of the nature of seeing as eternally abiding and truly pure.
This is because the nature of seeing is transparently luminous and thus easily pointed out directly. As for the faculty of hearing, if it were constant...
The meaning of abiding in true purity is fully elucidated in the sixth fascicle. In the verse where Mañjuśrī selects the perfect penetration, it says: "When sound exists, it is not born;
when sound is absent, it is not extinguished—this is the truth of permanence. This refers to the nature of hearing being neither born nor extinguished.
"When drums are struck throughout the ten directions, they are heard simultaneously in all ten places—this is the truth of pervasiveness. This refers to the nature of hearing being omnipresent.
It is all-pervasive. One can hear sounds through walls, whether they are distant or near; this is the reality of penetration, which is the true purity of the nature of hearing.
All of these points use the delusions of ordinary beings regarding phenomena to point toward the realization of principle.

If a practitioner can take this constant pervasiveness as a basis and expand upon it, their spiritual power will deepen and their virtuous capacity will increasingly excel. This is the subtle essence of the sutra’s substance.
It does not exceed what is seen and heard. As the Sūtra says: "If one can transform objects, one is identical to the Tathāgata.

With body and mind perfectly luminous, unmoving from the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), one manifests jeweled-king lands upon the tip of a single hair, universally containing and receiving all the lands of the ten directions."
This is its proof. Third, regarding the distinction between the specific and the general:

while various sutras generally take the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena as their primary essence, this present sutra specifically takes the eternally abiding true mind as its essence. Although the names differ, the meaning is no different.
As stated in the long passage of the "Expedient Means" chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*: "Only Buddhas and Buddhas can thoroughly exhaust the nature of all phenomena."
The true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). A verse states: "This Dharma abides in its own place; the characteristics of the world are eternally constant.

The "characteristics of the world" refer to all phenomena (*dharmas*), and "eternally constant" refers to the true mark. Now, at the beginning of this sutra, the "ever-abiding true mind" (*nityasthita-bhūtamanas*) is indicated;

in the subsequent text, it is extensively explained that the aggregates, sense bases, and elements are fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha, the wondrous nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*). This corresponds to the "characteristics of the world" in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

The meaning of "constant" (*chang*) is the same [as that of "eternal"]. Therefore, although it takes the eternally abiding true mind as its essence, in meaning it is truly identical to the true mark (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.
This wondrous essence spans horizontally across the ten voids, being neither coming nor going; this is what Tiantai refers to as "essence" (*ti*). Essence has its own ritual propriety (*li*):
the essence of a sovereign or a father is honorable, while the essence of a minister or a son is humble. One should know that essence possesses ritual propriety.
The term "zhī" (之) is a designation for the ultimate in nobility. This wondrous essence vertically exhausts the three periods of time, being neither born nor extinguished;

this is what Tiantai refers to as the meaning of "the fundamental ground" (*di*). To exhaust the source, reach the bottom, fully realize the principle within the profound treasury, and thoroughly penetrate the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*)—this is called "the ground.
This wondrous essence, as its very nature, is pure and undefiled, remaining unstained by delusions. This is what Tiantai... [refers to].

What the Platform Sutra calls "substance" (ti) has the meaning of "penetration. Attaining this substance means that the mind’s intent is thoroughly penetrating and unobstructed, like the wind moving through space, where there is no hindrance whatsoever.
Furthermore, it says: "The Tathāgatagarbha is the fundamentally wondrous, perfect, and round mind—neither mind nor emptiness, and so forth."

"Essence" (ti) refers to the fundamental ground. As it says: "The Tathāgatagarbha is originally luminous; the mind is wondrous—this very mind is emptiness. "Realization" (da) refers to thorough penetration. As it says:
"The Tathāgatagarbha is the wondrously luminous original mind; it is apart from both identity and difference, neither identical nor different. "Veneration" (li) refers to ritual homage.

Furthermore, the Ear-faculty’s Perfect Penetration (er-gen yuan-tong) possesses the three meanings of perfection, penetration, and constancy. "Perfection" (yuan) refers to veneration; "penetration" (tong) refers to realization; and "constancy" (chang) refers to the fundamental ground.
"Substance" (*ti*) refers to the virtue of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). "Foundation" (*di*) refers to the virtue of wisdom (*prajñā*).

"Realization" (*da*) refers to the virtue of liberation (*vimukti*). If these three virtues are correlated with the five chapters: the chapter on "Names" (*ming*) generally presents the characteristics of the teaching of the three virtues;

the chapter on "Substance" specifically pertains to the Dharma-body; the chapter on "Principle" (*zong*) specifically pertains to wisdom; the chapter on "Function" (*yong*) specifically pertains to liberation; and now, the chapter on "Substance" specifically pertains to the Dharma-body.

Regarding the phrase "one who clarifies the fundamental substance and penetrates its essence": as the *Myōshū* states, because emptiness is itself the Middle Way, the virtue of *prajñā* is the foundation of the *dharmakāya*;
because the provisional is itself the Middle Way, the virtue of liberation (*vimukti*) is the essence of sovereign mastery over all phenomena (and so forth).

The third major section, "Clarifying the Essential Tenet" (*zong*), states in the *Miaoxuan*: "The essential tenet is the throat and collarbone of practice; it is the vital path for manifesting the essence (*ti*).
It is like beams and pillars supporting a house, or the main ropes of a net. When the ropes are pulled, the mesh moves; when the beams are secure, the rafters remain.
This is because the essential tenet of cause and effect is the vital point for manifesting the essence of this sutra. This is explained in two parts. First:
Distinguishing the Essential Substance (*tattva*). Second, the correct elucidation of the essential substance. Regarding the distinction between the essential substance and the essence:

the *Miaoxuan* states, "Some say that the essence is the substance and the substance is the essence; this is not accepted here. Why? Since the essential aim (*zongchi*) consists of cause and effect, cause and effect are dual.
The principle-substance (*lititi*) is neither cause nor effect; the substance is non-dual. If the substance were dual, it would not be a substance. The substance...
If the non-dual nature were the thesis (*pakṣa*), then it would not be a thesis; if the thesis were non-dual, then the thesis would not be a thesis.
If the thesis were dual, then the thesis would not be the nature (*tattva*). How then can you say that the nature is the thesis and the thesis is the nature?

Furthermore, the beams and pillars are the structural framework of the house, while the void of the house is that which is occupied by the beams and pillars. One should not [conflate] the beams and pillars with the void of the house, nor the void of the house with the beams and pillars.

Beams and pillars. If the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the essence (*svabhāva*) were one, the fault would be as follows. Furthermore, if the thesis and the essence were different, then the two dharmas would exist in isolation from one another;

the thesis would not be a thesis that reveals the essence, and the essence would not be the essence belonging to the thesis. If the thesis is not a thesis that reveals the essence, it is erroneous and lacks the seal (*mudrā*) of truth.
If the essence is not the essence belonging to the thesis, then the essence is narrow and incomplete. Apart from the *dharmatā*, there would be something else.

Regarding cause and effect: if the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the essence (*svabhāva*) were different, the fault would be as described above. Now, because they are not different yet are different, there is the thesis;

because they are not one yet are one, there is the essence. The *Vyākhyāyukti* (Śāstra on Explanation) states: "Apart from the true nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*), everything else is the work of Māra.
The *Samantabhadra-darśana-sūtra* states: "The cause of the Mahāyāna is the true nature of all phenomena; the fruit of the Mahāyāna is the true nature of all phenomena."
This is precisely its meaning. One should know that the essence of the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) is pervasive and is neither cause nor effect. When practice begins, one distinguishes the cause;
when practice concludes, one discusses the effect. Thus, all Mahāyāna sūtras take the cause and effect of the true mark as their essential core.

Next, to clarify the central tenet: although all Mahāyāna sūtras generally take the real mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) and its causes and effects as their essential core, the substance of these causes and effects is pervasive and universally applicable to various designations, as seen in the *Commentary on the Contemplation Sūtra*.
Therein, the essential core of the sūtra is established as the attainment of the four pure lands through the wondrous contemplation of cultivating the mind;
this wondrous contemplation of cultivating the mind is the cause of the real mark, while the four kinds of pure lands are the [result].

This refers to the fruit of the marks. Now the Sūtra says: "If you wish to cast aside the vehicle of the Śrāvakas, cultivate the Bodhisattva vehicle, and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, you should carefully examine whether the mind generated at the stage of the causal ground is identical to or different from the awakening at the stage of the resultant ground.
If, at the causal ground, you take a mind of arising and ceasing as the fundamental practice for cultivation while seeking the fruit of the Buddha-vehicle—which is neither arising nor ceasing—"
This is impossible. This principle is precisely the same as that in the *Samantabhadra-darśana-sūtra*, wherein both Mahāyāna cause and effect are the true mark (*dharmatā*).

While the general meaning is thus, what is the specific meaning? In the past, Master Yuan of Gushan once judged this sūtra to take the "perfectly penetrating wondrous concentration" as its primary tenet;
this specifically refers to the perfect penetration of the ear-faculty of Avalokiteśvara, while generally encompassing all that is elucidated throughout the entire sūtra.
As for the practice of meditative concentration (samādhi), Master Yunjian took the wondrous samādhi of the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* as his primary tenet.

He maintained that because Ānanda initially requested instruction through the three types of cessation (*nirodha*), the beginning and end of the sutra do not discuss emptiness or the provisional, but rather expound the Middle Way; this, he said, was the essential core of the text.

Now, observing the positions established by these two masters, although both have grasped the underlying intent, they each rely on interpretation rather than the explicit text, and thus neither represents the actual meaning of the sutra.
This is the correct intention (*samyak-saṃkalpa*). This correct intention is precisely the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*jñāna-darśana*).

Taking this as the fundamental principle not only ensures that the encompassing of all phenomena is complete, but the textual meaning is also rendered manifest. As the Tathāgata first declared at the beginning of the sutra:

"The continuous succession of birth and death among all sentient beings is entirely due to their failure to know the eternally abiding true mind, the essence of pure luminosity. [This is] the investigation of the mind...
First, the Tathāgata asked: "Where now are the mind and the eyes? The disciple in turn requested: "Awaken the wondrously luminous mind and open my Dharma-eye.
The Tathāgata granted this, saying: "Enable all sentient beings to obtain the wondrous, subtle, and secret nature-pure, luminous mind, and attain the pure eye.
In the fourth fascicle, he rebukes the ordinary and the small-vehicle practitioners, saying: "Use worldly language to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision."
Ānanda requested to enter the Flower Hall and said, "I have attained the *dhāraṇī* for entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

The Tathāgata replied, "If you wish to cast aside the vehicle of the śrāvaka and cultivate the Bodhisattva vehicle to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, you should carefully examine the mind that was originally aroused at the causal stage.
The fifth fascicle states: "To establish knowing and seeing within knowing and seeing is the very root of ignorance; when knowing and seeing are free from seeing, this is *nirvāṇa*."

In these scriptural passages, found in numerous locations, the essence and function of knowledge and vision (*jñāna-darśana*) are explicitly revealed. Furthermore, "knowledge and vision" is mentioned here as a brief summary;
in full, they necessarily involve the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*). Thus, the Sūtra says: "That which brings you peace, bliss, and wondrous permanence is none other than these six faculties;

it is not some other thing. Since the faculties must encounter their respective objects, and such encounters necessarily give rise to consciousness, the first four fascicles of this Sūtra [discuss this].
The "Clarifying the Substance" section extensively employs the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), elements (*dhātu*), and the seven great elements to clarify the eternally abiding true mind.
The subsequent section, "Clarifying the Source," likewise presents each of the twenty-five sages with a single dharma from within that substance to demonstrate the perfect penetration.

Thus, there are as many as twenty-five sages to illustrate the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Therefore, the Sūtra says: "The Tathāgatas of the ten directions, regarding each of the eighteen realms..."
Through practice, all shall attain the perfection of Bodhi. The meaning of these sutras is entirely intended to elucidate and explain the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*jñāna-darśana*).

Regarding the statement that the encompassing of phenomena is complete: if knowledge and vision are already complete within the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya*), then the ear organ is included therein.
Since it is said that "knowledge and vision are without seeing," this is itself Nirvana; thus, the six sense organs must all universally be *Śūraṅgama*.
Great Samādhi is the foundation; it is called the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Therefore, at the beginning of the *Ānanda Sūtra*, there are two types of requests:

the general and the specific. Later in the text, the Tathāgata likewise provides two types of responses: the general and the specific. From the inquiry into the "mind" (*citta*) up to the "self-realization," these all serve as the response to the general request regarding *śamatha*.
From the request to "enter the jeweled chamber" up to the selection of the "perfect penetration" (*yuan-tong*), these all serve as the response to the specific request.
This is the initial expedient means. However, within the specific response, although the primary intent lies in the particular [instruction], the underlying meaning also encompasses the general.
As stated in the *Two Determinate Meanings for Beginners*: "If you wish to abandon the Śrāvaka [vehicle]... (and so forth).
This intends to lead one to cultivate the Great Samādhi based on the eternally abiding true mind; this is the general meaning. Next, it says: "You all..."
(And so forth). This, then, intends to mean that one should subdue the afflictions by means of the six sense organs; this is a distinct interpretation.
Furthermore, these two definitive meanings correspond to the two preceding fundamental principles.
As it says: "The first is the root of beginningless birth and death, which is the second definitive meaning. The second is the originally pure essence of beginningless bodhi and nirvana."
This is the first definitive determination (*niścaya*). One must know that the meaning elucidated in a single sutra does not transcend two kinds of definitive determinations.
The Tathāgata first established these two fundamental bases; thus, the general purport of the entire sutra has already been presented at the beginning of the first fascicle.
The subsequent textual passages merely elaborate in detail upon the meaning of these two determinations. Furthermore, regarding these two kinds...
The "Fundamental" and the "Definitive" also constitute a comprehensive response to Ānanda’s two requests—the general and the specific.
The first, the "Fundamental," and the second, the "Definitive," answer the specific request; the second, the "Fundamental," and the first, the "Definitive," answer the general request.

The reason why Ānanda necessarily made both the general and specific requests, and why the Tathāgata necessarily provided both the general and specific answers, is that if there were no particularity within the general, [the teaching would lack depth].
Thus, penetration is the gate that has no entry. If particularization were devoid of penetration, then particularization would become a mere practice of phenomenal characteristics.

Just as among worldly people who all possess the six sense faculties, the very act of establishing cognition based on knowledge and vision is the root of ignorance; how could the Buddhas be without the six sense faculties?
To know and see that there is no seeing is itself Nirvana. It is like a person with eyes who, when illuminated by the light of the sun, is able to see various forms and colors.
Question: If the Buddha’s knowledge and vision constitute the primary principle, then what was the purpose of the Buddha’s command to Mañjuśrī to select the faculty of hearing?
Answer: The reason the Buddha commanded Mañjuśrī specifically to select the faculty of hearing is as follows:
Although there are many gates for entering the Way, how could a beginner enter them all? Therefore, one is instructed to penetrate deeply through only a single gate.
Upon entering one gate without delusion, those six cognitive faculties become pure simultaneously. However, within the single gate entered, there must necessarily be a vital point;

if one truly attains this vital point, then compared to those with incomplete faculties, one’s progress will be many times greater over the course of days and eons. This is because the sentient beings of this region [possess...]
The faculties and consciousnesses are dull, with only the ear-faculty being the sharpest.

Therefore, Mañjuśrī, in accordance with the capacities of beings, selected this ear-faculty as the essential gateway for entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision through the "Perfect Penetration of the Ear-Faculty. This does not mean that perfect penetration applies solely to the ear-faculty.

This is analogous to the *Mahā-śraddhotpāda-śāstra* (Mohe Zhiguan), where one who begins their practice must first cultivate the internal mind; thus, among the three categories of phenomena, the "elements" (*dhātu*) are excluded.

One enters [the contemplation]. Furthermore, within the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), one again sets aside the first four and takes the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) as the object of observation.

This is like discarding the *zhang* to focus on the *chi*, or discarding the *chi* to focus on the *cun*; it is like cutting down a tree by reaching its root, or treating an ailment by finding the correct acupuncture point.

Thus, a thousand branches and a hundred ailments naturally wither away. While this is largely the same [as other methods], there is a slight difference. The difference lies in that this contemplation brings the sixth consciousness to completion as the perfect and wondrous Three Truths (*triratna-satya*).

This contemplation enters the perfect penetration by means of the ear-faculty (*śrotra-indriya*). Although the objects of contemplation differ, the principle revealed therein remains one and the same.

Now, the explanation of this selection of the faculty will be divided into two parts. First, the ear-faculty is elucidated by way of correspondence with the capacities of practitioners and through contrastive analysis.

Next, following the principle of non-reliance on opposites, the various objects of perception are clarified. First, following the capacity of sentient beings by relying on opposites, the faculty of hearing is clarified:
"The true essence of the teaching in this land is pure and resides in sound and hearing; those who wish to attain samādhi truly enter through hearing.
Here, "hearing" refers to the faculty of hearing (*śrotra-indriya*). By taking the faculty of hearing as the object of contemplation, one enters into perfect penetration. Thus, Avalokiteśvara—
The self-narration states: "At first, within the midst of hearing, one enters the flow and loses the object.

Now, since the ear-faculty serves as the object, one must ask: how can one contemplate it so as to enter the flow and lose the object? It should be understood that what is clarified here as the "principle" (zong) is the contemplating faculty;

what was previously clarified as the "essence" (ti) is the contemplated object. Contemplation arises based on the object, and the object is manifested through the support of contemplation. Herein, these points are briefly omitted.

Regarding the practice of "entering the stream" (*āyatanapraveśa*), this has already been fully explained in the preceding text. Therefore, the principle of entering the stream involves no other method than this:
at the very outset, within the midst of hearing, one contemplates according to the nature that the fundamental principle of this ear is thus eternally abiding and thus truly pure.
This is precisely what it means to enter the stream. What is called the "stream" is an alternative designation for perfect penetration (*pariṣphuṭa*). To not enter...
If one flows [with the stream], one has already ceased. If one can enter the stream, then one has already eliminated all objects of perception.
This is because the sphere of sound is the sphere of the ear. Thus, any statement that there is a locus for the dust of sound is merely following after sound and wandering through it.

Once one has entered perfect penetration, how could there be any such locus? Question: If one realizes that this faculty of the ear is eternally abiding, truly pure, and authentic, is this not itself entry into perfect penetration?
If that were so, then the triad of faculty, object, and consciousness could all equally enter [the state of permanence]; why, then, is the ear-faculty alone esteemed? Answer:
Although the triad of faculty, object, and consciousness are all eternally abiding, they can only be taken as objects of refuge and faith according to the measure of the Buddha’s correct teaching;

they are truly not within the scope of the cognitive faculties possessed by sentient beings. If the ear-faculty is eternally abiding, true, and pure, its principle is demonstrated from the perspective of the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of sentient beings.
Because it is manifest and clear. A verse by Mañjuśrī says: "As Avalokiteśvara has explained: 'For example, when a person dwells in quietude, drums are struck simultaneously in the ten directions;

they are heard all at once from the ten locations—this is the reality of perfection (pūrṇa-tattva). Hearing sounds through a wall, one can hear them both near and far—this is the reality of penetration (vyāpti-tattva).

Sound does not exist, yet there is no cessation; sound exists, yet it is not born. Birth and cessation are two [extremes]..."* *(Note: The original text fragment ends mid-sentence regarding the two extremes of birth and cessation.)*
To be perfectly detached from this is the eternal reality; "eternal reality" is the eternal. Perfect reality is abiding. Pervasive reality is identity.
These several verses can not only verify that the fundamental principle of the Ear is perfect and subtle, but practitioners should also maintain them to support their perfect cultivation.
It is like when a person dwells in stillness: regardless of where a sound originates, it issues forth from every direction.
Whether moving or still, one should remain outside of obstructions; yet my faculty of hearing is perfectly pervasive and constantly abides here, which can be fully utilized for realization.
As the Sūtra says: "In this Sahā world, the discourse on sound is proclaimed and made clear. It further states:
"The essence of the true teaching in this region is pure within sound and hearing. There is profound significance in these words. Below, it says: "That which is..."
Regarding the phrase "once entry has become still, the two marks of movement and stillness clearly do not arise":

this means that once the flow has entered [the source], the flow returns to its entirety as one, and both subject and object vanish. The wondrous, pure, and luminous mind stands forth in solitary liberation; all of this occurs spontaneously and naturally.

The wondrous realization occurs all at once and admits of no sequence; yet, when the Sūtras and treatises speak of such gradual increases and so forth, it is because some perceive that language and written characters are insufficient to convey the Way, and thus resort to this approach.

Students must not, however, attempt to grasp or comprehend this through sequential conceptualization. Regarding this principle, they may perhaps come close to it. Question: As previously stated, the six sense faculties...

Generally, it is held that the Great Śūraṅgama Samādhi serves as the foundation for the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Now, regarding the principle of "entering the stream," its method is nothing other than this:
simply to realize that this faculty of the ear is eternally abiding, true, and pure; this is itself "entering the stream.

Furthermore, how does this accord with the previous explanation of the names [of the samādhis], such as *śamatha* and so forth? Answer: Observing your question, it seems you must necessarily take *śamatha* as the basis.
To cease movement, one must necessarily observe; to observe its obscurity, one may then say that one is practicing *śamatha-vipaśyanā*.

Furthermore, one must necessarily use emptiness (*śūnyatā*) to shatter existence, the provisional (*prajñapti*) to shatter non-existence, and the Middle Way (*madhyamā pratipad*) to obliterate extremes;

only then may one say that one is practicing the three contemplations (*tri-vipaśyanā*). Such is the manner in which worldly people generally overlook the Perfect and Sudden *śamatha-vipaśyanā*. If this is so...

Then, the cultivation of the three contemplations at the initial stage of the *Sūtra of Adornment* and the cultivation of *śamatha* throughout the beginning and end of this scripture would both become conditioned activities (*sābhisaṃskāra*).
How, then, could they be called the stages of the sages? One must know that as for *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*: non-delusion is called *śamatha*, and non-obscuration is called *vipaśyanā*.

These are alternative designations for clarity and stillness, or quiescence and illumination, corresponding respectively to meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). For instance, at the moment one enters the stream, if there were even the slightest [disturbance] within the breast...
If there remains even a single thread of emotional attachment, then that nature of hearing cannot attain its perfect penetration and constancy;

how, then, could it suffice for "entering the stream"? Therefore, one who skillfully enters the stream, at that moment, is utterly detached from both sense faculties and their objects, revealing alone the true and constant.

One knows the cessation of opposites, leaving behind both agitation and stillness. As the verse says: "When hearing returns and the obscuring faculty is removed, the dust is extinguished and awareness becomes perfect."

Pure, pure, and profoundly luminous, it penetrates and reaches the limit of tranquil illumination, encompassing all of empty space. How could it be that contemplation and observation are not present therein?
Furthermore, one should know that the Dharma is fundamentally neither empty nor provisional, nor is it non-empty and non-provisional.

It is simply because the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is free from all relativity that we provisionally designate it as "the Middle. It is simply because the nature of phenomena is untainted that we provisionally designate it as "emptiness. It is simply because...

The Dharma-nature is fully endowed with all phenomena; this is designated as "provisional" based on these manifestations. This single Dharma-nature is itself beyond dependence, free from delusion, and replete with all phenomena.
It is like a mani jewel: it is luminous and transparent, it is replete with precious qualities, and its essence is perfect.

Although the three aspects are distinct, they are one single jewel; although it is one single jewel, the three aspects are perfectly manifest. The perfect penetration of the faculty of hearing is likewise so.

It is likewise so. When drums are struck simultaneously in the ten directions, they are heard all at once from ten locations; in relation to this, it is described as "the middle" because it is free from all relative distinctions.

To be able to contemplate this perfection is to contemplate the Middle Way. Therefore, the Sūtra says: "When the awareness of emptiness is perfectly perfected, that which is emptied by emptiness ceases."

When one hears sounds through a wall, they can be heard both from afar and nearby; this unimpeded state is called "emptiness. To be able to contemplate this penetration is to contemplate true emptiness.
Thus the Sūtra says: "Ceasing all hearing, one does not abide; that which perceives and that which is perceived are empty.
Sound being absent is not non-existence; sound being present is not birth. This state of non-arising is called "existence. To be able to contemplate this permanence is...
Contemplating the wondrous existence, the Sūtra says: "The two marks of movement and stillness are clearly seen as not arising. Tiantai said: "This arises entirely from the inherent nature;
it is truly not accomplished through cultivation. Is this not so? This is still explained in terms of sequential progression within the non-sequential.

If one were to speak of the non-sequential within the non-sequential, then to mention the Perfect (yuan) necessarily implies the Pervasive (tong) and the Eternal (chang); to mention the Pervasive necessarily implies the Perfect and the Eternal; and to mention the Eternal...

It must be perfect and it must be pervasive. Therefore, at the time of "returning the hearing," one simply contemplates its perfection; thus, both pervasiveness and constancy are both contained within this. Hence, Avalokiteśvara said:

"I have entered the Samādhi of the Perfect Illumination through the Ear-Gate, whereby the mind that conditions [objects] becomes sovereign, and by entering the phase of the flow, I have attained Samādhi.
It further says: "Because I contemplate the perfect clarity of the ten directions through hearing, I am called Avalokiteśvara."

"It is named as pervading the realms of the ten directions. This refers to observing in accordance with the nature (*dharmatā*) and illuminating through transcendence of all dependencies. Tiantai said:

"The person of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanren*) takes the Middle Way observation (*zhongguan*) as the essence from beginning to end. The first stage of faith (*xin*) in this sutra says: "One immediately enters the flow of the center within this mind.
The Tathāgata, manifesting his own realization, said: "I unite the non-extinguishing and non-arising with the Tathāgatagarbha," and thus the Tathāgata...
The *Zang* [commentary] states: "The wondrous awakening and clarity alone perfectly illumines the dharma-realm. The *Two Decisions* (*Er jueding lun*) says:

"It is formed based on the nature of non-arising and non-extinction, which is perfectly tranquil; by turning back that tranquility, one extinguishes the illusory arising and ceasing. Both of these express this same meaning. This wondrous contemplation is ever-quiescent while illuminating;
it is also called the "cessation of dualistic discrimination. All deluded thoughts are stilled by embodying this, and it is also called—
The "Cessation through Abiding in Reality" is also called the "Contemplation of Emptiness. Following all sounds heard, one realizes that the locus of these sounds is entirely the locus of the ear;

this is because the nature of hearing is perfect and pervasive. It is also called the "Cessation through Skillful Means following Conditions," and it is also called the "Contemplation of Provisionality.
This is cessation within contemplation, and contemplation within cessation; it is emptiness and provisionality within the Middle Way, and the Middle Way within emptiness and provisionality.
At the moment of entering the stream, the five abidings, the boulders, and the gravel all come to rest; this is called "cessation as cessation.
When the mind takes the Middle Way as its object and enters the wisdom of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), it is called "cessation as stopping.

This wisdom of the true mark is neither cessation nor non-cession (and so forth). As the verse says: "The proclamation of the Vajra King, the Illusory and Inconceivable Mother of Buddhas, the True Samādhi. Furthermore:
It is said: "The subtle power of the effortless Vajrasamādhi, cultivated through hearing and practiced through hearing, finds its ultimate aim here.

Question: In the sutras, it is said that "upon entering the stream, the object is forgotten. Ancient masters have interpreted this as the "stream of the dharma-nature," or as the "stream of the sages. Baoting Jian remarked:
"While these interpretations are generally applicable, they do not precisely accord with the intent of the sutra. Speaking according to the present [exegesis], this "one stream" refers to...
The term "characteristic" (*xiàng*) specifically points to the locus of the auditory faculty’s capacity for hearing; it is most subtle and ultimate, with no space between them even for a hair.

To err by a hair's breadth is to lose the mark by a thousand li. Now, regarding the Perfect, Constant, and Universal [Wisdom], it is commonly said that it is called "Middle" simply because the *dharmatā* (dharma-nature) is free from all opposition.
How is this so diametrically opposed to what Master Baiting established? Answer: As for *dharmatā*, there is both a general and a specific sense.

"Universal" means that all phenomena share the same nature, which is the single true Dharma-realm (*ekadharmadhātu*). "Particular" means that each phenomenon possesses its own individual self-nature (*svabhāva*).
However, since all phenomena are primordially present within the single true Dharma-realm, the universal is itself the particular, and the particular is itself the universal.

Therefore, there is no universality that is not particularity, and no particularity that is not universality. For this reason, the nature of the single true Dharma-realm is perfectly pervasive and universal, and so too are all phenomena.

The nature of these [senses] is likewise none other than universally pervasive and constant. Others, however, have explained this by conflating it with the *dharmatā* (dharma-nature). Therefore, [the text] distinguishes it, saying: "pervasive but not specific.

Now, we specifically point to the *dharmatā* of the ear-faculty; thus, what is meant by "universally pervasive and constant" resides precisely in that which is selected, not in that which is excluded.
Question: Tiantai clarifies that there are three kinds of *dharmatā*: first, the essence of nature (*xingti*).

This corresponds to the direct cause (*hetu*). Second is the nature-quantity (*prakṛti-pramāṇa*); this corresponds to the revealing cause (*vijñapti-hetu*). Third is the nature-endowment (*prakṛti-sampad*);
this corresponds to the conditional cause (*pratyaya-hetu*). Now, when contemplating the perfect penetration of the faculty of hearing, among these three natures, which nature is being contemplated?

Answer: As for the faculty of hearing, it is fundamentally a phenomenon of ignorance and birth-and-death. Because it is endowed with the nature [of enlightenment], it is able to be, in its very essence, perfect penetration. Perfect penetration...

"Constant" refers to the essence and the magnitude of the nature. To observe now by means of this term is precisely to observe the essence and magnitude of the nature through the principle of inherent inclusion (*xingju*). Question:

If it is a matter of inherent inclusion, then Buddhas and sentient beings must mutually include one another, and the sense organs and their objects must mutually encompass one another. What is the meaning of this in relation to the ear-faculty (*karṇendriya*) here and now?
Answer: The dharmas of inherent inclusion consist of both the self and the other. Buddhas and sentient beings arise from the self-mind; Buddhas and sentient beings arise from the other-mind.

The Buddha said: "In this very faculty of hearing, nothing is not fully present. The auditory faculty is perfectly pervasive; it is equally so for self and others, and for sentient beings and Buddhas.
Therefore, it is said that the aggregates, bases, and elements are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha. It is also said that they are pure by nature and pervade the entire Dharma-realm.
For example, it is like a thousand lamps in a single room: each lamp contains all the others, and each lamp pervades all the others. Thus, one should now simply observe..."

Regarding the faculty of hearing, both self and others—whether ordinary beings or Buddhas—are viewed with equal contemplation. Thus, at the time of Avalokiteśvara’s wondrous realization, it is said that he suddenly transcends the mundane and supramundane worlds;
above, he merges with the single awakened mind of all Buddhas of the ten directions, and below, he merges with the single shared longing for compassion of sentient beings in the six realms.
Instantly, he attains the thirty-two transformations, the fourteen fearlessnesses, and the four [unhindered powers].

It is inconceivable. If one does not cultivate [this practice], how could one suddenly harmonize with the Buddhas and sentient beings by means of a single thought-moment when contemplating the stage of fruition?

Furthermore, if one's own mind did not inherently possess the Buddhas and sentient beings of oneself and others, then the thirty-two manifestations and so forth would all become mere contrived supernatural powers (*manomaya-ṛddhi*).
It should be understood that this "conjunction" refers to the aforementioned non-arising and non-ceasing being conjoined with the Tathāgatagarbha—the ten realms and the three truths.

Cultivation in accordance with the nature is called "conjunction"; cultivation contrary to the nature is called "non-conjunction. Those who study the teachings should therefore achieve a comprehensive understanding.
The section on the Perfect Penetration of the Ear Organ is concluded. Next, following the principle of absolute transcendence, the various objects are elucidated.

What is called "returning to the source" is non-dual in its nature, yet there are many gates to the skillful means; the sagely nature is all-pervasive, such that both following and reversing are skillful means.
Within this, one must clarify two meanings regarding "absolute transcendence" (*juedai*). First, absolute transcendence is discussed in accordance with the principle of the ear-faculty;
second, absolute transcendence is discussed in accordance with the principles of all other objects. Regarding the first meaning: since the aforementioned ear-faculty is already perfect...

Generally speaking, if this is so, then one should realize that the Dharma-realm encompasses all phenomena without exception; there has never been a single phenomenon that is not the locus of the perfect penetration of the ear-faculty.
Therefore, for those who skillfully enter the stream [of liberation], why should they contemplate only the sphere of sound?

Indeed, the sphere of the ear, the sphere of taste, the sphere of fragrance, the sense faculties, the spheres of consciousness, and even the seven great elements can all serve as the entrance to the ear-gate for the Samādhi of Perfect Illumination. Free from...

Beyond the perfect penetration of the faculty of hearing, no other dharma can be obtained; therefore, it is said to be "transcending all dependencies" (*juedai*). Next, to clarify this transcendence of dependencies by following the principle of all objects:
while the previous discussion of transcending dependencies was merely incidental, if one were to speak of the primary argument, there is not a single phenomenon that is not perfect penetration.
Thus, the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) are all said to be fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha, the eternally abiding, wondrous [nature].

This clarifies the immovable, all-pervading, wondrous nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*). "Immovable and all-pervading" refers to its perfection (*pariniṣpanna*); "wondrous nature of True Suchness" refers to its penetration (*praveśa*).
"Constantly abiding in wondrous clarity" refers to its permanence (*nitya*). The *Seven Great Elements* state: "Pure and fundamentally so, it pervades the Dharma-realm.

"Pervading the Dharma-realm" refers to its perfection; "pure" refers to its penetration; "fundamentally so" refers to its permanence. Furthermore, in the first and second fascicles, the [nature of] seeing is revealed.

The nature is all-pervasive and perfect; it neither expands nor contracts, and thus it is penetrating. When one bends a finger and the light flies away, yet the vision remains unmoving, this verifies its constancy.
Therefore, speaking in terms of principle, there is nothing that is not perfect penetration. How could it be that only the faculty of hearing is to be adopted while other objects are to be discarded?

It is simply because the consciousnesses of the other faculties are dull for the sentient beings of this region, whereas the faculty of hearing is the sharpest. Thus, the Buddha followed [this capacity].
The Buddha initially commanded Mañjuśrī to select [the appropriate method]. Therefore, even among the various sages, their expositions of principle do not follow a single uniform standard;
this is because they abide by the Buddha’s command, namely the intent behind his words: "You all must first realize from what skillful means the eighteen realms enter into samādhi.
However, since the mental afflictions of sentient beings are manifold, it is difficult to treat them with a single medicine. This is just as in the case of worldly people—

If even those who skillfully manage their own lives can guide and nourish themselves so as to find their proper place, how much more so for one who studies the Buddha and understands skillful means (*upāya*)?

Furthermore, since people of the future will also attain the Way through this sutra, how could it be that one must necessarily be restricted by adapting to their ailments and conforming to their habits?

For this reason, I have taken the essence of the sutra and set forth two intentions: first, to conform to the literal text of the sutra; second, to conform to the underlying principles of the *piṭaka*. Regarding conformity to the sutra text, there are twenty...
The four gates differ in their relative scale; yet, according to the principle of the *pitakas*, the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) are of one flavor and equal.
Why is this? For when the World-Honored One commanded each to describe the skillful means first realized by them, the various sages ought to have followed the Buddha’s injunction.

Because they were proclaimed according to what was realized at the time [of their respective teachings], the twenty-five gates of the sutras differ distinctly in terms of the Great and Small Vehicles, the Partial and the Perfect;
this meaning is perfectly clear. Certainly, there is no need for the clamorous disputes of those who attempt to open up provisional means where none had been opened.

My present exposition intends to focus on practice and entry; it seeks to accord with the principles of the Tripitaka to open the gate of the Perfect, thereby remaining in harmony with the scriptural text.

This has already been explained according to various commentaries; here, I shall briefly clarify it in accordance with the principles of the Abhidharma-piṭaka. The general meaning consists of two parts: first, the condensation of the dharmas and the integration of their meanings;
second, the formal exposition of the various categories. Regarding the condensation of the dharmas and the integration of their meanings:

if each of the twenty-four categories were explained individually, the text would seem overly prolix; yet, if only the eighteen *dhātus* were explained, the meaning would seem incomplete. Therefore, [the text] condenses earth, water, fire, and...

The five great elements—wind and space—enter the six sense objects; the great element of seeing contracts to enter the six sense organs; and the great element of consciousness contracts to enter the six consciousnesses.
Thus, by treating them as the three categories, the seven elements are explained together with the meaning of the Tathāgatagarbha-nature, such as "form is true emptiness" and so forth.
Explained by way of these three categories, the text is concise yet exhaustive, and its meaning is profound and clear.
Moreover, since the *dhātu* (elements) take the "great" (*mahā*) as their essence, and "great" shares the same meaning as *dhātu*, they are thus condensed and unified.

If a practitioner can apply this condensed and unified textual meaning to traverse the six sense faculties, then every moment and every particle will become this wondrous contemplation. How much more so for the two [objects]?
There are only fifteen gates. Next, the correct elucidation of these gates is divided into three parts: first, the six objects; second, the six faculties;
and third, the six consciousnesses. As for the six objects—namely, form, sound, odor, taste, touch, and phenomena (*dharmas*)—although there are only six in number, each has three distinct meanings.
These are what are called colors that are contrary, colors that are favorable, and colors that are neither contrary nor favorable;

and so on, up to dharmas that are contrary, dharmas that are favorable, and dharmas that are neither contrary nor favorable. That which is disagreeable is contrary; that which is agreeable is favorable;

and that which is neither agreeable nor disagreeable is neither contrary nor favorable. These are the things encountered daily by sentient beings, from what is seen by the eyes up to what is perceived by the mind.

All that is knowable does not transcend these phenomena. Because sentient beings are blind and ignorant, they do not understand that the characteristics of these phenomena are illusory while their nature is truly real.

Therefore, they grasp at them as being substantially existent. Consequently, when they encounter agreeable forms, and so forth, up to agreeable mental objects (*dharma*), they immediately give rise to craving and attachment;
and when they encounter disagreeable forms, and so forth, up to disagreeable [mental objects]...
When encountering objects that are disagreeable to the mind, one immediately gives rise to anger;
when encountering objects that are neither agreeable nor disagreeable, one becomes dazed and indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). These three poisons are the root of all delusions.
Once the root is established, the branches and leaves flourish profusely, causing one to wander through birth and death without end. Now...

Once the practitioner has heard this principle of perfection, upon encountering such objects, they should immediately realize that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature and should take them as their own mind.
"The nature of form is true emptiness; the nature of emptiness is true form," and so on, up to "the nature of dharmas is true emptiness; the nature of emptiness is true dharmas."
It is pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm. It is without subject and without object; it is neither existent nor non-existent.

If one encounters circumstances that are either adverse or favorable, one should still them by means of these three modes of cessation that accord with the nature; thus, the minds of greed and anger can be subdued in advance.

If one encounters circumstances that are neither adverse nor favorable, one should illuminate and comprehend them by means of these three modes of contemplation that accord with the nature; thus, [the mind of delusion...]
The indeterminate mind is first eliminated. Next, regarding the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*):

one does not take the superficial, physical faculties (*tuccha-mūla-indriya*) as the essence of the faculties, but rather takes the ultimate faculties (*paramārtha-indriya*) that are capable of seeing and hearing. These six faculties are such that the eye depends upon light and darkness.
The ear depends on movement and stillness; the nose, on openness and obstruction; the tongue, on sweetness and blandness; the body, on separation and contact; and the mind, on arising and ceasing.

By inhaling these sensory phenomena, one takes them as the nature of seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and cognizing. Yet apart from these various objects, it ultimately has no substance. Sentient beings do not understand this;
they claim to see and hear, grasp at objects to give rise to consciousness, and moment by moment cling to them, wandering in the cycle of rebirth.
Birth and death cannot be severed. Now, the practitioner who has heard this perfect principle should immediately attain clear understanding regarding these faculties:
that phenomena have no self-nature and are the very substance of my own mind. The nature of seeing is luminous awareness, and luminous awareness is the essence of seeing;

even so with the nature of knowing and luminous awareness, and the essence of knowing and luminous awareness—they are pure and fundamental from the start, pervading the entire Dharma-realm, without subject and without object.

It is neither existent nor non-existent. When the eye-seeing arises due to light and darkness, and so on until the mental consciousness arises due to arising and ceasing, one should bring them to rest through these three modes of cessation that accord with the nature (*dharmatā*). Thus, thoughts of good and evil cannot arise.
When light, darkness, and so forth cease, the seeing also ceases accordingly; likewise, when arising and ceasing cease, the mind also ceases accordingly. By means of this—

By illuminating and comprehending through the three contemplations that accord with the nature (*dharmatā*), the indeterminate mind (*avyākṛta-citta*) is preemptively eliminated. Regarding the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*):

this refers to the arising of the mind whenever the sense organs and their objects encounter one another in the daily activities of sentient beings; the grasping of objects and subsequent discrimination is termed "consciousness.

These six consciousnesses arise as follows: with the eye and form as conditions, visual consciousness arises; and so on, up to the mind and mental phenomena (*dharma*) [as conditions, mental consciousness arises].
Consciousness arises dependent [on conditions]. Apart from these faculties and objects, it has no inherent nature of its own.

Sentient beings, failing to understand this, take it to be their "self-mind" and engage in conceptual discrimination moment by moment. As mind after mind arises and perishes, they are led through birth and death without end.
Now, the practitioner who already understands the perfect principle should realize that within these six consciousnesses, consciousness lacks self-nature; its very substance is wondrous.
The mind—its nature is conscious, clear, and aware; its enlightened clarity is the true consciousness, a wondrous awakening, profound and still, pervading the entire Dharma-realm.

When the sense organs and their objects arise in conjunction to produce discrimination, one should arrest this with these three types of cessation that accord with the nature, whereby such mental states are immediately stilled.
When the sense organs and their objects disengage to produce a state of non-discrimination (avyākṛta), one should [arrest this] with these three types of contemplation that accord with the nature.
Upon this illumination, this indeterminate mind is immediately broken and eliminated. This wondrous śamatha is the precious awakening of the Vajra King;
as soon as it encounters the various gates of affliction, they are dissolved. The practitioner should personally grasp its meaning and cultivate it;
there is no time for further elaboration. Question: When compared with other samādhis, how many levels of superiority or inferiority exist between this Ear-Gate Samādhi and the others?
Answer: The Ear-faculty’s Perfect Penetration (*karṇendriya-pariśuddha-avivarta*) is exceedingly superior and wondrous. Now, regarding its essential requirements, there are generally two.

First, as a method of complete cultivation, it must have a correspondence between cause and effect in its nomenclature. Second, it must possess levels of depth that allow for long-term practice. Regarding the correspondence of cause and effect:
as the Sūtra says, "Is the mind generated at the stage of the ground the same as, or different from, the awakening at the stage of fruition? If, regarding...
To seek the Buddha-vehicle—which is unborn and undying—by taking a mind of arising and ceasing as the fundamental cause on the stage of practice is impossible.
Furthermore, the Sūtra states that within the awakening of the stage of fruition, there are seven designations:
namely, bodhi, nirvāṇa, tathatā, buddha-nature, amala-vijñāna, the empty tathāgatagarbha, and the great perfect mirror-wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*). These are the names of these seven types.
This means that although they are distinct, there is none whose pure and perfect essence is not as firm and solid as a diamond-king, abiding eternally without decay.

Now, when observing the initial resolve of the twenty-five sages on the stage of cause, it is only the *samādhi* of Avalokiteśvara’s ear-door that possesses the qualities of perfection, penetration, and constancy;
its name and designation correspond to the awakening of the stage of fruition. As for the other *samādhis*, some may attain one [quality] but not others.
This is the second case; how much more so when all three are present? As in the twenty-fourth [chapter], if one selects that which is most beneficial, the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) is superior.

However, if we compare them, the experience of the finger pointing at the flying light to verify that seeing is immovable is precisely analogous to the experience of striking a bell to verify the permanence of the ear-faculty (*śrotra-indriya*).
Yet, regarding perfect penetration (*paripūrṇa-abhijñā*), although the nature of seeing (*darśana-svabhāva*) is clear and penetrating, it sees what is before it but does not see behind.
The latter four directions are deficient by half, and [the visual faculty] cannot perceive what lies beyond obstructions.
This is unlike the ear-faculty, which hears drums struck simultaneously in all ten directions and perceives sounds through walls, hearing both near and far at once.
Therefore, although the eye’s vision attains a certain kind of permanence and indestructibility that corresponds to the name of the stage of fruition, it does not attain completeness.
If it were associated with the common [sensory] faculties, then the qualities of purity and perfection at the stage of fruition could not correspond to it.

Furthermore, one should know that the present "perfect penetration of the ear faculty," where drums are struck in all ten directions and heard simultaneously in all ten locations, is precisely the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) of the fruition stage.
That sounds are heard through walls and can be perceived both far and near is precisely the Wisdom of Equality (*samatā-jñāna*) of the Tathāgata.

It is the treasury. Sound being non-existent does not mean sound is extinguished; sound being existent does not mean sound is born. This is precisely the *tathatā*, the Buddha-nature, and the *amala-vijñāna*.
When purity reaches its ultimate limit, light penetrates everywhere, and tranquil illumination contains the void; this is precisely *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*.

Furthermore, regarding the *ear-root samādhi*, if one seeks to harmonize it with the Great Assembly of Buddhas mentioned in the title: "When drums are struck in the ten directions, they are heard in all ten places as one."
"Qi" (Pervasion) means hearing; it immediately and extensively encompasses the Dharma-body and the Dharma-realm, which pervade all places—this is the meaning of "vastness.
Sound is neither non-existent nor extinguished, and sound is neither existent nor produced;

it immediately and extensively encompasses the wisdom-realm of the Sambhogakāya, wherein illumination and manifestation correspond inexhaustibly—this is the meaning of "encompassment. Even through a wall, one hears sounds; both the distant and the near are equally reached.
It can be heard. That which is "victorious" (*jaya*) means that the manifested body (*nirmāṇakāya*) emerges preeminently and acts with mastery, such that it cannot be obstructed or suppressed;
this is the meaning of "victory. This should be understood by correlating each of the ten kinds of great meanings and the ten kinds of triple dharmas.

Therefore, whether collectively or individually, the ear-faculty samādhi corresponds to the stage of fruition (*phala-bhūmi*). Next, regarding those who practice for a long time through shallow and deep stages, the others...
Regarding Dharma gates, some may be cultivated at a shallow stage but not at a deep stage, such as the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) practiced by Upānisaṭa.
Others may be cultivated at a deep stage but not at a shallow stage, such as the "Universal Worthy Mind-hearing that Penetrates the Ten Directions" which gives rise to the power of great causes.
Therefore, Mañjuśrī distinguished them, saying: "All other various skillful means are solely due to the Buddha’s majestic power."
To resolve worldly affairs and abandon defilement is not merely a matter of long-term cultivation; the teachings on the stages of depth and shallowness are spoken of as being identical.
Now, the Samādhi of the Ear-organ is complete, perfect, universal, and constant. Even for a beginner practicing this, it already accords with the names and designations of the ultimate fruit;

how much more so for those in other, deeper stages? Therefore, in the conclusion regarding the stages, it says: "These various stages are all, through diamond-like observation, like an illusion. Ten... [The text continues].
The various profound metaphors [illustrate] how, within *śamatha*, one employs the *vipaśyanā* of all Tathāgatas to purify, realize, and gradually penetrate deeper.
This is seen in the *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-darśana-sūtra*, which states: "That which is the cause of the Mahāyāna is the true mark of all phenomena (*dharmatā*).
That which is the fruit of the Mahāyāna is the true mark of all phenomena. It is evident therein.
The fourth major section clarifies "function" (*yòng*). Tiantai says: "Function is the wondrous capability of the Buddha and the supreme application of the Sūtra.

To extinguish evil and give rise to goodness constitutes the power and function of the Sūtra. Because it extinguishes evil, it is called 'power' (*lì*); because it gives rise to goodness, it is called 'function' (*yòng*).

Because it extinguishes evil, it is called 'merit' (*gōng*); because it gives rise to goodness, it is called 'virtue' (*dé*). These are all partial enumerations; a complete discussion must necessarily include them all. Some of the older [commentators] have...
