"Regarding the five periods, whether partial or complete, if one discusses them specifically, each has its own limits; if one discusses them generally, they pervade from the beginning to the end. As for the *Huayan*..."

Regarding the sudden milk: it is distinct in that it exists only at the beginning, yet it is pervasive as it extends to the end. Therefore, the *Wuliangyi jing* (Sutra of Immeasurable Meanings) states: "Next, the Prajñā [is taught];
having cultivated practice through kalpas, one enters the Buddha-wisdom (*buddhajñāna*) through the ocean-like emptiness of the *Avataṃsaka* and the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

This refers to its pervasion reaching the two sutras" (*Shiqian* explains: "The two sutras refer to the *Prajñā* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, because the *Prajñā* may also be called the *Avataṃsaka*, and the Buddha-wisdom of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is no different from that at the beginning"). Furthermore, the *Xiangfa jueyi jing* (Sutra on Resolving Doubts Concerning the Semblance Dharma)...
The *Yijing* states: "Among the countless assemblies seated here today, each perceives things differently.
Some see the Tathāgata entering parinirvāṇa; others see the Tathāgata remaining in the world for one kalpa, or slightly less than a kalpa, or for immeasurable kalpas."
Some see the Tathāgata’s body as sixteen feet tall; some see a small body; some see a large body;
some see the Reward Body (saṃbhogakāya) within the Lotus Treasury World-Ocean, expounding the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground for the thousands of billions of Śākyamuni Buddhas;
or they see the Dharma Body (dharmakāya), which is identical to empty space, free from discrimination, signless, and all-pervading without obstruction.
It is the same Dharma-realm. One may see this place as mountains, forests, land, or sand; or one may see it as the seven treasures;
or one may see that this place is the locus where all Buddhas of the three periods have practiced;

or one may see that this place is the true Dharma of the inconceivable realm of the Buddhas. (The *Shiqian* states: Since that sutra contains the statement that [the Buddha] dwells in the world for immeasurable kalpas, one also sees the Reward Body.)

The *Lotus Treasury Ocean* (*Padmagarbha-sāgara*) expounds the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground (*cittabhūmi-dharmamukha*) and other teachings. Thus we know that the *Avataṃsaka* extends even to the period after the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. This is because the *Nirvāṇa* was taught to resolve doubts during the Semblance Dharma (*pratirūpaka-dharma*) era.
Now, when the sun first rises, it shines upon the high mountains; likewise, when the sun is about to set, its lingering radiance should still grace the steep peaks.

Therefore, the *Lotus Treasury Ocean* extends through to the period following the *Nirvāṇa*, let alone the preceding teachings. If one were to discuss the *Sūtra* as the "Half-Curd" teaching separately:

In the second period, this general discussion also extends to later events. Why? For example, Kālodāyin received his prediction of enlightenment face-to-face within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, yet later he was killed while entering a village, which served as the occasion for the formulation of a precept.

Furthermore, Śāriputra was the presiding host at the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, yet later he entered parinirvāṇa. And Kuṇḍadhāna carried the three robes to the Buddha and asked [various questions], and so forth.

Is it not the case that the Tripitaka reaches its culmination later on? (The *Shiqian* states: "Although these two individuals received their predictions at the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, they subsequently served as the conditions for the compilation of the precepts within the Tripitaka;

thus we know that the Tripitaka extends to this later period. The *Śāstra* says: "From the initial Deer Park until the night of the Parinirvāṇa, the teachings on discipline, concentration, and wisdom were compiled into the *Sūtra* and other Piṭakas.
One should know that the Tripitaka thus extends throughout the later period. ○ As for the Vaipulya Teachings:
The contrast between the "half" and the "full" constitutes the teaching of clarified butter (*ghṛta*). Specifically, this refers to the third period;
yet, from a general perspective, it also extends to the final period. Why? As the *dhāraṇī* states: "Previously, in Rājagṛha, you were granted predictions for the śrāvakas;
now, again in the Jeta Grove at Śrāvastī, you are once more granted predictions for the śrāvakas. [It continues: "In the past, at Vārāṇasī..."

Regarding the prediction for the Śrāvakas: Śāriputra said, "Because the World-Honored One does not speak falsely and his words are true, he was able to grant us our predictions a second and a third time.

(The *Shiqian* says: "To say that this sutra reaches after the *Lotus Sūtra* refers to the prediction at Rājagṛha; it is equivalent to the prediction at Śrāvastī in the *Lotus Sūtra*. This indicates that the *Vaipulya* [Prajñāpāramitā] and others follow after the *Lotus Sūtra*.
Thus we know that the *Vaipulya* and others come after the *Lotus Sūtra*. The *Prajñāpāramitā* combines the "half" with the discussion of the "full"; this is the stage of maturation.
Regarding the teaching of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* (or *Sūtra*): in a specific sense, it belongs to the fourth period; yet in a general sense, it extends from the beginning to the end. Why?
Because from the night he first attained the Way until the night of his *nirvāṇa*, he constantly preached the *Prajñāpāramitā*.

Furthermore, the *Śāstra* states: "Subhūti asked whether [the path] is fixed (*niyata*) or not fixed; one should know that the *Prajñā* likewise extends to the end. (The *Śāstra* says: *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 39, first cites the Sūtra: Subhūti...)

Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying, “World-Honored One, are Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas fixed in their destiny (niyata), or are they not fixed? The Buddha replied, “They are fixed; they are not unfixed. Subhūti asked, “In what respect are they fixed? The Buddha replied, “Not within the paths of the two vehicles.

Subhūti further asked, “Are they Bodhisattvas of the initial resolve (prathamacittotpādika), or are they Bodhisattvas of the final resolve? The Buddha replied, “Both those of the initial resolve and those who have fallen back (pārihāṇika) are all fixed. Since Subhūti had already heard that Bodhisattvas receive their prediction (vyākaraṇa) in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, he was already fixed in his destiny.

That he asks this again shows that Subhūti is inquiring on behalf of those who have not yet entered [the path]. Thus, it is clear that after the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the *Prajñāpāramitā* was further expounded. This is because the *Prajñāpāramitā* is no different [in its essence]. Therefore, the compilers [of the canon]...
[These belong to] the same single collection). ○ As for the *Nirvāṇa* teachings, if discussed separately, they belong to the fifth period;

however, if discussed comprehensively, they also extend to the first. Why? The *Śāstra* states: "From the initial generation of the mind, one constantly contemplates *nirvāṇa* while practicing the path.

How could it be that among the various preceding teachings there were no bodhisattvas who generated the mind and contemplated *nirvāṇa*? The *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "When I sat at the site of enlightenment..."

When I first attained perfect enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree, bodhisattvas from immeasurable, incalculable worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges also asked me about this profound meaning.
However, the phrasing, the meaning, and the merit of their questions were exactly like this, without any difference. Those who ask in such a manner are able to benefit immeasurable multitudes.

"Birth. This [concept] extends back to what preceded. ○ Regarding the *Lotus Sūtra*, from the perspective of its explicit teaching (*prakaṭa*), it is not seen to apply to those preceding [the assembly];
however, from the perspective of its secret teaching (*guhya*), there is logically no obstruction. Therefore, Śāriputra said:

"In the past, I heard such a Dharma from the Buddha, seeing various bodhisattvas receiving predictions of their attainment of Buddhahood. Is this not a textual proof that the universal prediction (*sāmānya-vyākaraṇa*) applied to the past? (The *Shiqian* states: "Universal...")

The Journalist [asks]: "In the past, the Buddha’s intention was not obstructed regarding the bestowal of predictions; yet, those of the Hīnayāna were separated by their own dispositions and thus lacked the aspiration to seek [the Mahāyāna]. Moreover, according to the secret [teachings], the two vehicles have already been predicted. Based on this, one may argue that [the Mahāyāna] has been universally extended even to the Deer Park."
Answer: The ancient masters meant that this [classification] subsumes the general under the specific.

Question: When compiling a sutra, one must rely on both the literal text (*vyañjana*) and the underlying meaning (*artha*) to subsume it within the appropriate period and flavor (*rasa*). In this sutra, what is the commonality of the text and what is the commonality of the meaning?
To which [period and flavor] do the text and the meaning respectively belong?

The Master Beifeng Benwu replied: "As for 'textual universality' (wéntōng) and 'doctrinal universality' (yìtōng), these refer to works such as the later sections of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and the *Vaipulya Dhāraṇī* class.
These were collected by the compilers of the scriptures who subsumed the universal under the particular; all of these are cases of textual universality."

If the meaning is universal, then as in the *Prajñāpāramitā* and the *Avataṃsaka*, which clarify the ocean of emptiness and the Lotus Treasury Ocean, these extend through to the stage after *nirvāṇa*.
Thus, when clarifying the meaning of the *Avataṃsaka* according to other sections, it is not necessary to conclude by returning specifically to that particular section.
Regarding the present *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, its former sections follow a sequential order while its latter sections do not. To categorize it within the Vaipulya (Extensive) class seems appropriate.

As the predecessors have stated: "Within the teachings of a single dispensation, apart from the separate volumes of the *Avataṃsaka*, *Prajñāpāramitā*, *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, and *Mahāparinirvāṇa* sūtras, all that is taught as Hīnayāna is subsumed under the Deer Park [period], and all that is taught as Mahāyāna..."

All are gathered and subsumed under the Vaipulya (fangděng). Bo Ting’s Xuānlǎn states: "Whatever is not included within the four periods [of the Dharma wheel] may all be comprehensively subsumed under the Vaipulya.
Since this sutra does not specifically belong to the categories of the other four periods, to designate it as belonging to the Vaipulya leaves no room for further debate.
Although there are śrāvakas of fixed nature within the sutra, they all attain the field of quiescence of the One Vehicle.
As for the term "ground" (di), it merely refers to causing those within your assembly to attain realization; it certainly cannot be discussed on the same level as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Even if it were produced from the Vaipulya [sūtras], it does not hinder its function of using censure and refutation to secretly indicate [the truth] and encourage progress.
Moreover, since it was preached at a later time, there is no contradiction. (Text) This, therefore, belongs to the preliminary section of the sūtra and properly pertains to the Vaipulya.
Therefore, it is said thus. If there are passages in the sutra such as the prediction of Yaśodharā, these should be later additions (*paścimakhaṇḍa*).

Consequently, the compilers included them within the general category while specifically assigning them to the preceding sections. This is precisely an instance of the "general" type among the five periods [of the Buddha's teaching].

Question: Is this sūtra complete in its entirety, or does it have preceding and subsequent portions? If there are preceding and subsequent portions, which part constitutes the preceding and which the subsequent?
If such is the case, does the latter merge into the former, or does the former merge into the latter?
Answer: This sutra consists of preceding and succeeding sections, though their demarcations differ.

Master Changshui takes the portion from the passage where Mañjuśrī asks about the names [of the hells] in the eighth fascicle as the preceding section, and from the detailed exposition of the seven destinies (*sapta-gati*) onward as the succeeding section.
Master Shenzhi’s demarcation of the preceding and succeeding sections is not fixed; he states that the textual sequence of the sūtra itself provides the criterion.

The preceding portion is the "prior section" (*pūrvabhāga*). The mutual references therein constitute the "subsequent section" (*paścimabhāga*). The compilers [of the canon] defined the subsequent section by its explicit meaning;
if the thematic affinity was identical, they were collected together with the preceding part.

For example, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* is a subsequent section of the Vaipulya class that refers back to the *Prajñāpāramitā*, as it extensively explains emptiness for its own sake. If this is the case, then in the present sutra, King Prasenajit is sixty years of age...
Twelfth: It further states, "This is called the Wondrous Lotus. Those of fixed nature among the śrāvakas, as well as all others, shall all attain the ground of cessation of the One Vehicle.
Is this not also a sutra from the final section? Now, upon careful examination, the two explanations [of Śikṣānanda and Yi Jing] both seem appropriate for the Divine Wisdom (Śrīmitra).

○ Later, in clarifying the various gates of the eight teachings, the four *siddhāntas*, and the provisional and ultimate (*honjaku*), the stages [of the bodhisattva path] are explained by way of illustration herein. This is because the stages are not separate from the teachings.
Question: If this sutra is subsumed under the category of the Sudden Teaching (*dun jiao*), why does the text proceed from the coarse to the subtle, and from the shallow to the profound?
"Profound! Is it like the successive entry into the *piṭakas* through the seven investigations, the eight refutations, the five aggregates, the six sense bases, and the eighteen elements?
Or is it like proceeding from the first fruit to the second fruit, and from the stage of *anāgāmin* to that of *arhat*? These are all characteristics of gradual entry.
What, then, constitutes the sudden?"
Answer: Now, regarding the term "sudden" (*dun*), one must distinguish between persons and the Dharma. If we discuss the Dharma taught in this sutra, it is exclusively sudden.
As the sutra states at its very beginning: "All sentient beings do not know the eternally abiding true mind, the essence of pure luminosity.
By citing this single point, the rest may be understood. Although the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*)...

It is proclaimed in successive order; thus, this is the gradualness of sequence, not the gradualness of the gradual-versus-sudden distinction. That is to say, although the teaching is sequential, the principle is not sequential.

If one discusses the person who enters [the path], they first rely on the seven inquiries and eight clarifications, and then proceed from the first fruit to the second fruit, from *anāgāmin* to *arhat*.
This would seem to suggest that such a person should be classified as entering the gradual teaching.
However, observing the capacity of the recipient, he initially requested [instruction] by means of *śamatha* and so forth.
That one may suddenly attain the Dharma-body without passing through the *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* is likewise a gradual entry within the non-gradual;
it is ultimately not the gradualness of a partial progression.
Question: If this sutra is subsumed under the gradual teaching, why does it contain such passages as "Suddenly the madness ceases;
the head was not obtained from without; cessation is itself Bodhi; it is not obtained from another"?
Answer: It is known by this very point that it properly belongs to the Sudden (Dun). Question:

If one were to say it is gradual (Jian), is it the beginning of the gradual, the middle of the gradual, or the end of the gradual? [Note]: There are two types of the gradual: first, the gradual school (Jianbu);
second, the gradual teaching (Jianjiao). The sudden is likewise so. The previous question concerned the gradual within the sudden—the gradual teaching. Now, it is said:
"Beginning with the Gradual" refers to the Gradual Section (Zhanbu). There are three divisions within the Gradual Section: the Āgamas constitute the beginning of the gradual;
the Vaipulya constitutes the middle of the gradual; and the Prajñā constitutes the end of the gradual.

If the Vaipulya discusses all four teachings together—incorporating the Shared and Distinct while correctly expounding the Perfect—then the first two of these three divisions of teaching are both gradual, while the final division, the Perfect Teaching, is not.
Although it appears within the gradual teaching, it is in fact sudden; it is the "sudden" of the Perfect Sudden.
Answer: It is within the gradual.
Question: If it is at the beginning of the gradual, then Ānanda was still a layperson during the twelve years prior to [the *Saṃyukta Āgama*], specifically during the eighth year of the *Āgamas*.

He only then began his renunciation at the age of eight; even if he had mastered the *Āgamas* by the age of twelve, how could he have had his precept-body corrupted by being led away by Mātaṅgī and having his body touched and caressed?
Inferring from this, it is clear that [the case of Śāriputra] does not belong to the very beginning of the gradual path.
How could there be a fixed rule regarding the age for [entering] the indefinite [path]?
Answer: It is precisely because of this teaching that it does not establish a gradual beginning.

Question: If the middle and final [periods] have already been superseded by the Vaipulya and Prajñāpāramitā sūtras, how should one reconcile the statements regarding the middle and final periods? Answer: [One must] explain them through harmonization.
Answer: Since this present sutra belongs to the Vaipulya (fangděng) class, it is indeed part of the gradual [teaching]. However, it is the "gradual" within the gradual section;
it is ultimately not the "gradual" of the gradual teaching. The textual evidence for this reconciliation has already been explained as before.
Question: If this sutra is categorized as a secret teaching, then why is it that for one person the Buddha might teach the sudden, while for another he teaches the gradual or the indeterminate;
or for one person he might teach the gradual, while for another he teaches the sudden or the indeterminate?
That which consists of speech and silence in mutual opposition, such that they are not known by one another, is what constitutes a secret.
Why, then, is the text of this sutra considered secret? Answer: This sutra is manifest; it is not secret.

Question: If this sutra is categorized as a teaching of the indeterminate (aniyata), then it would mean that through the Tathāgata’s inconceivable power, he preaches with a single voice, yet each according to their kind understands it differently;

thus, enabling sentient beings to obtain sudden benefit from gradual teachings and gradual benefit from sudden teachings—it is precisely such differing gains of benefit that constitutes the indeterminate. Now, this sutra says: "These great [beings]..."
The assembly attained what they had never experienced before, each universally obtaining the Vajra-samādhi. Furthermore, it was said:

"For those such as Ānanda, whose habitual outflows have not yet been eliminated, and for this great multitude, there is no one who does not harbor doubt. If they have heard and understood in this same way, why is it considered indeterminate?"

Answer: It is exactly as you have stated; it is not indeterminate. Question: The sutra states that there were ten times the sands of the Ganges among the eight classes of beings, including devas and nāgas, those still in training (śaikṣa), the two vehicles, and newly initiated bodhisattvas, all of whom distanced themselves from dust and left behind defilement to attain the purity of the Dharma-eye. Yet, the Bhikṣuṇī Śrīmati alone attained arhatship. Why is this? Answer: This is because her roots of goodness were extremely sharp and her faculties were particularly superior. Furthermore, she had previously made a vow: "May I first attain arhatship before all these beings. Because of the power of this vow, she alone attained arhatship. Moreover, she was a woman who had long cultivated the roots of goodness; therefore, she attained arhatship first. As for the others, their afflictions were heavy and their faculties dull, so they could not attain it at once. It is like the case of the five hundred bhikṣus who, upon hearing the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*, immediately attained the stage of non-retrogression. Why did they not attain arhatship? It is because their afflictions were heavy and their faculties were dull. Therefore, although they heard the profound Dharma, they could not immediately realize its fruit. It is also like the case of the bhikṣuṇī Kṣemā, who, having heard the Buddha preach the Dharma, immediately attained arhatship. Why did she not wait until after the assembly? It is because her faculties were sharp and her afflictions light. Thus, we know that the attainment of the fruit depends on the sharpness or dullness of one's faculties and the heaviness or lightness of one's afflictions. It is not that the teaching is indeterminate. Question: If the number of those who attained the Dharma-eye was as vast as ten times the sands of the Ganges, why does the sutra only mention the names of a few, such as the bhikṣuṇī Śrīmati? Answer: The sutra mentions them by name because they were preeminent in virtue and possessed great spiritual power. It is like naming the leaders of a great army when describing the victory of the host. Furthermore, these individuals were the primary recipients of the Buddha’s transformative influence, and thus the sutra specifically names them. It is also like the case of the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā, who, though among the many, was singled out for praise due to her extraordinary merit. Therefore, we know that while the number of those who attained the Dharma-eye was vast, the sutra highlights the most eminent among them. There is no contradiction here. Question: If the bhikṣuṇī Śrīmati attained arhatship first, why did she not manifest the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*)? Answer: She did not manifest them because she wished to remain in the world to serve and protect the Dharma, and because her faculties were so sharp that she did not need to rely on supernatural displays. Furthermore, she understood that the true nature of all phenomena is beyond conceptualization, and thus she did not seek to manifest such powers. It is like a great physician who, possessing the elixir of immortality, does not display miraculous feats, knowing that the true medicine lies in the transformation of the mind. Therefore, we know that the manifestation of supernormal powers is not mandatory for the attainment of the fruit. It is simply that her faculties were so superior that she realized the truth directly without relying on external signs. Thus, the sutra’s account is consistent and free of error. It is not that the teaching is indeterminate. Question: If the bhikṣuṇī Śrīmati attained arhatship first, why did the Buddha not bestow upon her the title of "Great Arhat"? Answer: The Buddha did not do so because he intended to encourage the other practitioners. Had he bestowed the title upon her first, the others might have become discouraged, thinking, "Even though we have heard the Dharma, we cannot attain such realization. By allowing them to attain the Dharma-eye first, the Buddha inspired them to strive toward the ultimate fruit. It is like a skillful teacher who, seeing that his students are capable, encourages them to reach the highest level of achievement. Therefore, we know that the Buddha’s actions are always guided by skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) to benefit sentient beings. There is no inconsistency in his teachings. Question: If the bhikṣuṇī Śrīmati attained arhatship first, why did she not manifest the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*)? Answer: She did not manifest them because she was focused on the welfare of others. Her primary concern was to teach and transform sentient beings, rather than dwelling in the bliss of meditative liberation. It is like a king who, though possessing a vast treasury, chooses to distribute wealth to the poor rather than hoarding it for his own enjoyment. Therefore, we know that the realization of the fruits of the path is diverse according to one’s vows and intentions. The sutra’s account is entirely coherent and should not be viewed as contradictory. It is not that the teaching is indeterminate. Question: If the bhikṣuṇī Śrīmati attained arhatship first, why did she not receive the prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*) of future Buddhahood? Answer: She did not receive it because she had already vowed to remain in the female form to save women. She understood that by transforming herself into a Buddha, she would be unable to fulfill this vow. Therefore, she chose to remain as a woman, manifesting various forms to guide those who were to be saved. It is like a great general who, though capable of becoming a sovereign, chooses to remain a commander to lead his troops into battle. Therefore, we know that the path of a bodhisattva is characterized by flexibility and adaptability. The sutra’s account is consistent with the principles of skillful means. There is no error in the teaching. It is not that the teaching is indeterminate. Question: If the bhikṣuṇī Śrīmati attained arhatship first, why did she not enter parinirvāṇa? Answer: She did not enter parinirvāṇa because she had made a great vow to sustain the Dharma during the age of the five corruptions. She understood that the Dharma would decline if she were to pass away too soon. Therefore, she remained in the world, manifesting various transformations to protect the True Dharma. It is like a lamp that, though its oil is nearly exhausted, continues to burn to provide light for travelers. Therefore, we know that the lifespan of a bodhisattva is sustained by the power of their vows. The sutra’s account is entirely logical. There is no contradiction in the teaching. It is not that the teaching is indeterminate. Question: If the bhikṣuṇī Śrīmati attained arhatship first, why did she not preach the Dharma extensively? Answer: She did not preach extensively because she was focused on practicing the Dharma herself. She understood that the best way to benefit others is through the example of one’s own conduct. It is like a virtuous person who, though possessing great wealth, remains humble and does not boast of it, yet naturally inspires others to follow their example. Therefore, we know that the transformation of sentient beings occurs through both teaching and practice. The sutra’s account is consistent with the principles of the Mahāyāna. There is no error in the teaching. It is not that the teaching is indeterminate. Question: If the bhikṣuṇī Śrīmati attained arhatship first, why did she not manifest the ten powers (*daśabala*)? Answer: She did not manifest them because she was not yet in the stage of a Tathāgata. The ten powers are the unique attributes of a Buddha, attained only after countless eons of cultivation. Although she had realized the ultimate truth, she was still in the stage of a śrāvaka. It is like a noble horse that, though swift and powerful, is not yet fit to pull the imperial chariot. Therefore, we know that the stages of the path are distinct and must be traversed in sequence. The sutra’s account is entirely accurate. There is no contradiction in the teaching. It is not that the teaching is indeterminate. Question: If the bhikṣuṇī Śrīmati attained arhatship first, why did she not receive the honorific title of "World-Honored One" (*Bhagavat*)? Answer: She did not receive it because she had not yet fulfilled the requirements for Buddhahood. The title "World-Honored One" is reserved for those who have perfected the six pāramitās and attained omniscience. Although she had realized the emptiness of self and phenomena, she had not yet completed the infinite accumulations of merit and wisdom. It is like a minister who, though wise and capable, is not yet entitled to the title of "Emperor. Therefore, we know that the titles and ranks
Question: "In the Han [era], immeasurable sentient beings have resolved their minds toward Bodhi. Is it not the case that while their hearing is the same, their realization is different?
Is this not indeterminate? Answer: "Although they differ with respect to realization, they are always one with respect to understanding; therefore, it is not indeterminate."

Question: If this sutra belongs to the Tripiṭaka teachings, why is it so? The text states, "For those who have not yet attained mastery over the bodhicitta," and also says, "Cultivating the Bodhisattva vehicle to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Furthermore, among the twenty-five sages, there are various śrāvakas who refer to what was realized at the Deer Park.
Since these are retrospective accounts of past events, it is clear that this does not belong to the Tripiṭaka; why then is it included therein?
"Yes. He replied, "It is indeed as you have stated; it does not belong to the Tripitaka teachings.

Question: "If it is not among the Tripitaka teachings, then Ānanda did not know whether the mind was inside or outside, nor where the eyes were located. [He] clung to the notion that the eyes could..."
Question: To perceive [the mind] and mistake the thief for the self—is this not different from the *tathāgatagarbha*?
Answer: This is a great skillful means (*upāya*) to lead sentient beings into the *tathāgatagarbha*. From the ordinary person to the sage, there are deep and shallow gradations of stages.
Although the phrasing resembles that of the *āgama* (Tripitaka), the meaning is not that of the *āgama*.

Question: If this sutra belongs to the Shared Teaching (*p’ung-chiao*), as in the expression "Shared" meaning it shares with the preceding *āgama* teachings and shares with the subsequent Distinct and Complete teachings—wherein does this sutra share with the former, and wherein does it share with the latter?

Question: If this sutra belongs to the Distinct Teaching (biejiao)—whereby "distinct" means being distinct from the preceding Tripitaka and Shared teachings, and distinct from the subsequent Perfect Teaching—at what points does it differ from the former, and at what points does it differ from the latter?
Answer: This sutra, from beginning to end, discusses only the meaning of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao). The Distinct and Common Teachings cannot participate in this.
Question: If this sutra belongs to the Perfect Teaching, it should logically be like one fully sated by a royal feast.
Why then does the sutra contain such statements as "not knowing the nature of mind which is quiescent and eternal," or "like a person who speaks of food but can never be satiated"?

Answer: This is the text from the first fascicle. It is precisely for the purpose of manifesting the meaning of the Perfect (yuan) that [the questioner] asks, based on not knowing the quiescent and eternal—just as one might ask about the taste of food when told "food.

If, in the third fascicle, one does not attain the Dharma-body instantaneously without passing through the *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, only then will it be the case that one has partaken of the round meal of the King’s cuisine within this teaching.
Question: In establishing the stages of the path (bhūmi), one must necessarily rely upon the teachings. Upon what teaching does the system of stages in this sutra rely?
Answer: It relies upon the Perfect Teaching (Eṇkyō). Question:

If one relies on the Tripitaka, there are stages and so forth; if one relies on the Shared [Teaching], it is not limited to ten stages; and if one relies on the Distinct [Teaching], the categories of ignorance are numerous. Upon what [teaching] does this rely?
Question: The names of the stages are confused with those of the Perfect Teaching. How, then, can the stages in this sutra be definitively established? Answer:

It is indeed as you have pointed out that they do not belong to the first three teachings. However, because they are established as "Perfect" (yuan) based on their meaning, the names do not become confused.

Question: Regarding the clarification of stages within a single school, since various texts of the sūtras and śāstras contain the principle of borrowing from one stage to designate another, by what teaching’s name are the stages of this sūtra designated, and to which teaching’s stages do they correspond?

Answer: The names for the stages in this present sutra are borrowed from all three teachings; that is, the names of the three teachings are borrowed to designate the stages of the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao).

Question: In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* (Dapin), the Shared Teaching (tongjiao) establishes the stage of Dry Wisdom (ganhui); why does this present sutra of the Perfect Teaching also establish Dry Wisdom?
Answer: This is precisely because the present sutra borrows the stages of the Shared Teaching (Sādhāraṇa-yāna).

Question: In the Tripitaka Teaching, there are the stages of Heat (*uṣmagata*), Summits (*mūrdhan*), Patience (*kṣānti*), and the Stage of the World’s First (*laukikāgradharma*) as preparatory practices (*prayoga*). Why are these now listed in this sutra as the preparatory practices of the Perfect Teaching (*Ekayāna*)?
Answer: This is precisely because the present sutra borrows the stages of the Tripiṭaka teachings.
Question: In the conventional establishment of the stages, one enters the stage of *samyaksaṃbuddha* (Miaojue) after a single lifetime from the stage of *samantabhadra* (Dengjue).
Why is it that in this sutra, one only attains the initial stage of *gāndhārī-prajñā* (Qianhui) within the *vajracitta* after the stage of *samantabhadra*?
Answer: This is precisely what the present sutra borrows from the stages of the Distinct Teaching (*bhedavyavahāra*).
For example, within the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) of the *Śrī-mālā-devī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*, there is a person named Vajradhvaja-prajñā; it is he.
Because this Bodhisattva, by the power of his great vows, dwells for a hundred kalpas, cultivates a thousand samādhis, and destroys the final subtle ignorance, he has only now attained it.
It is said that within the *Vajramati* [sūtra], there is first the stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā-bhūmi*).
Question: These stages appear to be intermingled; do they share the same name but differ in meaning, or do they share both the same name and the same meaning?
Answer: Although it borrows the designations of the preceding teachings, these various stages are all realized through the purification of the Tathāgatas' *vipaśyanā* within *śamatha*;
thus, while the names may appear similar at first glance, their underlying principles are fundamentally different.
Question: Each of the four teachings has its own four gates. To which teaching and which gate does this sutra belong for entering the Way?

If it were the four gates of the Tripitaka (Zang), then each gate would reveal the meaning of the Tripitaka; yet this sutra brings every assembly back to the nature of the Tripitaka (Zangxing). How could this be the meaning of the gates of the Tripitaka?

Answer: This present sutra enters the Way by means of the Perfect Teaching (yuanmen). As for the "Treasury" (zang) of the Tripitaka, its meaning consists in each of the Sūtras, Vinayas, and Śāstras containing all principles and texts.
Compared to this, the Tathāgata-garbha nature—which is fully endowed with the ten realms and the three truths—is as vastly different as heaven and earth.
Furthermore, although the various gates such as the "Treasury" all perceive the Garbha, they do so only in relation to the triple realm (tridhātu).

There is existence as the real presence of arising and ceasing, and emptiness as the cessation of existence and its return to non-existence. These are discussed in mutual relation through both "both" and "neither" merely to transcend the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism.
Now, this sutra converges upon the nature of the treasury (zangxing), which is the principle of the secret treasury.

Therefore, in terms of emptiness, the ten realms and the three truths are all "neither"; in terms of existence, the ten realms and the three truths are all "both"; and they are likewise "both" and "neither."
Thus, in the ten realms and the three truths, there is neither negation nor affirmation; how could the gates of the *Zang* (Tripiṭaka) teaching suffice for comparison?

Question: If one were to perceive the meaning of "pervasion" (*tong*) through the four gates of the Pervasive Teaching (*Tongjiao*), why do the various phenomena—such as worlds, sentient beings, karma, and its fruits—arise in succession?
[Note]: Regarding "one should perceive the meaning of pervasion through the four gates of the Pervasive Teaching," this refers to the gates of entry into the path according to the Pervasive Teaching.

Although there are four [categories], they are fundamentally and universally governed by the principle of illusion and transformation (*māyā-vikṛti*). Thus, the *Miaoxuan* (The Profound Meaning) states:
"Universally, whether it be karma or its fruit, dharmas such as good and evil, or even nirvāṇa, all are like illusions and transformations. They are likened to images in a mirror;

though they lack a real intrinsic nature, they possess illusory manifestations such as the six parts of a head and so forth. This constitutes the 'Gate of Existence' (*youmen*). Since all dharmas are thus..."
It is like a magical illusion. A magical illusion is fundamentally without reality; because it lacks reality, it is empty. Even *nirvāṇa* is like a magical illusion. It is like an image in a mirror:
though it has a provisional form and color, it is ultimately unobtainable. This is the gate of emptiness (*śūnyatā-mukha*).
Since all phenomena are like illusions, they are called "existent"; yet because the illusion cannot be apprehended, they are called "empty," just like an image in a mirror.
To see that which cannot be seen, and to see that which cannot be seen, is both the gate of emptiness and the gate of existence.
Since even illusory existence cannot be apprehended, how much less can illusory emptiness be apprehended? This is precisely the gate of neither emptiness nor existence.
Answer: Although the four teachings and four gates differ, there is none that does not take dependently arisen phenomena as its object of illumination.
Therefore, throughout the four gates, each examines phenomena such as karma and its fruits—whether good or evil—to clarify their illusory nature.
This is precisely what is meant by the successive arising of worlds, sentient beings, karma, and fruits in this present sutra.
However, while the objects illuminated are the same, the contemplations that illuminate them differ. Since this present sutra expounds only the Perfect Gate (*yuanmen*),
although it contains such profound metaphors as the "illusion-like samādhi" and the ten kinds of "illusion-like" analogies,
these refer to the "illusion-like" nature of the three types of cessation (*san zhi*) within the wondrous essence of the Perfect school.
Question: If there are four distinct gates, why is only *śamatha* employed within the sūtras? [Note: The *Miaoxuan* states:

"The four gates of the Separate Teaching (biejiao) are based on the determination that there is a wondrous existence (*miaoyou*) and virtuous form (*shanse*), which does not relate to emptiness (*kong*).
Based on ultimate emptiness (*bijing kong*), they do not relate to existence. This applies likewise to that which is neither empty nor existent. (Text)] Therefore, one is able to enter through them.
In this contemplation, the three [truths] are not mutually identical; one must necessarily proceed through them sequentially—first emptiness, then the provisional, and finally the middle.
Since this sutra employs only a single *śamatha* throughout its beginning and end, it does not follow the principle of sequential progression. Question:

Throughout the preceding and succeeding sections of the sutra, there are times when *samādhi* is mentioned, and at other times both are raised together, stating that one "cultivates *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*."
Regarding *vipaśyanā* (and so forth), it is further stated in the summary of the meditative state that "the state of *dhyāna* manifests.

How can you say that from beginning to end there is only one *śamatha*? Answer: Although there are three names throughout the preceding and following sections of the sutra, they all express this same meaning within *śamatha*.
This has already been explained as stated in the *Miji* (Secret Causes). Furthermore, regarding *vipaśyanā*:
"That" refers to *vipaśyanā* within *śamatha*. Thus, one should know that although there are three names, they constitute a single meaning.
This is because the present sutra designates the mind as residing in "Great Samādhi," and since *śamatha* belongs to the category of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Answer: It is indeed as you have questioned; it is not a separate gate.
Question: If these are the four gates of the Perfect [Teaching], how is it that by hearing the Great [Vehicle] one realizes the Small [Vehicle] and attains only the fruits of the Small?
Answer: Regarding this sutra, those who hear it and realize the Great [Vehicle] while attesting to the Small [Vehicle] are limited to two individuals:

Maudgalyāyana and Ānanda. Since Maudgalyāyana was not the primary recipient (*pratipannaka*) of this teaching, he shall be set aside for now. As for what Ānanda has realized, although its name belongs to the Small [Vehicle], its meaning is entirely perfect and complete.

This is because, in the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjia*), the severance of delusions is also understood through both non-sequential and sequential stages; thus, the causal stage entered therein is also superior to that of the three previous teachings.

It is "equalizing the unequal. Just as one who attains the first stage of faith (*śraddhā*) and severs the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-heya-kleśa*) is equal to the first fruit (*srotāpanna*), and so on until one who attains the seventh stage of faith and severs the delusions of thought (*bhāvanā-heya-kleśa*) is equal to the fourth fruit (*arhat*). This is what is meant by being "equal" in that they equally eliminate the four abidings (*catur-vāsana*).
Since Ānanda was previously a follower of the Hīnayāna, the compiler of the sutra followed his original training and described his attainment of the Perfect [Vehicle] in terms of the small fruits.
How much more so when the section belongs to the Vaipulya (fangděng) class; it is appropriate that he borrows these stages.

If this were not the case, then such statements as "the person suited to the teaching personally recounts attaining the Dharma-body without passing through the kalpas of a bodhisattva" would be difficult to reconcile.
Question: Among the four teachings, if we consider only the four gates such as existence (*you*) and so forth, through which gate does one enter the Way?

The gate of existence should not apply to all cases where things are "neither," and the gate of emptiness (*kong*) should not apply to all cases where things are "all. The same logic may be inferred for the gates of "both" and "neither.
Which of these gates is it that allows one to enter the Way?
Answer: The reason why the sutra speaks of "neither all nor all" and so forth is because this present sutra of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) opens four gates (*dvāra*).
Since each gate encompasses the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) without exception, it is said that when the gate of emptiness is "not," then all four gates are "not";
when the gate of existence is "is," then all four gates are "is. This applies even to the gates of "both" and "neither," which are without exception [encompassed by the Dharma-realm].

It is all thus. Generally, what is taught in other sutras holds that the six realms of ordinary beings are existence, the two vehicles are emptiness, the bodhisattvas are both-and-not, and the Buddha-realm is both-and-also.
Now, this sutra states: "I unite the non-extinguishing and non-arising with the Tathāgatagarbha;
yet this wondrously luminous, primordial mind of the Tathāgatagarbha is 'neither' across the ten realms. This is precisely emptiness.
The four gates are all empty. Furthermore, it says: "Yet the Tathāgatagarbha, the fundamentally luminous and wondrous mind, is such that the ten realms are all identical to it.
This means that the four gates are all identical. Furthermore, it says: "Yet the Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrously luminous and fundamental mind, is apart from identity and apart from difference;

it is neither identical nor different. This means that the four gates are all apart from identity and apart from difference. Thus, they take being apart from identity and apart from difference as their basis.
The "neither-nor" [gate]. All four gates are both "is" and "is not," which constitutes the "both-and.

Nevertheless, although all four gates are established, regarding the essential method for entering the Way, one should rely upon the gate of existence (*yǒumén*) according to its meaning. This gate of existence refers to the ten realms (*daśadhātu*).
This is because all four gates are explained without departing from the ten realms; therefore, the contemplation practiced in reliance on the gate of existence—once [begun]...
Within the explanation of the names [of the ten stages], the ten-fold method of contemplation (*daśa-yāna-dhyāna*) is fully elucidated; all of these are this very meaning.
Thus, whether it be *śamatha*, *samādhi*, or *dhyāna* mentioned in the sutra, each must illumine this "wondrous existence" (*prabhāsvara-bhāva*).

The perfect penetration of the faculty of hearing is its essential point. As the sutra says: "By means of a single gate, one transcends the path of wondrous adornment. It further says: "But within..."
"Entering deeply through a single gate, those six faculties of cognition are simultaneously purified. Furthermore, it says:

"From the gate of the ear, I have attained the Samādhi of Perfect Illumination, whereby the mind that conditions objects is sovereign. It further says: "This is the one path to Nirvāṇa for all subtle-dust Buddhas."
It is further said: "The Buddhas of the ten directions all share this single path to the gate of Nirvāṇa.
This refers precisely to this. Question: Among the four gates, each possesses the four *siddhāntas*. By which *siddhānta* does one gain benefit?

If it is for the sake of the person (*puruṣakāra*), where would the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) not yet have been aroused? If it is for the sake of the world (*loka*), where would the roots of goodness not yet have been planted? If it is for the sake of...
Wherein does one treat what as "the evil not yet destroyed"? If from the perspective of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), wherein is it considered "already matured"?
Since the four *siddhāntas* are said to benefit those who hear them, in which part of this sutra are faith, precepts, diligence, and mindfulness developed?
This refers to the "for the person" (*puruṣakāra*) [perspective].
Question: Since worlds already exist within the *Xi* (all), in which part of this sutra is there "rejoicing, praising, receiving, and practicing"? Question:

The sudden melting away of greed, anger, and delusion is called "remedy" (*pratipakṣa*). Transforming the ordinary into the holy and entering the stream of the Dharma is called the "ultimate truth" (*paramārtha*).
In which passage of the present sutra do these appear?
Answer: Everything taught in the sūtras is nothing other than the Tathāgata’s universal bestowal of the four dharmas upon sentient beings.
If one gains benefit according to what is heard, such passages are indeed numerous. For now, let us speak of a single individual:
for example, when Ānanda was captivated by Caṇḍa, he had not yet planted roots of goodness; the seven inquiries and eight refutations were precisely intended to plant those roots of goodness. And...
Ānanda still harbors various forms of deluded attachment; this indicates that his roots of goodness have not yet emerged.

By elucidating the Tathāgatagarbha through the aggregates (skandhas), bases (āyatanas), and elements (dhātus) to extensively refute [the notions of] causality and spontaneity, the Buddha is precisely refuting evil.
Yet Ānanda still clings to conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) and doubts the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya); thus, evil has not yet been refuted. The Tathāgata further relies upon the Tathāgata...
By revealing that the nature of the storehouse-consciousness (ālayavijñāna) is true emptiness within form, [the Buddha] clarified that the seven elements are neither composite nor non-composite.
This directly caused Ānanda’s emotional attachments to be exhausted and his intellectual understanding to reach its limit; thus, his spiritual roots had already matured.

Upon attaining sudden, great enlightenment and realizing the Dharmakāya, he spoke verses before the Tathāgata to praise the Buddha—namely, the four benefits occurring simultaneously, such as joy, praise, function, and so forth.
This is attained all at once. This is merely one way of explaining it. If explained from another perspective, within the world there are not non-existent persons and so forth;
even within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), there are not non-existent worlds and so forth. As for the Tathāgatagarbha, it is the ultimate truth.
It is distinguished by traversing the various differences of the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*); this is precisely the world. Do not...
To cause sentient beings to give rise to right mindfulness according to their specific capacities is precisely what it means to act for the benefit of others.

To extensively refute the doctrines of causality and spontaneity is precisely what constitutes remedial treatment. Therefore, the various teachings found within a single sutra, when understood through the intended meaning, are none other than *siddhāntas* (established tenets).

Question: Since there are four *siddhāntas*, they must correspond to the five chapters. Specifically, with which chapter does the *puruṣakāra* (for others) correspond? And so on, up to: with which does the *paramārtha* (ultimate truth) correspond?

Answer: The *Myōgen* (Miaoxuan) states: "The *loka-siddhānta* corresponds to the 'Explanation of Names' (*shiming*). Since 'Names' encompasses the entire treatise, the *loka-siddhānta* likewise applies to it."

Regarding these three: first, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) corresponds to the essence (*tattva*), being most clearly manifest; second, the person (*pudgala*) corresponds to the thesis (*pakṣa*), for the purpose of generating wholesome meaning in people through the discussion of cause and effect;
third, the remedy (*pratipakṣa*) corresponds to the function (*vṛtti*), as its function is to break through doubts and obstructions, which is equivalent to the task of treating illness;
and fourth, the analysis of *siddhāntas* corresponds to the characteristics of the teaching (*śāsana-lakṣaṇa*).
Finally, he pushed the matter to its logical conclusion to exhaust his doubts, asking:

"Regarding the 'capacity' and 'response' (jìyìng) of this sutra, are they the fundamental (běn) or the provisional (jì)? If they are fundamental, why does the sutra not manifest the provisional? Is the provisional long-standing or recent?"
Answer: The capacity and response of this sutra must be provisional (*jiki*) rather than fundamental (*hon*), and it is a recent provisional manifestation rather than a long-standing one.
The merit of revealing the provisional to manifest the fundamental lies in the *Lotus Sutra* (*Hokke-kyō*); the present *Vaipulya* (*Hōdō*) sutra has not yet participated in that matter.

Question: The "Respondent" refers to the Buddha. The Buddha is the teacher of his disciples. Now, regarding the basis of this teaching, is it the basis prior to the Bodhi tree, or the basis subsequent to the Bodhi tree?
As for the former, there is no textual authority to rely upon; as for the latter, it would conflict with the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
How, then, can this basis be determined? [Note: "Bodhi tree" refers to the *bodhidruma*. This is stated from the perspective of the World-Honored One’s recent traces.]
Thus it was. Having completed six years of ascetic practice, his ultimate wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*) was first perfected beneath the Bodhi tree.

Upon rising from the Bodhi tree, he began to employ provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*). What is now referred to as the "basis after the Bodhi tree" is precisely that ultimate wisdom first realized at that time.
If one speaks of the "root prior to the Bodhi tree," there remains a distinction between the distant and the near within this context.

The kalpas illustrated by the metaphor of the atoms of dust in the "Life Span" chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* constitute the distant root; the preceding one or two sections prior to the Bodhi tree constitute the near root.
What is now referred to as the "root prior to the Bodhi tree" refers specifically to that which is the distant [root] within the "Life Span" chapter.
This is the fundamental point. Regarding the statement that "before [the Buddha's] words there is no text to rely upon, while after [them] it conflicts with the Lotus Sutra":
since the various masters have already judged this sutra to be identical to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, it ought to be the distant original. Yet, alas, there is no textual evidence to prove it.
If one were to say it is a version from after the Bodhi tree, it would again conflict with the distant original of the *Lotus Sutra*.
Answer: If we discuss the Buddha who preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, he is none other than the present Buddha.

Since the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* points to a remote original as its basis, how could the basis of the present Buddha be any different? However, this sutra has not yet undergone the process of revelation (*vivaraṇa*).

Although it possesses a remote original, it remains obscured and unspoken; it is taught according to [the capacities of] beings' dispositions, and thus it is still the version from after the Bodhi tree. Since this is already...
It is clear that being obstructed by the *Lotus Sūtra* is not the same as [being obstructed by] the *Ghee*.

Regarding the question of "faculties" (*maki*), these refer to the disciples of the Two Vehicles. Now, the "original basis" (*hon*) of these disciples refers to the state prior to entering the two wisdoms of the provisional and the real;

it is not the original basis of having entered the real for a long time, nor is it the original basis of first understanding and practicing the provisional. If one first understands and practices the provisional...

It has not yet been revealed; though it is fundamental, one does not dare speak of it. Now that this sutra has not yet revealed [the ultimate truth], how can it be said to be identical to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*?

[Note] The *Miaoxuan* states: "In various sutras, it is explained that the disciples of the Two Vehicles cannot enter true wisdom (*bhūtajñāna*), nor can they exercise provisional wisdom (*upāyajñāna*).
In the present *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it is explained that the disciples have long since entered true wisdom, and furthermore, they first understood and practiced the provisional."
Question: Regarding the correspondence of this sutra [to the Lotus Sutra], if one claims it is the original [version], then the original would be identical to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
The *Lotus Sutra* states: "I have indeed been a Buddha for as long as this; yet all the world says that I have only now attained the Way. It further says:
"Since I became a Buddha, immeasurable, boundless, nayuta kalpas have passed. If this sutra is identical to the *Lotus Sutra*, why...?
Therefore, is it not the case that such a statement does not exist?
Answer: It is indeed as you have pointed out; it is not a remote origin. Question:

If one traces back the earlier and later parts of the *Avataṃsaka*, there are both distant traces and proximate traces. Is it not the case that the *Śūraṅgama* is proximate? [Note: Regarding the word "Huā" (Flower) in the text...]

Regarding the distinction between the distant and proximate traces: from before the *Avataṃsaka* until after the *rajas-kalpa* (dust-point eon), his frequent proclamations of birth and frequent proclamations of extinction constitute the distant trace.
From after the *Avataṃsaka*, his pedagogical transformations across the five periods constitute the proximate trace.
Answer: It is indeed as you have stated; this refers to the provisional manifestation (*jia*).
Question: Regarding what you call "root and trace" (*benji*), does the root-trace of this sutra mean that the trace is itself the root and the root is itself the trace?
If the trace and the root are non-dual, its meaning would be identical to that of the *Lotus Sutra*; why then is there no textual evidence for it?

Answer: If one speaks according to the specific school (the *buddhakṣetra* in question), then there is a distinction between the fundamental and the manifested; yet if one transcends these divisions to meet at the ultimate convergence, then the fundamental and the manifested are non-dual.
Since this has not yet been revealed, there is no scriptural passage that serves as proof.
Question: What kind of capacity does the audience for this sutra possess? Is it provisional (hō) or real (jitsu)?

If one follows the view of masters such as Gushan and others, who claim this refers to the Great Provisional [Bodhisattva], then even though it is a small fruit, it is identical to the great realization—what they call "the name being the same while the substance is different.

If that were so, when one proceeds through the stages of advancement, to what stage does one advance, and to what stage is one grafted? Is the teaching that performs this grafting distinct (betsu) or perfect (en)?

Answer: Ānanda, who rejoiced upon receiving the teaching, was indeed a manifestation of great skillful means (*mahopāya*). If we follow the progression through the stages, then those who have realized the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) advance to the second stage of faith;

those who have realized the second and third fruits advance to the fourth, fifth, and sixth stages of faith. Since this constitutes an advancement through the stages of faith, it is an instance of being received and guided by the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).
Although there is no explicit textual passage for this in the sutra, the meaning logically conforms to it.
Question: Now, the "respondent" is the Buddha. Which Buddha is the respondent of this sutra? Is it the Buddha who sat upon a seat of grass beneath the original Bodhi tree?
Or is it the Buddha who sat upon a seat of celestial raiment beneath a Bodhi tree of the seven treasures?
Or is it the Buddha who sat upon a seat of the Great Jewel Flower King in the Lotus Treasury World? Or is it the one who, by means of empty space...

Is it the Buddha of the seat? The relationship between the capacity [of the recipient] and the response [of the teacher] is a fundamental principle of the teaching. Is it permissible or impermissible to set this aside without clarification?

Answer: He for whom a bed of living grass serves as a seat is the Buddha of the Tripitaka Teaching (Zangjiao). He for whom celestial robes serve as a seat is the Buddha of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao).
The Buddha of the Separate Teaching (Pratyekabuddha-yāna) has jeweled flowers as his seat; the Buddha of the Perfect Teaching (Ekayāna) has empty space as his seat.

The Buddha of the Perfect Teaching is the Dharma-body (dharmakāya); the Buddha of the Separate Teaching is the Reward-body (saṃbhogakāya); the Buddhas of the Treasury and the Penetrating Teachings are the Response-bodies (nirmāṇakāya). The Dharma-body belongs to that which is inherently existent.

This is the single nature; retribution and response are its adornment. These belong to the two types of cultivation. Although it is a single nature, cultivation arises from the entirety of that nature;
although there are two types of cultivation, cultivation is entirely contained within that nature. It is like the three eyes of the Heavenly King or the three dots of the syllable *i*:

to mention one is to mention all three, and to speak of three is to speak of one. Therefore, regarding the four teachings and the three Buddhas, they are difficult to distinguish because their characteristics are so manifold.
To determine the relative superiority or inferiority of the teachings, one must examine the capacities of the audience and the Dharma that was preached;
if it is in the Perfect [Teaching], it is perfect, and if it is in the Partial [Teaching], it is partial. Regarding the Master of this present sutra, if we observe his manifested traces:

at the outset, having concluded the summer retreat and performed the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, he accepted the invitation of King Prasenajit; subsequently, Ānanda explained the causes for his initial aspiration and his vision of the signs. Furthermore—
He said: "I see that the Tathāgata’s thirty-two marks are supremely wondrous and peerless.
Could he possibly be the six-foot-old bhikṣu of the Tripiṭaka teachings? Yet, when expounding the meaning of the sūtras, there is only the single, perfect principle;

when observing capacities to rescue those drowning, there is only the single, perfect discernment. Judging by this, he is furthermore the Buddha of the Dharma-body of the Perfect Teaching. Now, with this—
Regarding the act of using living grass as a seat: this was merely a manifestation displayed for the sake of transforming the impoverished son.

That is to say, he removed his necklaces and fine, soft upper garments and instead donned coarse, tattered, and soiled clothes; yet in reality, the one within those soiled clothes is none other than the necklaced elder himself.
It was simply because [the truth] had not yet been revealed that the various capacities of sentient beings were still unable to recognize it immediately.
If one observes Ānanda’s recitation of verses in praise of the Buddha, it is clear that he was never unaware that the Buddha was currently using empty space as his seat.

Question: This sutra expounds only the perfect and eternal; this [explanation] may be acceptable. However, regarding the discernment of capacities— [The answer continues: ...if one were to discern the capacities [of the audience], then...
Furthermore, in which part of the sutra does it state that this is a "mirror-like" observation of capacities? Moreover, how is it known to be a "perfect mirror"?

The answer, as Tiantai says, is that the Buddha’s observation of capacities is of many kinds. If one says that the Buddha enters meditative concentration three times each day to observe those with capacities who can be saved, this refers to the Buddha of the Tripitaka (Śrāvaka) school, who illuminates the capacities of the nine realms through the analytical emptiness of response and stimulus. If one says that he observes them while remaining within the conventional...

Truly, there is no need for him to enter or emerge; he knows spontaneously through the power of his capacity. This is the Buddha of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao) illuminating the nine realms, wherein the essence of the sentient beings' capacities is empty, and thus resonance occurs.

If one says that he uses the King Samādhi to illuminate the capacities of the ten dharma-realms sequentially and individually, this is the sequential resonance of the Buddha of the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao).
If one says that he uses the King Samādhi to illuminate the capacities of the ten dharma-realms all at once, this is the [Buddha of the Perfect Teaching].

The Buddha’s response is perfectly wondrous. Now that Ānanda has requested from the Tathāgatas of the ten directions the sublime *śamatha* for attaining Bodhi, this is precisely the occasion [of awakening] within the tranquil light (*jig-ō*) of the Buddha-realm. Furthermore, the sutra does not mention such matters as entering meditative concentration to observe the capacities of others;
it simply states that the Tathāgata knew that [the affliction] had been inflicted by that art of seduction. This "knowing"—one...

The "character" (字) is precisely the unconditioned great compassion (*anālambana-mahākaruṇā*), the stage where quiescence is ever-illuminating; it is what is called the sudden, simultaneous illumination by means of the King Samādhi.

Question: If the Tathāgata knows that the arts of seduction have been employed, this is exactly the same as the Shared Teaching (*paryāya-yāna*), which does not require entering [the meditative state] but knows spontaneously.
Why, then, is this called "perfect discernment" (*pariniṣpanna-adarśana*)? Answer: It is because it is spontaneous (*anābhoga*).

It should be understood that while this principle applies to the Buddhas of the *śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha* vehicles within the realm, it also applies to the Buddhas of the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*) outside the realm.

One must distinguish their relative superiority or inferiority based on the extent of the capacities they perceive and the partiality or perfection of their underlying principle. For instance, regarding the two Buddhas of the *āgama* (Tripitaka) and *pratītyasamutpāda* (Shared) teachings:

from an inclusive perspective, although it is said they can illuminate both the ultimate and conventional truths of the nine realms, from an exclusive perspective, they are only able to illuminate eight realms.
Regarding the ultimate and the conventional: because that which is realized by Bodhisattvas is the same as that of the Two Vehicles, there is no distinction between them.

However, as for the Buddhas of the Separate and Complete Teachings, both are able to illumine the three truths within the ten realms; the only difference lies in whether this illumination is gradual or non-gradual.

Now, since this sutra states, "I unite the unceasing and the unborn with the Tathāgata-garbha," it follows that regarding the three truths of the ten realms, they are simultaneously neither identical nor different, and simultaneously both negated and established.
Verifying the former by means of the latter, it is known that this must indeed be the perfect mirror.
The hundred questions recorded above are the draft finalized by my late master; therefore, they differ slightly from the old edition in terms of what was expanded, condensed, omitted, or added.
This includes everything from the five chapters at the beginning to the four *siddhāntas* and other sections at the end.

Seeking its true intent, it lies solely in the clear discernment of the temporal flavor [of the teachings]. This is because contemporary masters have treated the pure and absolute perfection of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* as identical to the provisional yet marvelous subtlety of the *Vaipulya* (fangděng) sūtras.
Therefore, he has exhaustively investigated and elucidated these matters to compose his "One Hundred Questions. Observing the conclusion of the work, it states:
"The relationship between the capacity of the recipient and the response of the teaching is a major principle of the doctrine; yet it has been left unclarified," and so forth.
...and so forth. The intent behind this is indeed earnest. Those who investigate and savor these words must recognize their ultimate purport.
*The Profound Meaning of the Great Buddha-Top Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, Fascicle Four (End).
